abstract: This paper presents a model of nondeterministic adaptive automata that are constructed from simpler nondeterministic adaptive information processing elements. The first half of the paper describes the model. The second half discusses some of its significant adaptive properties using computer simulation examples. Chief among these properties is that network aggregates of the model elements can adapt appropriately when a single reinforcement channel provides the same positive or negative reinforcement signal to all adaptive elements of the network at the same time. This holds for multiple-input, multiple-output, multiple-layered, combinational and sequential networks. It also holds when some network elements are "hidden" in that their outputs are not directly seen by the external environment.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a model of nondeterministic adaptive automata that are constructed from simpler nondeterministic adaptive information processing elements. The first half of the paper describes the model. The second half discusses some of its significant adaptive properties using computer simulation examples. Chief among these properties is that network aggregates of the model elements can adapt appropriately when a single reinforcement channel provides the same positive or negative reinforcement signal to all adaptive elements of the network at the same time. This holds for multiple-input, multiple-output, multiple-layered, combinational and sequential networks. It also holds when some network elements are "hidden" in that their outputs are not directly seen by the external environment.

paragraphs: This paper builds a model of adaptive automata from simpler, nondeterministic information-processing elements. The individual elements can change their behavior, and the research asks what adaptive capabilities emerge when they are connected into a network. The model description is followed by computer simulations illustrating significant properties of the resulting systems.

The central finding is that a network can adapt appropriately when every element receives the same positive or negative reinforcement signal at the same time. There is only one reinforcement channel for the whole network. This matters because the feedback does not separately identify which internal element should receive a different evaluation.

The reported property holds across networks with multiple inputs, multiple outputs, and multiple layers, as well as both combinational and sequential organizations. It also holds when some elements are hidden, meaning their outputs are not directly visible to the external environment. The simulations therefore illustrate adaptation under shared reinforcement even when the network contains internal processing that the environment cannot observe directly.
summary.tldr: Networks of nondeterministic adaptive elements learn appropriate behavior from a single shared reinforcement signal, including when internal elements are hidden.

title: Learning in Networks of Nondeterministic Adaptive Logic Elements

abstract: We describe an adaptive network, TIN2, that learns the transition function of a sequential system from observations of its behavior. It integrates two subnets, TIN-I (Winter, Ryan and Turner, 1987) and TIN-2. TIN-2 constructs state representations from examples of system behavior, and its dynamics are the main topics of the paper. TIN-I abstracts transition functions from noisy state representations and environmental data during training, while in operation it produces sequences of transitions in response to variations in input. Dynamics of both nets are based on the Adaptive Resonance Theory of Carpenter and Grossberg (1987). We give results from an experiment in which TIN2 learned the behavior of a system that recognizes strings with an even number of l's .
originalAbstract: We describe an adaptive network, TIN2, that learns the transition function of a sequential system from observations of its behavior. It integrates two subnets, TIN-I (Winter, Ryan and Turner, 1987) and TIN-2. TIN-2 constructs state representations from examples of system behavior, and its dynamics are the main topics of the paper. TIN-I abstracts transition functions from noisy state representations and environmental data during training, while in operation it produces sequences of transitions in response to variations in input. Dynamics of both nets are based on the Adaptive Resonance Theory of Carpenter and Grossberg (1987). We give results from an experiment in which TIN2 learned the behavior of a system that recognizes strings with an even number of l's .

paragraphs: TIN2 learns how a sequential system changes state by observing its behavior. A transition function describes how the system's current state and incoming information determine what happens next. Learning such a function requires a useful representation of state as well as a way to connect states through transitions.

The architecture divides these responsibilities between two subnets. TIN-2 constructs state representations from behavioral examples, and its dynamics receive particular attention in the paper. TIN-I learns transition functions from noisy state representations and environmental data. During operation, TIN-I generates sequences of transitions as the input changes. Both subnets use dynamics based on Adaptive Resonance Theory.

The reported experiment concerns a system that recognizes strings containing an even number of ones. This provides a concrete sequential task in which recognition depends on the accumulated history of the input. The paper reports that TIN2 learns this system's behavior, illustrating how learned state representations and learned transition rules can work together within one adaptive network.
summary.tldr: TIN2 combines learned state representations with learned transition rules to reproduce a sequential system's behavior.

title: An Adaptive Network That Learns Sequences of Transitions

abstract: A time delay in the response of the neurons in a network can induce sustained oscillation and chaos. We present a stability criterion based on local stability analysis to prevent sustained oscillation in symmetric delay networks, and show an example of chaotic dynamics in a non-symmetric delay network.
originalAbstract: A time delay in the response of the neurons in a network can induce sustained oscillation and chaos. We present a stability criterion based on local stability analysis to prevent sustained oscillation in symmetric delay networks, and show an example of chaotic dynamics in a non-symmetric delay network.

paragraphs: This paper examines how delayed neuron responses affect the behavior of analog neural networks. The central issue is whether activity settles or continues changing indefinitely. A response delay can alter that outcome: the authors identify sustained oscillation and chaos as behaviors that delays can induce.

For networks with symmetric connections, the paper develops a criterion intended to prevent sustained oscillation. It derives this criterion through local stability analysis, which examines behavior near an equilibrium. This links a property of the network's dynamics to a practical question about its operation: whether delayed responses allow activity to settle rather than keep cycling.

The authors also present an example of chaotic dynamics in a network with nonsymmetric connections. The two contributions address different settings: a stability condition for symmetric delay networks and an example of chaos in a nonsymmetric one. Together, they show why response timing belongs in the analysis of analog networks. Understanding the connections alone is insufficient when delayed activity can change the network's eventual behavior.
summary.tldr: Response delays can produce oscillation or chaos, motivating a stability criterion for symmetric analog neural networks.

title: Dynamics of Analog Neural Networks with Time Delay

abstract: We have used information-theoretic ideas to derive a class of prac(cid:173) tical and nearly optimal schemes for adapting the size of a neural network. By removing unimportant weights from a network, sev(cid:173) eral improvements can be expected: better generalization, fewer training examples required, and improved speed of learning and/or classification. The basic idea is to use second-derivative informa(cid:173) tion to make a tradeoff between network complexity and training set error. Experiments confirm the usefulness of the methods on a real-world application.
originalAbstract: We have used information-theoretic ideas to derive a class of prac(cid:173) tical and nearly optimal schemes for adapting the size of a neural network. By removing unimportant weights from a network, sev(cid:173) eral improvements can be expected: better generalization, fewer training examples required, and improved speed of learning and/or classification. The basic idea is to use second-derivative informa(cid:173) tion to make a tradeoff between network complexity and training set error. Experiments confirm the usefulness of the methods on a real-world application.

paragraphs: Optimal Brain Damage addresses how to adapt the size of a neural network by removing weights that contribute little to its performance. The authors derive practical, nearly optimal pruning schemes from information-theoretic ideas. The underlying design problem is how much network complexity is worth retaining for a given level of training error.

The method uses second-derivative information to guide this tradeoff. Such information describes the curvature of the error function as weights change, helping assess the effect of removing a connection. This gives the pruning decision a connection to the training objective: a weight's importance is evaluated through its expected effect on error.

The abstract identifies better generalization, reduced training-data requirements, and faster learning or classification as potential benefits of removing unimportant weights. It also reports that experiments on a real-world application confirm the methods' usefulness. The contribution is a principled way to simplify a trained network while accounting for the cost of simplification in training performance.
summary.tldr: Optimal Brain Damage uses second-derivative information to prune weights while balancing network complexity against training error.

title: Optimal Brain Damage

abstract: Prediction, estimation, and smoothing are fundamental to signal processing. To perform these interrelated tasks given noisy data, we form a time series model of the process that generates the data. Taking noise in the system explicitly into account, maximum(cid:173) likelihood and Kalman frameworks are discussed which involve the dual process of estimating both the model parameters and the un(cid:173) derlying state of the system. We review several established meth(cid:173) ods in the linear case, and propose severa! extensions utilizing dual Kalman filters (DKF) and forward-backward (FB) filters that are applicable to neural networks. Methods are compared on several simulations of noisy time series. We also include an example of nonlinear noise reduction in speech.

To perform these interrelated tasks given noisy data, we form a time series model of the process that generates the data. Taking noise in the system explicitly into account, maximum(cid:173) likelihood and Kalman frameworks are discussed which involve the dual process of estimating both the model parameters and the un(cid:173) derlying state of the system. We review several established meth(cid:173) ods in the linear case, and propose severa! extensions utilizing dual Kalman filters (DKF) and forward-backward (FB) filters that are applicable to neural networks. Methods are compared on several simulations of noisy time series. We also include an example of nonlinear noise reduction in speech.

paragraphs: Noisy time-series data create two connected uncertainties: the underlying state of the process is hidden, and the model describing that process may also be unknown. This paper treats prediction, estimation, and smoothing through that joint problem. It explicitly includes system noise when modeling how the observations are generated.

The authors discuss maximum-likelihood and Kalman frameworks that estimate both model parameters and system states. After reviewing established linear methods, they propose extensions using dual Kalman filters and forward-backward filters that can be applied to neural networks. The dual viewpoint keeps parameter learning and state estimation connected, since each depends on the other when observations are noisy.

The methods are compared in simulations involving several noisy time series, and the paper includes nonlinear speech-noise reduction as an application. These examples place the proposed extensions in concrete signal-processing settings. The contribution is a framework for carrying uncertainty about both dynamics and state into nonlinear modeling, with prediction and reconstruction treated as related uses of the same underlying process model.
summary.tldr: The paper extends dual and forward-backward filtering to neural-network models that jointly estimate noisy system states and model parameters.

title: Dual Kalman Filtering Methods for Nonlinear Prediction, Smoothing and Estimation

abstract: We explore methods for incorporating prior knowledge about a problem at hand in Support Vector learning machines. We show that both invari(cid:173) ances under group transfonnations and prior knowledge about locality in images can be incorporated by constructing appropriate kernel functions.
originalAbstract: We explore methods for incorporating prior knowledge about a problem at hand in Support Vector learning machines. We show that both invari(cid:173) ances under group transfonnations and prior knowledge about locality in images can be incorporated by constructing appropriate kernel functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how knowledge about a problem can be built into a support vector learning machine. Its central mechanism is the kernel function, which determines how inputs are compared within the learning method. Constructing that function appropriately provides a way to make known structure part of the model's treatment of data.

The authors address two forms of knowledge. One is invariance under group transformations: specified transformations should preserve the relevant interpretation of an input. The other is locality in images, where spatially local organization matters to the problem. The paper shows that both can be incorporated through kernel construction.

The significance is that prior knowledge receives a concrete mathematical entry point into support vector learning. Invariance can shape which transformed inputs are treated consistently, while locality can shape how image structure participates in comparisons. The stated contribution is a method for expressing these requirements through the kernel, connecting assumptions about the task directly to the representation used for learning.
summary.tldr: Appropriately constructed support vector kernels can incorporate transformation invariance and knowledge about image locality.

title: Prior Knowledge in Support Vector Kernels

abstract: This paper presents a novel practical framework for Bayesian model averaging and model selection in probabilistic graphical models. Our approach approximates full posterior distributions over model parameters and structures, as well as latent variables, in an analyt(cid:173) ical manner. These posteriors fall out of a free-form optimization procedure, which naturally incorporates conjugate priors. Unlike in large sample approximations, the posteriors are generally non(cid:173) Gaussian and no Hessian needs to be computed. Predictive quanti(cid:173) ties are obtained analytically. The resulting algorithm generalizes the standard Expectation Maximization algorithm, and its conver(cid:173) gence is guaranteed. We demonstrate that this approach can be applied to a large class of models in several domains, including mixture models and source separation.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a novel practical framework for Bayesian model averaging and model selection in probabilistic graphical models. Our approach approximates full posterior distributions over model parameters and structures, as well as latent variables, in an analyt(cid:173) ical manner. These posteriors fall out of a free-form optimization procedure, which naturally incorporates conjugate priors. Unlike in large sample approximations, the posteriors are generally non(cid:173) Gaussian and no Hessian needs to be computed. Predictive quanti(cid:173) ties are obtained analytically. The resulting algorithm generalizes the standard Expectation Maximization algorithm, and its conver(cid:173) gence is guaranteed. We demonstrate that this approach can be applied to a large class of models in several domains, including mixture models and source separation.

paragraphs: Bayesian model selection and averaging require reasoning about uncertainty in models, rather than committing immediately to one fitted configuration. This paper presents a practical framework for probabilistic graphical models that approximates posterior distributions over parameters, model structures, and latent variables. It therefore addresses several sources of uncertainty within a single analytical approach.

The posterior approximations emerge from a free-form optimization procedure that naturally accommodates conjugate priors. They are generally non-Gaussian, unlike the large-sample approximations discussed in the abstract, and the method does not require computing a Hessian. Predictive quantities can also be obtained analytically, connecting the approximated uncertainty directly to predictions.

The resulting algorithm extends Expectation Maximization and has a convergence guarantee. That guarantee concerns convergence of the algorithm; the framework still approximates the full Bayesian posterior. Applications include mixture models and source separation across several domains. The central contribution is a common computational framework that makes Bayesian selection, averaging, and prediction accessible across a broad class of graphical models.
summary.tldr: A variational framework analytically approximates Bayesian uncertainty over graphical-model parameters, structures, and latent variables.

title: A Variational Baysian Framework for Graphical Models

abstract: The most popular algorithms for object detection require the use of exhaustive spatial and scale search procedures. In such approaches, an object is defined by means of local features. fu this paper we show that including contextual information in object detection pro(cid:173) cedures provides an efficient way of cutting down the need for exhaustive search. We present results with real images showing that the proposed scheme is able to accurately predict likely object classes, locations and sizes.
originalAbstract: The most popular algorithms for object detection require the use of exhaustive spatial and scale search procedures. In such approaches, an object is defined by means of local features. fu this paper we show that including contextual information in object detection pro(cid:173) cedures provides an efficient way of cutting down the need for exhaustive search. We present results with real images showing that the proposed scheme is able to accurately predict likely object classes, locations and sizes.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the search burden in object detection. When a detector defines an object through local visual features, it may need to check many image locations and object sizes. The authors investigate how contextual information can help focus that search by indicating which objects are likely and where they may appear.

The proposed scheme incorporates context into the detection procedure. Its predictions concern three related aspects of a target: its class, its location, and its size. Each addresses part of the uncertainty that an exhaustive search would otherwise explore. The approach therefore uses information beyond an object’s local features to guide where and at what scale detection should concentrate.

Results on real images show that the scheme can accurately predict likely object classes, locations, and sizes. The authors present this as an efficient way to reduce the need for exhaustive search. The finding supports using context to prioritize plausible targets and search regions; the stated benefit is a reduction in search requirements, with predictions about likely objects guiding the process.
summary.tldr: Context helps predict likely object types, positions, and sizes, reducing the need for exhaustive detection searches.

title: Contextual Modulation of Target Saliency

abstract: The nearest neighbor technique is a simple and appealing method to address classification problems. It relies on t he assumption of locally constant class conditional probabilities. This assumption becomes invalid in high dimensions with a finite number of exam(cid:173) ples due to the curse of dimensionality. We propose a technique that computes a locally flexible metric by means of Support Vector Machines (SVMs). The maximum margin boundary found by the SVM is used to determine the most discriminant direction over the query's neighborhood. Such direction provides a local weighting scheme for input features. We present experimental evidence of classification performance improvement over the SVM algorithm alone and over a variety of adaptive learning schemes, by using both simulated and real data sets.
originalAbstract: The nearest neighbor technique is a simple and appealing method to address classification problems. It relies on t he assumption of locally constant class conditional probabilities. This assumption becomes invalid in high dimensions with a finite number of exam(cid:173) ples due to the curse of dimensionality. We propose a technique that computes a locally flexible metric by means of Support Vector Machines (SVMs). The maximum margin boundary found by the SVM is used to determine the most discriminant direction over the query's neighborhood. Such direction provides a local weighting scheme for input features. We present experimental evidence of classification performance improvement over the SVM algorithm alone and over a variety of adaptive learning schemes, by using both simulated and real data sets.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification relies on nearby examples having approximately constant class probabilities. With many input dimensions and only finitely many examples, that local assumption becomes unreliable because of the curse of dimensionality. The paper addresses this problem by changing how distance is measured around the point being classified.

The proposed method uses a support vector machine to construct a locally flexible metric. Its maximum-margin boundary identifies the direction that best distinguishes classes within the query’s neighborhood. That direction then determines local weights for the input features, so the neighborhood used for classification reflects the local discrimination problem.

This combines a boundary-based learning method with neighborhood-based prediction. The support vector machine supplies information about which local differences matter, and the nearest-neighbor procedure uses that information in its distance calculation. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show improved classification performance over an SVM alone and several adaptive learning schemes. These are empirical improvements in the evaluated settings, supporting locally learned distance as a useful component of classification.
summary.tldr: Using a local SVM boundary to weight features improves nearest-neighbor classification in experiments on simulated and real data.

title: Adaptive Nearest Neighbor Classification Using Support Vector Machines

abstract: Spectral clustering enjoys its success in both data clustering and semisupervised learning. But, most spectral clustering algorithms cannot handle multi-class clustering problems directly. Additional strategies are needed to extend spectral clustering algorithms to multi-class clustering problems. Furthermore, most spectral clustering algorithms employ hard cluster membership, which is likely to be trapped by the local optimum. In this paper, we present a new spectral clustering algorithm, named "Soft Cut". It improves the normalized cut algorithm by introducing soft membership, and can be efficiently computed using a bound optimization algorithm. Our experiments with a variety of datasets have shown the promising performance of the proposed clustering algorithm.
originalAbstract: Spectral clustering enjoys its success in both data clustering and semisupervised learning. But, most spectral clustering algorithms cannot handle multi-class clustering problems directly. Additional strategies are needed to extend spectral clustering algorithms to multi-class clustering problems. Furthermore, most spectral clustering algorithms employ hard cluster membership, which is likely to be trapped by the local optimum. In this paper, we present a new spectral clustering algorithm, named "Soft Cut". It improves the normalized cut algorithm by introducing soft membership, and can be efficiently computed using a bound optimization algorithm. Our experiments with a variety of datasets have shown the promising performance of the proposed clustering algorithm.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering uses relationships among data points to organize them into groups. The paper identifies two difficulties with many existing algorithms: handling multiple clusters requires additional strategies, and hard membership decisions can leave optimization trapped at a local optimum. These issues motivate a more flexible treatment of which groups a point belongs to.

The proposed algorithm, Soft Cut, modifies normalized cut by introducing soft cluster membership. Instead of expressing membership solely through an exclusive assignment, it allows a probabilistic treatment. This changes the clustering formulation so that membership can remain flexible during optimization, directly addressing the concern about hard assignments raised by the authors.

The authors use a bound optimization algorithm to compute Soft Cut efficiently and report promising results across a variety of datasets. The contribution combines a different treatment of membership with a practical optimization procedure. The experimental findings support the usefulness of that combination, while the abstract does not claim that soft membership guarantees avoidance of every local optimum.
summary.tldr: Soft Cut introduces probabilistic membership into normalized-cut clustering and uses efficient bound optimization, with promising experimental results.

title: A Probabilistic Approach for Optimizing Spectral Clustering

abstract: The Maximum Margin Planning (MMP) (Ratliff et al., 2006) algorithm solves imitation learning problems by learning linear mappings from features to cost functions in a planning domain. The learned policy is the result of minimum-cost planning using these cost functions. These mappings are chosen so that example policies (or trajectories) given by a teacher appear to be lower cost (with a lossscaled margin) than any other policy for a given planning domain. We provide a novel approach, M M P B O O S T , based on the functional gradient descent view of boosting (Mason et al., 1999; Friedman, 1999a) that extends MMP by "boosting" in new features. This approach uses simple binary classification or regression to improve performance of MMP imitation learning, and naturally extends to the class of structured maximum margin prediction problems. (Taskar et al., 2005) Our technique is applied to navigation and planning problems for outdoor mobile robots and robotic legged locomotion.
originalAbstract: The Maximum Margin Planning (MMP) (Ratliff et al., 2006) algorithm solves imitation learning problems by learning linear mappings from features to cost functions in a planning domain. The learned policy is the result of minimum-cost planning using these cost functions. These mappings are chosen so that example policies (or trajectories) given by a teacher appear to be lower cost (with a lossscaled margin) than any other policy for a given planning domain. We provide a novel approach, M M P B O O S T , based on the functional gradient descent view of boosting (Mason et al., 1999; Friedman, 1999a) that extends MMP by "boosting" in new features. This approach uses simple binary classification or regression to improve performance of MMP imitation learning, and naturally extends to the class of structured maximum margin prediction problems. (Taskar et al., 2005) Our technique is applied to navigation and planning problems for outdoor mobile robots and robotic legged locomotion.

paragraphs: Maximum Margin Planning learns from demonstrations by constructing a cost function for a planning problem. A planner then chooses a policy that minimizes that cost. Training seeks costs under which the teacher’s demonstrated behavior is preferable to competing behavior, with a separation that depends on how much the alternatives differ from the desired result.

The original approach learns a linear mapping from supplied features to costs. This paper introduces MMPBOOST, which expands that representation by adding features through boosting. It uses the functional gradient descent interpretation of boosting to guide these additions, allowing simple binary classification or regression procedures to improve the imitation learning system.

This matters because learning a useful planning cost depends on the features available to express it. The contribution provides a way to improve those features within the learning process. The authors also extend the approach to structured maximum margin prediction and apply it to outdoor robot navigation and planning, as well as robotic legged locomotion.
summary.tldr: MMPBOOST adds learned features through boosting to improve cost learning from demonstrations for planning and structured prediction.

title: Boosting Structured Prediction for Imitation Learning

abstract: Maximum variance unfolding (MVU) is an effective heuristic for dimensionality reduction. It produces a low-dimensional representation of the data by maximiz- ing the variance of their embeddings while preserving the local distances of the original data. We show that MVU also optimizes a statistical dependence measure which aims to retain the identity of individual observations under the distance- preserving constraints. This general view allows us to design “colored” variants of MVU, which produce low-dimensional representations for a given task, e.g. subject to class labels or other side information.
originalAbstract: Maximum variance unfolding (MVU) is an effective heuristic for dimensionality reduction. It produces a low-dimensional representation of the data by maximiz- ing the variance of their embeddings while preserving the local distances of the original data. We show that MVU also optimizes a statistical dependence measure which aims to retain the identity of individual observations under the distance- preserving constraints. This general view allows us to design “colored” variants of MVU, which produce low-dimensional representations for a given task, e.g. subject to class labels or other side information.

paragraphs: Maximum variance unfolding creates a low-dimensional representation by spreading embedded observations apart while preserving distances between nearby observations. This balances a global objective, increasing variance, against local constraints that retain neighborhood geometry. The paper revisits this dimensionality-reduction heuristic to explain its objective from a statistical perspective and use that explanation to construct variants.

The authors show that maximum variance unfolding also optimizes a measure of statistical dependence. Under the distance-preserving constraints, this measure aims to retain the identity of individual observations. This connects the geometric operation of unfolding data with an information-preservation objective: the representation remains statistically connected to which observation each point represents.

That interpretation leads to colored versions of the method, where class labels or other side information help determine the low-dimensional representation. Here, colored refers to supplying information relevant to a particular task. The contribution is a route from a general geometric embedding method to task-directed embeddings, using a shared statistical view to explain both the original method and its extensions.
summary.tldr: A statistical interpretation of maximum variance unfolding leads to embeddings guided by labels or other task information.

title: Colored Maximum Variance Unfolding

abstract: We devise a graphical model that supports the process of debugging software by guiding developers to code that is likely to contain defects. The model is trained using execution traces of passing test runs; it reflects the distribution over transitional patterns of code positions. Given a failing test case, the model determines the least likely transitional pattern in the execution trace. The model is designed such that Bayesian inference has a closed-form solution. We evaluate the Bernoulli graph model on data of the software projects AspectJ and Rhino.
originalAbstract: We devise a graphical model that supports the process of debugging software by guiding developers to code that is likely to contain defects. The model is trained using execution traces of passing test runs; it reflects the distribution over transitional patterns of code positions. Given a failing test case, the model determines the least likely transitional pattern in the execution trace. The model is designed such that Bayesian inference has a closed-form solution. We evaluate the Bernoulli graph model on data of the software projects AspectJ and Rhino.

paragraphs: The paper develops a graphical model to help developers locate defects in software. Its evidence comes from execution traces: records of the code positions visited during program runs. Training uses passing tests, allowing the model to learn a probability distribution over transition patterns associated with those successful executions.

When a test fails, the model examines its execution trace and identifies the least likely transition pattern under the learned distribution. That pattern guides attention toward code that may contain a defect. The method therefore turns differences between passing and failing executions into a probabilistic clue about where a developer should investigate.

The authors design the Bernoulli graph model so that Bayesian inference has a closed-form solution. This supplies an explicit computational procedure for analyzing the traces and identifying the unusual pattern. They evaluate the approach using data from AspectJ and Rhino. The contribution is a debugging aid that uses learned execution behavior to prioritize suspicious code locations for further inspection.
summary.tldr: A graphical model trained on passing executions flags unlikely transitions in failing runs to guide bug localization.

title: Localizing Bugs in Program Executions with Graphical Models

abstract: Upstream supervised topic models have been widely used for complicated scene understanding. However, existing maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) schemes can make the prediction model learning independent of latent topic discovery and result in an imbalanced prediction rule for scene classification. This paper presents a joint max-margin and max-likelihood learning method for upstream scene understanding models, in which latent topic discovery and prediction model estimation are closely coupled and well-balanced. The optimization problem is efficiently solved with a variational EM procedure, which iteratively solves an online loss-augmented SVM. We demonstrate the advantages of the large-margin approach on both an 8-category sports dataset and the 67-class MIT indoor scene dataset for scene categorization.
originalAbstract: Upstream supervised topic models have been widely used for complicated scene understanding. However, existing maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) schemes can make the prediction model learning independent of latent topic discovery and result in an imbalanced prediction rule for scene classification. This paper presents a joint max-margin and max-likelihood learning method for upstream scene understanding models, in which latent topic discovery and prediction model estimation are closely coupled and well-balanced. The optimization problem is efficiently solved with a variational EM procedure, which iteratively solves an online loss-augmented SVM. We demonstrate the advantages of the large-margin approach on both an 8-category sports dataset and the 67-class MIT indoor scene dataset for scene categorization.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models for scene understanding must both discover hidden topics and learn to predict scene categories. The paper identifies a problem with existing maximum-likelihood training schemes: they can make prediction-model learning independent of topic discovery. That separation can produce an imbalanced prediction rule, weakening the connection between the learned representation and classification.

The proposed method combines maximum-margin and maximum-likelihood learning in a joint objective. This closely couples discovery of the latent topics with estimation of the prediction model. The authors solve the optimization efficiently through variational expectation-maximization, which repeatedly solves an online loss-augmented support vector machine problem as part of the training procedure.

Experiments demonstrate advantages of the large-margin approach on an eight-category sports dataset and the 67-class MIT indoor scene dataset. The reported findings support training the representation and prediction rule together for these scene-categorization tasks. The contribution is an integrated learning method that makes classification requirements part of the process that discovers latent scene structure.
summary.tldr: Joint maximum-margin and maximum-likelihood training couples latent topic discovery with scene classification and improves results on two scene datasets.

title: Large Margin Learning of Upstream Scene Understanding Models

abstract: During the last years support vector machines (SVMs) have been successfully applied even in situations where the input space $X$ is not necessarily a subset of $R^d$. Examples include SVMs using probability measures to analyse e.g. histograms or coloured images, SVMs for text classification and web mining, and SVMs for applications from computational biology using, e.g., kernels for trees and graphs. Moreover, SVMs are known to be consistent to the Bayes risk, if either the input space is a complete separable metric space and the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $H\subset L_p(P_X)$ is dense, or if the SVM is based on a universal kernel $k$. So far, however, there are no RKHSs of practical interest known that satisfy these assumptions on $\cH$ or $k$ if $X \not\subset R^d$. We close this gap by providing a general technique based on Taylor-type kernels to explicitly construct universal kernels on compact metric spaces which are not subset of $R^d$. We apply this technique for the following special cases: universal kernels on the set of probability measures, universal kernels based on Fourier transforms, and universal kernels for signal processing.
originalAbstract: During the last years support vector machines (SVMs) have been successfully applied even in situations where the input space $X$ is not necessarily a subset of $R^d$. Examples include SVMs using probability measures to analyse e.g. histograms or coloured images, SVMs for text classification and web mining, and SVMs for applications from computational biology using, e.g., kernels for trees and graphs. Moreover, SVMs are known to be consistent to the Bayes risk, if either the input space is a complete separable metric space and the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $H\subset L_p(P_X)$ is dense, or if the SVM is based on a universal kernel $k$. So far, however, there are no RKHSs of practical interest known that satisfy these assumptions on $\cH$ or $k$ if $X \not\subset R^d$. We close this gap by providing a general technique based on Taylor-type kernels to explicitly construct universal kernels on compact metric spaces which are not subset of $R^d$. We apply this technique for the following special cases: universal kernels on the set of probability measures, universal kernels based on Fourier transforms, and universal kernels for signal processing.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can operate on inputs such as probability measures, trees, and graphs, beyond ordinary finite-dimensional vectors. Yet their successful use does not by itself supply the function-space properties needed for known consistency results. This paper addresses the construction of universal kernels for certain nonstandard input spaces.

The authors develop a general technique based on Taylor-type kernels that explicitly constructs universal kernels on compact metric spaces outside the usual Euclidean setting. Universality supplies a sufficiently rich function space for approximation and is one route to the consistency guarantees discussed for support vector machines. Compactness is part of the stated construction setting.

The paper applies the technique to spaces of probability measures, kernels based on Fourier transforms, and signal-processing kernels. These constructions address the gap between theoretically useful assumptions and kernels of practical interest for nonstandard inputs. The contribution is therefore a method for building kernels with the desired theoretical property, rather than an empirical comparison of prediction accuracy across applications.
summary.tldr: A Taylor-type construction produces universal kernels on compact nonstandard metric spaces, including spaces of probability measures.

title: Universal Kernels on Non-Standard Input Spaces

abstract: We present a technique for exact simulation of Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs), which can be interpreted as locally injecting noise to each Gaussian factor independently, followed by computing the mean/mode of the perturbed GMRF. Coupled with standard iterative techniques for the solution of symmetric positive definite systems, this yields a very efficient sampling algorithm with essentially linear complexity in terms of speed and memory requirements, well suited to extremely large scale probabilistic models. Apart from synthesizing data under a Gaussian model, the proposed technique directly leads to an efficient unbiased estimator of marginal variances. Beyond Gaussian models, the proposed algorithm is also very useful for handling highly non-Gaussian continuously-valued MRFs such as those arising in statistical image modeling or in the first layer of deep belief networks describing real-valued data, where the non-quadratic potentials coupling different sites can be represented as finite or infinite mixtures of Gaussians with the help of local or distributed latent mixture assignment variables. The Bayesian treatment of such models most naturally involves a block Gibbs sampler which alternately draws samples of the conditionally independent latent mixture assignments and the conditionally multivariate Gaussian continuous vector and we show that it can directly benefit from the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Drawing samples from a very large Gaussian Markov random field can be computationally demanding. This paper presents an exact simulation technique with a local construction: independently inject noise into each Gaussian factor, then compute the mean or mode of the perturbed model. The resulting optimization calculation produces a sample from the original Gaussian model.

Combined with standard iterative solvers for symmetric positive definite systems, the technique yields an efficient algorithm with essentially linear time and memory requirements. This makes it suitable for extremely large probabilistic models. The same construction also provides an efficient unbiased estimator of marginal variances, allowing it to quantify uncertainty as well as generate data.

Introducing latent mixture assignments makes the continuous variables jointly Gaussian conditional on those assignments. A block Gibbs sampler can then alternate between sampling assignments and the continuous vector, using the proposed algorithm for the Gaussian step.
summary.tldr: Independent local noise followed by a Gaussian mean computation enables exact sampling and efficient uncertainty estimation in large Gaussian graphical models.

title: Gaussian sampling by local perturbations

abstract: We present a novel multilabel/ranking algorithm working in partial information settings. The algorithm is based on 2nd-order descent methods, and relies on upper-confidence bounds to trade-off exploration and exploitation. We analyze this algorithm in a partial adversarial setting, where covariates can be adversarial, but multilabel probabilities are ruled by (generalized) linear models. We show $O(T^{1/2}\log T)$ regret bounds, which improve in several ways on the existing results. We test the effectiveness of our upper-confidence scheme by contrasting against full-information baselines on real-world multilabel datasets, often obtaining comparable performance.

The algorithm is based on 2nd-order descent methods, and relies on upper-confidence bounds to trade-off exploration and exploitation. We analyze this algorithm in a partial adversarial setting, where covariates can be adversarial, but multilabel probabilities are ruled by (generalized) linear models. We show $O(T^{1/2}\log T)$ regret bounds, which improve in several ways on the existing results. We test the effectiveness of our upper-confidence scheme by contrasting against full-information baselines on real-world multilabel datasets, often obtaining comparable performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies multilabel prediction and ranking when the learner receives only partial information. An algorithm in this setting must make useful predictions while also acquiring information that can improve later decisions. The proposed method combines second-order descent with upper-confidence bounds to manage this exploration–exploitation trade-off.

The analysis allows the covariates, or input features, to be adversarial. It assumes, however, that multilabel probabilities follow linear or generalized linear models. Under this partially adversarial setup, the authors establish regret bounds of O(√T log T), reporting improvements over existing results in several respects. The modeling assumption is part of the setting in which the guarantee applies.

Experiments on real-world multilabel datasets compare the confidence-based scheme with baselines that receive full information. The partial-feedback method often reaches comparable performance, providing empirical support for its information-selection strategy. Together, the theory and experiments show how confidence-guided exploration can support effective multilabel learning despite incomplete feedback, without claiming equivalence to full-information learning in every case.
summary.tldr: A confidence-guided second-order algorithm learns multilabel predictions from partial feedback, with regret guarantees under a partially adversarial model.

title: On Multilabel Classification and Ranking with Partial Feedback

abstract: This paper suggests a learning-theoretic perspective on how synaptic plasticity benefits global brain functioning. We introduce a model, the selectron, that (i) arises as the fast time constant limit of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons equipped with spiking timing dependent plasticity (STDP) and (ii) is amenable to theoretical analysis. We show that the selectron encodes reward estimates into spikes and that an error bound on spikes is controlled by a spiking margin and the sum of synaptic weights. Moreover, the efficacy of spikes (their usefulness to other reward maximizing selectrons) also depends on total synaptic strength. Finally, based on our analysis, we propose a regularized version of STDP, and show the regularization improves the robustness of neuronal learning when faced with multiple stimuli.

paragraphs: This paper connects a local rule for changing synaptic connections with questions about learning and useful neural communication. It introduces the selectron, a model obtained as a fast-time-constant limit of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons equipped with spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The simplified model makes it possible to analyze aspects of neuronal learning mathematically.

The authors show that selectron spikes encode estimates of reward. They derive an error bound controlled by a spiking margin and the total synaptic weight. Total synaptic strength also affects how useful those spikes are to other selectrons pursuing reward. The analysis therefore links properties of a neuron's connections to both its own output quality and that output's usefulness downstream.

Using these results, the authors propose a regularized form of spike-timing-dependent plasticity. They show that this modification improves robustness when neuronal learning encounters multiple stimuli. The broader contribution is a learning-theoretic route from an analyzable neuron model to a modified plasticity rule, with synaptic strength playing a central role in the reasoning.
summary.tldr: An analyzable neuron model links spike quality to synaptic strength and motivates a more robust, regularized plasticity rule.

title: Towards a learning-theoretic analysis of spike-timing dependent plasticity

abstract: Implementing inference procedures for each new probabilistic model is time-consuming and error-prone. Probabilistic programming addresses this problem by allowing a user to specify the model and then automatically generating the inference procedure. To make this practical it is important to generate high performance inference code. In turn, on modern architectures, high performance requires parallel execution. In this paper we present Augur, a probabilistic modeling language and compiler for Bayesian networks designed to make effective use of data-parallel architectures such as GPUs. We show that the compiler can generate data-parallel inference code scalable to thousands of GPU cores by making use of the conditional independence relationships in the Bayesian network.

We show that the compiler can generate data-parallel inference code scalable to thousands of GPU cores by making use of the conditional independence relationships in the Bayesian network.

paragraphs: Augur addresses the effort involved in implementing inference for probabilistic models. Writing a separate inference procedure for every new model takes time and creates opportunities for errors. Probabilistic programming moves that responsibility into software: a user specifies a model, and a system generates the procedure needed to perform inference.

The paper focuses on making that generated procedure efficient on parallel hardware. Augur combines a probabilistic modeling language with a compiler for Bayesian networks, targeting data-parallel architectures such as GPUs. Its central resource is the network's conditional independence structure. Relationships that specify which variables become independent when others are known help the compiler organize inference computations for parallel execution.

The authors show that this approach can generate inference code that scales to thousands of GPU cores. The contribution connects a model's statistical structure to its implementation on modern hardware. It makes automatic inference generation more practically useful by addressing execution performance alongside the convenience of expressing a model in a dedicated language.
summary.tldr: Augur compiles Bayesian networks into parallel inference code by exploiting conditional independence, scaling execution to thousands of GPU cores.

title: Augur: Data-Parallel Probabilistic Modeling

abstract: This paper proposes a new hybrid architecture that consists of a deep Convolutional Network and a Markov Random Field. We show how this architecture is successfully applied to the challenging problem of articulated human pose estimation in monocular images. The architecture can exploit structural domain constraints such as geometric relationships between body joint locations. We show that joint training of these two model paradigms improves performance and allows us to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes a new hybrid architecture that consists of a deep Convolutional Network and a Markov Random Field. The architecture can exploit structural domain constraints such as geometric relationships between body joint locations. We show that joint training of these two model paradigms improves performance and allows us to significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques.

paragraphs: Estimating human pose from a single image requires locating body joints while accounting for how those joints fit together. The paper addresses this articulated pose-estimation problem with a hybrid architecture. It combines a deep convolutional network with a Markov random field, bringing two modeling approaches into the same system.

The architecture can exploit structural knowledge about the task, including geometric relationships between joint locations. These relationships provide information beyond the appearance of an isolated location in the image. The graphical component offers a way to incorporate that structure alongside the convolutional network, so pose estimation can use visual evidence together with constraints on relationships between body parts.

The authors show that training the two components jointly improves performance and allows their system to significantly outperform the existing state-of-the-art techniques considered. The central finding is therefore about learning the combined architecture, as well as choosing its components. It supports coordinating visual representation learning with structured pose modeling for the monocular image task evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: Jointly training a convolutional network and a Markov random field improves single-image human pose estimation by incorporating structural relationships.

title: Joint Training of a Convolutional Network and a Graphical Model for Human Pose Estimation

abstract: Probabilistic inference serves as a popular model for neural processing. It is still unclear, however, how approximate probabilistic inference can be accurate and scalable to very high-dimensional continuous latent spaces. Especially as typical posteriors for sensory data can be expected to exhibit complex latent dependencies including multiple modes. Here, we study an approach that can efficiently be scaled while maintaining a richly structured posterior approximation under these conditions. As example model we use spike-and-slab sparse coding for V1 processing, and combine latent subspace selection with Gibbs sampling (select-and-sample). Unlike factored variational approaches, the method can maintain large numbers of posterior modes and complex latent dependencies. Unlike pure sampling, the method is scalable to very high-dimensional latent spaces. Among all sparse coding approaches with non-trivial posterior approximations (MAP or ICA-like models), we report the largest-scale results. In applications we firstly verify the approach by showing competitiveness in standard denoising benchmarks. Secondly, we use its scalability to, for the first time, study highly-overcomplete settings for V1 encoding using sophisticated posterior representations. More generally, our study shows that very accurate probabilistic inference for multi-modal posteriors with complex dependencies is tractable, functionally desirable and consistent with models for neural inference.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models of sensory processing can have posterior distributions with many modes and complex dependencies among hidden variables. Accurately representing these features becomes difficult in very high-dimensional spaces. This paper studies how approximate inference can preserve that structure while remaining scalable, using spike-and-slab sparse coding as a model of V1 processing.

The proposed select-and-sample approach combines selection of a latent subspace with Gibbs sampling. It can retain numerous posterior modes and dependencies that factored variational approximations do not preserve, while scaling to higher-dimensional latent spaces than pure sampling. The combination targets both the complexity of the posterior representation and the computational cost of obtaining it.

The authors report their largest-scale results within the stated class of sparse coding approaches with nontrivial posterior approximations. They demonstrate competitive denoising results and use the method to study highly overcomplete V1 encoding with sophisticated posterior representations. The findings support the tractability and functional value of rich approximate inference in this setting, as well as its consistency with models of neural inference.
summary.tldr: Combining latent subspace selection with Gibbs sampling makes richly structured posterior inference scalable for spike-and-slab sparse coding.

title: Select-and-Sample for Spike-and-Slab Sparse Coding

abstract: We propose a vector-valued regression problem whose solution is equivalent to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) embedding of the Bayesian posterior distribution. This equivalence provides a new understanding of kernel Bayesian inference. Moreover, the optimization problem induces a new regularization for the posterior embedding estimator, which is faster and has comparable performance to the squared regularization in kernel Bayes' rule. This regularization coincides with a former thresholding approach used in kernel POMDPs whose consistency remains to be established. Our theoretical work solves this open problem and provides consistency analysis in regression settings. Based on our optimizational formulation, we propose a flexible Bayesian posterior regularization framework which for the first time enables us to put regularization at the distribution level. We apply this method to nonparametric state-space filtering tasks with extremely nonlinear dynamics and show performance gains over all other baselines.

paragraphs: Kernel Bayesian inference represents probability distributions through embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This paper shows that a Bayesian posterior embedding can be understood as the solution to a vector-valued regression problem. That equivalence gives posterior estimation an optimization formulation, providing a new way to reason about both its computation and its regularization.

The formulation induces a regularization method that is faster than the squared regularization used in kernel Bayes' rule while achieving comparable performance. It also matches an earlier thresholding approach used in kernel partially observable decision processes. The authors establish consistency analysis in regression settings, addressing the previously unresolved consistency of that approach.

Building on the optimization view, the paper develops a flexible framework for imposing regularization at the distribution level. This makes the posterior distribution itself the object of regularization. Applications to nonparametric state-space filtering with extremely nonlinear dynamics show performance gains over all baselines included in the experiments, linking the theoretical reformulation to improved filtering results.
summary.tldr: A regression formulation of kernel Bayesian inference supports faster regularization, consistency analysis, and distribution-level posterior constraints.

title: Kernel Bayesian Inference with Posterior Regularization

abstract: The quest for algorithms that enable cognitive abilities is an important part of machine learning. A common trait in many recently investigated cognitive-like tasks is that they take into account different data modalities, such as visual and textual input. In this paper we propose a novel and generally applicable form of attention mechanism that learns high-order correlations between various data modalities. We show that high-order correlations effectively direct the appropriate attention to the relevant elements in the different data modalities that are required to solve the joint task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our high-order attention mechanism on the task of visual question answering (VQA), where we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the standard VQA dataset.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires a model to use both an image and a textual question. The relevant information depends on how these inputs relate: answering the joint task requires directing attention toward useful elements across the modalities. This paper studies an attention mechanism designed to learn those relationships and use them to guide what the model attends to.

The proposed mechanism learns high-order correlations between different data modalities. These correlations provide a basis for selecting relevant elements in the inputs. The authors present the mechanism as generally applicable, with the central idea that relationships across modalities can help determine attention for a task that depends on those modalities together.

The paper demonstrates the approach on visual question answering and reports state-of-the-art performance on the standard VQA dataset. This supplies empirical support for using high-order cross-modal correlations to guide attention in that task. The broader contribution is an attention formulation intended for multiple modalities, while the stated performance evidence specifically comes from the visual question answering evaluation.
summary.tldr: An attention mechanism learns high-order relationships across modalities and achieves state-of-the-art results on the standard visual question answering dataset.

title: High-Order Attention Models for Visual Question Answering

abstract: This article introduces an energy-based model that is adversarial regarding data: it minimizes the energy for a given data distribution (the positive samples) while maximizing the energy for another given data distribution (the negative or unlabeled samples). The model is especially instantiated with autoencoders where the energy, represented by the reconstruction error, provides a general distance measure for unknown data. The resulting neural network thus learns to reconstruct data from the first distribution while crushing data from the second distribution. This solution can handle different problems such as Positive and Unlabeled (PU) learning or covariate shift, especially with imbalanced data. Using autoencoders allows handling a large variety of data, such as images, text or even dialogues. Our experiments show the flexibility of the proposed approach in dealing with different types of data in different settings: images with CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (not-in-training setting), text with Amazon reviews (PU learning) and dialogues with Facebook bAbI (next response classification and dialogue completion).

paragraphs: Reconstruct & Crush Network learns to distinguish two data distributions by assigning them opposing energy values. Training lowers the energy of positive samples and raises it for samples from another distribution, which may be negative or unlabeled. The adversarial relationship is therefore between how the model treats the two supplied populations.

In the autoencoder implementation, reconstruction error supplies the energy. The network learns to reproduce samples from the first distribution while reconstructing those from the second poorly. That error then serves as a general distance measure for unfamiliar data. The approach can address positive-and-unlabeled learning and covariate shift, including settings with imbalanced data.

The authors demonstrate the method across several data types and tasks: CIFAR images in a not-in-training setting, Amazon review text for positive-and-unlabeled learning, and Facebook bAbI dialogues for response classification and completion. The reported experiments support the approach's flexibility across these settings. Its unifying contribution is to use the same reconstruct-versus-crush training principle across different forms of data.
summary.tldr: An energy-based autoencoder learns to reconstruct positive samples and poorly reconstruct another population, supporting several learning settings and data types.

title: Reconstruct & Crush Network

abstract: Learning latent representations from long text sequences is an important first step in many natural language processing applications. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have become a cornerstone for this challenging task. However, the quality of sentences during RNN-based decoding (reconstruction) decreases with the length of the text. We propose a sequence-to-sequence, purely convolutional and deconvolutional autoencoding framework that is free of the above issue, while also being computationally efficient. The proposed method is simple, easy to implement and can be leveraged as a building block for many applications. We show empirically that compared to RNNs, our framework is better at reconstructing and correcting long paragraphs. Quantitative evaluation on semi-supervised text classification and summarization tasks demonstrate the potential for better utilization of long unlabeled text data.

The proposed method is simple, easy to implement and can be leveraged as a building block for many applications. paragraphs: Representing a long paragraph as a latent code is useful only if that code preserves information needed by later tasks. The paper identifies a difficulty with recurrent neural network autoencoders: the quality of reconstructed sentences decreases as the text gets longer. This makes long passages a particularly demanding test of representation learning.

The authors propose a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder built entirely from convolutional and deconvolutional operations. It learns a representation by encoding text and reconstructing the sequence from that representation. They describe the framework as computationally efficient, simple to implement, and free of the length-related reconstruction issue motivating their work.

Experiments show better reconstruction and correction of long paragraphs than the recurrent models used for comparison. Evaluations on semi-supervised text classification and summarization also indicate potential for making better use of long unlabeled text. These downstream results matter because they test whether the learned representation is useful beyond reproducing its input, supporting the framework's proposed role as a component in language-processing systems.
summary.tldr: A convolutional and deconvolutional autoencoder improves long-paragraph reconstruction and shows promise for learning useful representations from unlabeled text.

title: Deconvolutional Paragraph Representation Learning

abstract: We consider a modification of the covariance function in Gaussian processes to correctly account for known linear constraints. By modelling the target function as a transformation of an underlying function, the constraints are explicitly incorporated in the model such that they are guaranteed to be fulfilled by any sample drawn or prediction made. We also propose a constructive procedure for designing the transformation operator and illustrate the result on both simulated and real-data examples.
originalAbstract: We consider a modification of the covariance function in Gaussian processes to correctly account for known linear constraints. By modelling the target function as a transformation of an underlying function, the constraints are explicitly incorporated in the model such that they are guaranteed to be fulfilled by any sample drawn or prediction made. We also propose a constructive procedure for designing the transformation operator and illustrate the result on both simulated and real-data examples.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process model may need to respect known linear constraints on the function it represents. This paper incorporates those constraints by modifying the covariance function, which describes how function values vary together. The goal is to make the known relationships part of the model's structure, so they hold throughout its predictions and samples.

The construction represents the target function as a transformation of an underlying function. By designing that transformation around the constraints, the authors ensure that every sampled function and every prediction satisfies them. The guarantee therefore applies to the model's possible outputs, rather than only to agreement with constraints at particular observed examples.

The paper also provides a constructive procedure for designing the transformation operator. This turns the modeling principle into a way to build constrained Gaussian processes for a given problem. Illustrations on simulated and real data demonstrate the resulting approach. The contribution connects explicit prior knowledge about linear relationships with a covariance construction that enforces those relationships by design.
summary.tldr: A transformed Gaussian process covariance guarantees that all samples and predictions satisfy specified linear constraints.

title: Linearly constrained Gaussian processes

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a model-based approach for gradient-free black-box function optimization, such as hyperparameter optimization. Typically, BO relies on conventional Gaussian process (GP) regression, whose algorithmic complexity is cubic in the number of evaluations. As a result, GP-based BO cannot leverage large numbers of past function evaluations, for example, to warm-start related BO runs. We propose a multi-task adaptive Bayesian linear regression model for transfer learning in BO, whose complexity is linear in the function evaluations: one Bayesian linear regression model is associated to each black-box function optimization problem (or task), while transfer learning is achieved by coupling the models through a shared deep neural net. Experiments show that the neural net learns a representation suitable for warm-starting the black-box optimization problems and that BO runs can be accelerated when the target black-box function (e.g., validation loss) is learned together with other related signals (e.g., training loss). The proposed method was found to be at least one order of magnitude faster that methods recently published in the literature.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model to guide evaluations of an unknown function, such as a model's validation loss under different hyperparameters. Conventional Gaussian process regression has cubic complexity in the number of evaluations. That cost makes it difficult to use large histories of evaluations to initialize optimization on related tasks.

The paper replaces this modeling setup with a multitask adaptive Bayesian linear regression approach whose complexity is linear in the number of function evaluations. Each optimization task gets its own Bayesian linear regression model. A shared deep neural network connects those models, allowing information learned across tasks to shape a common representation.

Experiments show that the shared representation supports warm-starting new optimization problems. They also show that optimization can accelerate when the target function is learned alongside related signals, such as learning validation loss together with training loss. The method is reported to be at least an order of magnitude faster than the compared recently published approaches.
summary.tldr: Task-specific Bayesian linear models coupled through a shared neural network enable scalable transfer for hyperparameter optimization.

title: Scalable Hyperparameter Transfer Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a low dimensional representation for compositional data. Compositional data consists of a collection of nonnegative data that sum to a constant value. Since the parts of the collection are statistically dependent, many standard tools cannot be directly applied. Instead, compositional data must be first transformed before analysis. Focusing on principal component analysis (PCA), we propose an approach that allows low dimensional representation learning directly from the original data. Our approach combines the benefits of the log-ratio transformation from compositional data analysis and exponential family PCA. A key tool in its derivation is a generalization of the scaled Bregman theorem, that relates the perspective transform of a Bregman divergence to the Bregman divergence of a perspective transform and a remainder conformal divergence. Our proposed approach includes a convenient surrogate (upper bound) loss of the exponential family PCA which has an easy to optimize form. We also derive the corresponding form for nonlinear autoencoders. Experiments on simulated data and microbiome data show the promise of our method.

Compositional data consists of a collection of nonnegative data that sum to a constant value. Focusing on principal component analysis (PCA), we propose an approach that allows low dimensional representation learning directly from the original data. Our approach combines the benefits of the log-ratio transformation from compositional data analysis and exponential family PCA. paragraphs: Compositional data contains nonnegative parts that sum to a fixed total. This constraint makes the parts statistically dependent, complicating the direct use of standard analysis tools. The paper studies how to learn a low-dimensional representation while accounting for that structure, with principal component analysis as its starting point.

The proposed approach combines benefits of log-ratio transformations with exponential family PCA, allowing representation learning directly from the original data. Its derivation generalizes the scaled Bregman theorem, relating transformed divergences through an additional remainder term. This mathematical connection supports a surrogate loss that upper-bounds the exponential family PCA loss and has a form that is easier to optimize.

The authors also derive a corresponding formulation for nonlinear autoencoders, extending the approach beyond linear representations. Experiments on simulated and microbiome data show promise. The contribution brings the dependence inherent in fixed-total data into the representation-learning objective, and supplies a practical optimization surrogate. The stated empirical evidence supports the approach's potential without claiming superiority for every kind of compositional dataset.
summary.tldr: A compositional-data objective combines log-ratio ideas with exponential family PCA and extends to nonlinear autoencoders.

title: Representation Learning of Compositional Data

abstract: Generative adversarial training for imitation learning has shown promising results on high-dimensional and continuous control tasks. This paradigm is based on reducing the imitation learning problem to the density matching problem, where the agent iteratively refines the policy to match the empirical state-action visitation frequency of the expert demonstration. Although this approach has shown to robustly learn to imitate even with scarce demonstration, one must still address the inherent challenge that collecting trajectory samples in each iteration is a costly operation. To address this issue, we first propose a Bayesian formulation of generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL), where the imitation policy and the cost function are represented as stochastic neural networks. Then, we show that we can significantly enhance the sample efficiency of GAIL leveraging the predictive density of the cost, on an extensive set of imitation learning tasks with high-dimensional states and actions.

paragraphs: Imitation learning teaches an agent to act from demonstrations. Generative adversarial imitation learning, or GAIL, does this by matching how frequently an expert visits different combinations of states and actions. The agent repeatedly updates its policy to make its own behavior resemble that pattern. Even when relatively few expert demonstrations suffice, collecting new agent trajectories during training can remain expensive.

The paper introduces a Bayesian version of GAIL in which both the policy and the cost function are stochastic neural networks. This formulation represents these components probabilistically. In particular, the cost has a predictive distribution that provides information beyond a single predicted value, and the proposed approach uses that distribution to improve learning efficiency.

Across an extensive collection of imitation tasks with high-dimensional states and actions, the authors report significantly better sample efficiency. The contribution therefore addresses the cost of gathering experience during imitation, rather than only the scarcity of demonstrations. Its stated result is that probabilistic cost predictions can make the adversarial imitation process more economical in its use of samples.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian formulation of adversarial imitation learning uses probabilistic cost predictions to improve sample efficiency.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning

abstract: Flow-based generative models are conceptually attractive due to tractability of the exact log-likelihood, tractability of exact latent-variable inference, and parallelizability of both training and synthesis. In this paper we propose Glow, a simple type of generative flow using invertible 1x1 convolution. Using our method we demonstrate a significant improvement in log-likelihood and qualitative sample quality. Perhaps most strikingly, we demonstrate that a generative model optimized towards the plain log-likelihood objective is capable of efficient synthesis of large and subjectively realistic-looking images.
