paragraphs: Glow is a generative model built around a flow architecture using invertible 1x1 convolutions. The paper’s motivation is that flow-based models combine several attractive computational properties: exact log-likelihood can be evaluated, latent variables can be inferred exactly, and both training and generation can be parallelized. These properties connect image generation with a tractable probabilistic model.

The proposed architecture uses an invertible convolution as a central component of a comparatively simple generative flow. Invertibility matters because the model retains the ability to move between observed data and its latent representation. The paper therefore focuses on an architectural choice within a family that already supports exact likelihood and latent-variable inference.

The authors report significant improvements in log-likelihood and qualitative sample quality. They also demonstrate efficient generation of large images that look realistic by subjective assessment, despite training with the plain log-likelihood objective. This finding shows that likelihood-focused training can produce visually convincing samples in their setting; the stated visual-quality assessment remains qualitative.
summary.tldr: Glow uses invertible 1x1 convolutions to improve flow-based image generation while retaining exact likelihood and latent inference.

title: Glow: Generative Flow with Invertible 1x1 Convolutions

abstract: In this paper we consider the dynamic assortment selection problem under an uncapacitated multinomial-logit (MNL) model. By carefully analyzing a revenue potential function, we show that a trisection based algorithm achieves an item-independent regret bound of O(sqrt(T log log T), which matches information theoretical lower bounds up to iterated logarithmic terms. Our proof technique draws tools from the unimodal/convex bandit literature as well as adaptive confidence parameters in minimax multi-armed bandit problems.
originalAbstract: In this paper we consider the dynamic assortment selection problem under an uncapacitated multinomial-logit (MNL) model. By carefully analyzing a revenue potential function, we show that a trisection based algorithm achieves an item-independent regret bound of O(sqrt(T log log T), which matches information theoretical lower bounds up to iterated logarithmic terms. Our proof technique draws tools from the unimodal/convex bandit literature as well as adaptive confidence parameters in minimax multi-armed bandit problems.

paragraphs: Dynamic assortment selection concerns choosing which items to offer over time while learning how to earn revenue. This paper studies the problem under an uncapacitated multinomial-logit model, so its result concerns that particular choice model without a capacity restriction on the assortment. Performance is measured by regret, the revenue lost relative to the relevant optimal policy.

The authors analyze a revenue potential function and use that analysis to justify an algorithm based on trisection. The proof combines ideas from unimodal and convex bandit problems with adaptive confidence parameters from minimax multi-armed bandit analysis. These tools connect the structure of the revenue objective with how the algorithm manages uncertainty during repeated choices.

The resulting regret bound is O(√(T log log T)) and does not depend on the number of items. It matches information-theoretic lower bounds up to iterated logarithmic factors, making the policy near-optimal in the stated sense. The notable finding is that, under this model, the guarantee can avoid an explicit item-count penalty while remaining close to the fundamental regret limit.
summary.tldr: A trisection-based assortment policy achieves item-independent regret close to the information-theoretic limit under an uncapacitated MNL model.

title: Near-Optimal Policies for Dynamic Multinomial Logit Assortment Selection Models

abstract: Semi-supervised learning has proven to be a powerful paradigm for leveraging unlabeled data to mitigate the reliance on large labeled datasets. In this work, we unify the current dominant approaches for semi-supervised learning to produce a new algorithm, MixMatch, that guesses low-entropy labels for data-augmented unlabeled examples and mixes labeled and unlabeled data using MixUp. MixMatch obtains state-of-the-art results by a large margin across many datasets and labeled data amounts. For example, on CIFAR-10 with 250 labels, we reduce error rate by a factor of 4 (from 38% to 11%) and by a factor of 2 on STL-10. We also demonstrate how MixMatch can help achieve a dramatically better accuracy-privacy trade-off for differential privacy. Finally, we perform an ablation study to tease apart which components of MixMatch are most important for its success. Code is attached.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning tries to make useful training data out of examples that lack labels, reducing dependence on expensive labeled datasets. MixMatch combines several dominant ideas in this area into one algorithm. Its central contribution is an integrated training procedure that brings labeled and unlabeled examples into a shared learning process.

The algorithm guesses low-entropy labels for augmented unlabeled examples, meaning its guessed label distributions are relatively concentrated. It then uses MixUp to mix labeled and unlabeled data. These steps connect the creation of training targets for unlabeled examples with the way the combined data is presented during learning.

The paper reports substantial improvements across multiple datasets and amounts of labeled data. On CIFAR-10 with 250 labels, error falls from 38% to 11%; on STL-10, the reported reduction is by a factor of two. The authors also demonstrate an improved accuracy–privacy trade-off under differential privacy and use an ablation study to examine which components contribute most to MixMatch’s success.
summary.tldr: MixMatch combines guessed labels for augmented unlabeled data with MixUp to substantially improve semi-supervised learning.

title: MixMatch: A Holistic Approach to Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We introduce a gradient-based learning method to automatically adapt Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) proposal distributions to intractable targets. We define a maximum entropy regularised objective function, referred to as generalised speed measure, which can be robustly optimised over the parameters of the proposal distribution by applying stochastic gradient optimisation. An advantage of our method compared to traditional adaptive MCMC methods is that the adaptation occurs even when candidate state values are rejected. This is a highly desirable property of any adaptation strategy because the adaptation starts in early iterations even if the initial proposal distribution is far from optimum. We apply the framework for learning multivariate random walk Metropolis and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin proposals with full covariance matrices, and provide empirical evidence that our method can outperform other MCMC algorithms, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo schemes.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo uses proposed moves to explore a target probability distribution that is difficult to handle directly. Its effectiveness depends on the proposal distribution, which determines the candidate moves. This paper introduces a gradient-based method for learning that distribution automatically, reducing reliance on a well-chosen proposal at the start.

The authors define an entropy-regularized objective called a generalized speed measure and optimize proposal parameters using stochastic gradients. A central feature is that learning continues even when a proposed state is rejected. Rejection therefore does not prevent the adaptation mechanism from updating the proposal. This matters especially in early iterations, when a poor initial proposal may make successful moves difficult.

The framework is applied to multivariate random-walk Metropolis and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin proposals, including full covariance matrices that describe relationships among movement directions. Experiments provide evidence that the method can outperform other MCMC algorithms, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo schemes. The stated finding is empirical and establishes potential advantages of the adaptation strategy rather than a universal ranking of samplers.
summary.tldr: A gradient-based MCMC adaptation method learns proposal distributions even from rejected moves and empirically can outperform other samplers.

title: Gradient-based Adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo

abstract: Aggregated data is commonplace in areas such as epidemiology and demography. For example, census data for a population is usually given as averages defined over time periods or spatial resolutions (cities, regions or countries). In this paper, we present a novel multi-task learning model based on Gaussian processes for joint learning of variables that have been aggregated at different input scales. Our model represents each task as the linear combination of the realizations of latent processes that are integrated at a different scale per task. We are then able to compute the cross-covariance between the different tasks either analytically or numerically. We also allow each task to have a potentially different likelihood model and provide a variational lower bound that can be optimised in a stochastic fashion making our model suitable for larger datasets. We show examples of the model in a synthetic example, a fertility dataset and an air pollution prediction application.

We also allow each task to have a potentially different likelihood model and provide a variational lower bound that can be optimised in a stochastic fashion making our model suitable for larger datasets. We show examples of the model in a synthetic example, a fertility dataset and an air pollution prediction application.

paragraphs: Data about related quantities are often reported at different scales, such as averages over different regions or time periods. Those differences complicate learning the quantities together because their observations describe different aggregations. This paper develops a Gaussian process model that explicitly includes the aggregation scale of each task in a shared statistical representation.

Each task combines latent processes that are integrated at its own scale. Sharing these underlying processes connects tasks, while task-specific integration represents how their measurements were collected. The authors derive ways to calculate cross-covariances between tasks analytically or numerically. These covariances express how observations remain related even when they summarize different spatial or temporal scales.

The framework also permits different likelihood models for different tasks. A variational lower bound can be optimized stochastically, making the approach suitable for larger datasets. Demonstrations include synthetic data, fertility data, and air-pollution prediction. Together, these examples illustrate a modeling approach that incorporates aggregation into joint learning instead of requiring all observations to share one input scale.
summary.tldr: A multi-task Gaussian process model jointly learns related quantities observed at different aggregation scales using shared, integrated latent processes.

title: Multi-task Learning for Aggregated Data using Gaussian Processes

abstract: A dynamic treatment regime (DTR) consists of a sequence of decision rules, one per stage of intervention, that dictates how to determine the treatment assignment to patients based on evolving treatments and covariates' history. These regimes are particularly effective for managing chronic disorders and is arguably one of the key aspects towards more personalized decision-making. In this paper, we investigate the online reinforcement learning (RL) problem for selecting optimal DTRs provided that observational data is available. We develop the first adaptive algorithm that achieves near-optimal regret in DTRs in online settings, without any access to historical data. We further derive informative bounds on the system dynamics of the underlying DTR from confounded, observational data. Finally, we combine these results and develop a novel RL algorithm that efficiently learns the optimal DTR while leveraging the abundant, yet imperfect confounded observations.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies a treatment decision at each intervention stage, using the patient's evolving treatment and covariate history. The paper studies how to learn such decision rules through online reinforcement learning. It also considers how observational records can help, even when confounding makes those records imperfect evidence about treatment dynamics.

The first contribution is an adaptive online algorithm with near-optimal regret that does not require historical data. Regret measures the loss incurred while learning relative to optimal decision-making. This establishes a learning procedure for the online setting before introducing the separate question of how existing observations should influence it.

The authors then derive informative bounds on the underlying treatment-regime dynamics from confounded observational data. They combine those bounds with the online learning results to obtain an algorithm that efficiently learns an optimal regime while using the available observations. The key connection is that imperfect historical information can still constrain learning usefully; the contribution concerns algorithmic learning guarantees rather than a reported clinical treatment trial.
summary.tldr: Near-optimal online learning for sequential treatment decisions is combined with informative bounds derived from confounded observational data.

title: Near-Optimal Reinforcement Learning in Dynamic Treatment Regimes

abstract: In this paper we consider the nonparametric least square regression in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We propose a new randomized algorithm that has optimal generalization error bounds with respect to the square loss, closing a long-standing gap between upper and lower bounds. Moreover, we show that our algorithm has faster finite-time and asymptotic rates on problems where the Bayes risk with respect to the square loss is small. We state our results using standard tools from the theory of least square regression in RKHSs, namely, the decay of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operator and the complexity of the optimal predictor measured through the integral operator.
originalAbstract: In this paper we consider the nonparametric least square regression in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We propose a new randomized algorithm that has optimal generalization error bounds with respect to the square loss, closing a long-standing gap between upper and lower bounds. Moreover, we show that our algorithm has faster finite-time and asymptotic rates on problems where the Bayes risk with respect to the square loss is small. We state our results using standard tools from the theory of least square regression in RKHSs, namely, the decay of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operator and the complexity of the optimal predictor measured through the integral operator.

paragraphs: This paper studies least-squares regression in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a mathematical setting for learning flexible prediction functions. Its objective is to understand how accurately a randomized learning algorithm can predict under squared loss. The authors propose an algorithm with optimal generalization error bounds, closing a previously unresolved gap between upper and lower bounds.

The analysis also examines problems with small Bayes risk under squared loss. Bayes risk describes the error of the best possible predictor for the underlying problem. When that risk is small, the proposed algorithm has faster rates both at finite stages and asymptotically. This acceleration is explicitly tied to that favorable property of the problem.

The guarantees are expressed through two standard ingredients of kernel regression theory: how quickly the associated integral operator’s eigenvalues decay, and the complexity of the optimal predictor as measured through that operator. These ingredients specify the setting of the results. The contribution combines optimal generalization guarantees with a more favorable analysis for low-noise problems.
summary.tldr: A randomized kernel regression algorithm achieves optimal generalization bounds and faster rates when the problem’s squared-loss Bayes risk is small.

title: Kernel Truncated Randomized Ridge Regression: Optimal Rates and Low Noise Acceleration

abstract: This paper presents a provable and strong algorithm, termed Innovation Search (iSearch), to robust Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and outlier detection. An outlier by definition is a data point which does not participate in forming a low dimensional structure with a large number of data points in the data. In other word, an outlier carries some innovation with respect to most of the other data points. iSearch ranks the data points based on their values of innovation. A convex optimization problem is proposed whose optimal value is used as our measure of innovation. We derive analytical performance guarantees for the proposed robust PCA method under different models for the distribution of the outliers including randomly distributed outliers, clustered outliers, and linearly dependent outliers. Moreover, it is shown that iSearch provably recovers the span of the inliers when the inliers lie in a union of subspaces. In the challenging scenarios in which the outliers are close to each other or they are close to the span of the inliers, iSearch is shown to outperform most of the existing methods.

paragraphs: This paper approaches outlier detection through the idea of innovation: how much a point contributes that is not shared by the low-dimensional structure supported by many other points. The same idea supports robust principal component analysis, where the aim is to recover the structure of the inliers despite the presence of outliers.

The proposed algorithm, Innovation Search or iSearch, assigns each point an innovation score using the optimal value of a convex optimization problem. It then ranks the points by those scores. This turns the qualitative distinction between shared structure and unusual contributions into a mathematical quantity that can guide outlier detection and recovery of the inlier span.

The authors derive guarantees for several outlier models, including random, clustered, and linearly dependent outliers. They also establish recovery of the inlier span when inliers occupy a union of subspaces. In challenging scenarios where outliers cluster together or lie near the inlier span, iSearch outperforms most existing methods in the reported comparisons. The findings cover both modeled recovery guarantees and evidence of effectiveness in difficult geometric configurations.
summary.tldr: iSearch ranks points using a convex innovation measure to detect outliers and recover low-dimensional inlier structure.

title: Outlier Detection and Robust PCA Using a Convex Measure of Innovation

abstract: Meta-materials are an important emerging class of engineered materials in which complex macroscopic behaviour--whether electromagnetic, thermal, or mechanical--arises from modular substructure. Simulation and optimization of these materials are computationally challenging, as rich substructures necessitate high-fidelity finite element meshes to solve the governing PDEs. To address this, we leverage parametric modular structure to learn component-level surrogates, enabling cheaper high-fidelity simulation. We use a neural network to model the stored potential energy in a component given boundary conditions. This yields a structured prediction task: macroscopic behavior is determined by the minimizer of the system's total potential energy, which can be approximated by composing these surrogate models. Composable energy surrogates thus permit simulation in the reduced basis of component boundaries. Costly ground-truth simulation of the full structure is avoided, as training data are generated by performing finite element analysis of individual components. Using dataset aggregation to choose training data allows us to learn energy surrogates which produce accurate macroscopic behavior when composed, accelerating simulation of parametric meta-materials.

paragraphs: Metamaterials obtain complex large-scale behavior from modular internal structures. Simulating those structures can require detailed finite element meshes, making the governing partial differential equations expensive to solve. This paper uses the modular structure to learn component-level approximations that can be assembled into a cheaper model of the full material.

A neural network predicts a component's stored potential energy from its boundary conditions. The component models are then composed, and the material's macroscopic behavior is determined by minimizing the approximate total potential energy. This formulation reduces simulation to variables on component boundaries while retaining an energy-based relationship between the components and the full structure.

Training examples come from finite element analyses of individual components, avoiding costly ground-truth simulations of the complete structure for that purpose. Dataset aggregation guides the selection of training data so that the component models work accurately when combined. The reported result is accurate macroscopic behavior from the composed surrogates and accelerated simulation of parametric metamaterials.
summary.tldr: Neural component-energy models compose into reduced simulations that accurately reproduce macroscopic metamaterial behavior while accelerating computation.

title: Learning Composable Energy Surrogates for PDE Order Reduction

abstract: The support/query (S/Q) episodic training strategy has been widely used in modern meta-learning algorithms and is believed to improve their generalization ability to test environments. This paper conducts a theoretical investigation of this training strategy on generalization. From a stability perspective, we analyze the generalization error bound of generic meta-learning algorithms trained with such strategy. We show that the S/Q episodic training strategy naturally leads to a counterintuitive generalization bound of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, which only depends on the task number $n$ but independent of the inner-task sample size $m$. Under the common assumption $m<<n$ for few-shot learning, the bound of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ implies strong generalization guarantees for modern meta-learning algorithms in the few-shot regime. To further explore the influence of training strategies on generalization, we propose a leave-one-out (LOO) training strategy for meta-learning and compare it with S/Q training. Experiments on standard few-shot regression and classification tasks with popular meta-learning algorithms validate our analysis.

paragraphs: Modern meta-learning often trains on episodes with separate support and query data. This strategy is widely believed to help a learner generalize to test environments. The paper examines that belief theoretically, focusing on how the training strategy influences a generalization bound rather than treating episodic training as an unexplained design choice.

Using a stability perspective, the authors analyze generic meta-learning algorithms trained with support/query episodes. They obtain a bound of order 1/√n, where n is the number of tasks. Its notable feature is that it does not depend on m, the number of samples within each task. This describes the dependence of the bound; it does not say that within-task data can never affect actual performance.

Under the common few-shot assumption that m is much smaller than n, the result supplies strong generalization guarantees. The authors also propose leave-one-out training to investigate how changing the training strategy affects generalization. Experiments using popular meta-learning algorithms on standard few-shot regression and classification tasks support their analysis.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis gives support/query meta-learning a generalization bound depending on the number of tasks rather than samples per task.

title: A Closer Look at the Training Strategy for Modern Meta-Learning

abstract: Coreset is usually a small weighted subset of $n$ input points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, that provably approximates their loss function for a given set of queries (models, classifiers, etc.). Coresets become increasingly common in machine learning since existing heuristics or inefficient algorithms may be improved by running them possibly many times on the small coreset that can be maintained for streaming distributed data. Coresets can be obtained by sensitivity (importance) sampling, where its size is proportional to the total sum of sensitivities. Unfortunately, computing the sensitivity of each point is problem dependent and may be harder to compute than the original optimization problem at hand. We suggest a generic framework for computing sensitivities (and thus coresets) for wide family of loss functions which we call near-convex functions. This is by suggesting the $f$-SVD factorization that generalizes the SVD factorization of matrices to functions. Example applications include coresets that are either new or significantly improves previous results, such as SVM, Logistic regression, M-estimators, and $\ell_z$-regression. Experimental results and open source are also provided.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small, weighted selection of data points that provably approximates the full dataset's loss across a specified collection of models or queries. It can make expensive algorithms more practical because they operate on much less data. This is particularly useful when an algorithm must run repeatedly or data arrives through streaming or distributed systems.

One way to construct coresets is importance sampling based on each point's sensitivity. The total sensitivity determines the resulting coreset size, but calculating these sensitivities can itself be harder than the original optimization problem. This paper develops a common framework for computing them across a broad family of losses called near-convex functions.

The technical device is an f-SVD factorization, which extends the idea of matrix singular value decomposition to functions. It provides a shared route from the structure of a loss to sensitivities and then to coresets. Applications include support vector machines, logistic regression, M-estimators, and l_z regression, with coreset results that are new or substantially improve earlier results. The paper also provides experiments and open-source material.
summary.tldr: A function-level generalization of SVD provides a common way to construct provable coresets for a broad family of near-convex losses.

title: Coresets for Near-Convex Functions

abstract: Deep learning algorithms are well-known to have a propensity for fitting the training data very well and often fit even outliers and mislabeled data points. Such fitting requires memorization of training data labels, a phenomenon that has attracted significant research interest but has not been given a compelling explanation so far. A recent work of Feldman (2019) proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon based on a combination of two insights. First, natural image and data distributions are (informally) known to be long-tailed, that is have a significant fraction of rare and atypical examples. Second, in a simple theoretical model such memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed. However, no direct empirical evidence for this explanation or even an approach for obtaining such evidence were given. In this work we design experiments to test the key ideas in this theory. The experiments require estimation of the influence of each training example on the accuracy at each test example as well as memorization values of training examples. Estimating these quantities directly is computationally prohibitive but we show that closely-related subsampled influence and memorization values can be estimated much more efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate the significant benefits of memorization for generalization on several standard benchmarks. They also provide quantitative and visually compelling evidence for the theory put forth in Feldman (2019).
originalAbstract: Deep learning algorithms are well-known to have a propensity for fitting the training data very well and often fit even outliers and mislabeled data points. Such fitting requires memorization of training data labels, a phenomenon that has attracted significant research interest but has not been given a compelling explanation so far. A recent work of Feldman (2019) proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon based on a combination of two insights. First, natural image and data distributions are (informally) known to be long-tailed, that is have a significant fraction of rare and atypical examples. Second, in a simple theoretical model such memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed. However, no direct empirical evidence for this explanation or even an approach for obtaining such evidence were given. In this work we design experiments to test the key ideas in this theory. The experiments require estimation of the influence of each training example on the accuracy at each test example as well as memorization values of training examples. Estimating these quantities directly is computationally prohibitive but we show that closely-related subsampled influence and memorization values can be estimated much more efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate the significant benefits of memorization for generalization on several standard benchmarks. They also provide quantitative and visually compelling evidence for the theory put forth in Feldman (2019).

paragraphs: Deep networks often fit individual training labels closely, including unusual or mislabeled examples. This paper tests an explanation for why memorization can help generalization: natural datasets contain many rare examples, and learning those examples can matter for predicting other uncommon cases. Earlier theory established a necessity for memorization in a simple model with a long-tailed distribution.

Testing that explanation requires measuring how individual training examples affect accuracy on individual test examples, together with how strongly training examples are memorized. Directly estimating these quantities is computationally prohibitive. The authors develop more efficient estimates of closely related subsampled influence and memorization quantities, making an empirical investigation feasible.

Experiments on several standard benchmarks show substantial generalization benefits from memorization and provide quantitative and visual evidence supporting the long-tail explanation. The distinction between the theoretical and empirical claims matters: necessity was established in the earlier simple model, while this work supplies evidence from benchmark learning problems. Its contribution links efficient influence estimation to a concrete account of why remembering particular examples can support prediction beyond the training set.
summary.tldr: Efficient subsampled influence estimates provide empirical evidence that memorizing rare training examples can improve generalization on long-tailed data.

title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation

abstract: We present a novel approach to estimating discrete distributions with (potentially) infinite support in the total variation metric. In a departure from the established paradigm, we make no structural assumptions whatsoever on the sampling distribution. In such a setting, distribution-free risk bounds are impossible, and the best one could hope for is a fully empirical data-dependent bound. We derive precisely such bounds, and demonstrate that these are, in a well-defined sense, the best possible. Our main discovery is that the half-norm of the empirical distribution provides tight upper and lower estimates on the empirical risk. Furthermore, this quantity decays at a nearly optimal rate as a function of the true distribution. The optimality follows from a minimax result, of possible independent interest. Additional structural results are provided, including an exact Rademacher complexity calculation and apparently a first connection between the total variation risk and the missing mass.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete distribution becomes especially challenging when it may assign probability to infinitely many outcomes. This paper makes no structural assumptions on the distribution and measures estimation error using total variation. In that setting, distribution-free risk bounds are impossible, so the authors seek bounds calculated from the observed data.

Their central result identifies the empirical distribution’s half-norm as a quantity that gives tight upper and lower estimates of empirical risk. This provides an observable basis for assessing error without first assuming a particular form for the unknown distribution. The resulting bounds are shown to be best possible in a specified sense.

The authors also establish nearly optimal decay as a function of the true distribution, supported by a minimax result. Additional analysis gives an exact Rademacher complexity calculation and connects total variation risk with missing mass, the probability associated with outcomes absent from the sample. The contribution replaces an unavailable universal guarantee with a sharp, data-dependent account of what can be learned in this unrestricted setting.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharp data-dependent error bounds for learning discrete distributions without structural assumptions, including infinite-support distributions.

title: Learning discrete distributions with infinite support

abstract: Neural networks have been shown to perform incredibly well in classification tasks over structured high-dimensional datasets. However, the learning dynamics of such networks is still poorly understood. In this paper we study in detail the training dynamics of a simple type of neural network: a single hidden layer trained to perform a classification task. We show that in a suitable mean-field limit this case maps to a single-node learning problem with a time-dependent dataset determined self-consistently from the average nodes population. We specialize our theory to the prototypical case of a linearly separable dataset and a linear hinge loss, for which the dynamics can be explicitly solved in the infinite dataset limit. This allow us to address in a simple setting several phenomena appearing in modern networks such as slowing down of training dynamics, crossover between feature and lazy learning, and overfitting. Finally, we asses the limitations of mean-field theory by studying the case of large but finite number of nodes and of training samples.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a neural network changes during training, using classification with a single hidden layer as a setting that permits detailed analysis. The goal is to explain aspects of the learning trajectory, including why progress can slow and how the character of learning can change over time.

In a suitable mean-field limit, the authors reduce the network's dynamics to a single-node learning problem. That node sees a time-dependent dataset determined by the average behavior of the node population. This self-consistent construction preserves the influence of the wider network while simplifying the equations needed to describe training.

For linearly separable data and linear hinge loss, the dynamics can be solved explicitly in the infinite-data limit. The solution allows the authors to examine slowing training, transitions between feature learning and lazy learning, and overfitting within this simple setting. They also study large but finite networks and datasets to assess where the mean-field description has limitations. The analysis supplies a controlled account of these phenomena under its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: A mean-field analysis makes shallow-network training explicitly solvable in a particular classification setting and illuminates several learning dynamics.

title: An analytic theory of shallow networks dynamics for hinge loss classification

abstract: One fundamental problem in the empirical sciences is of reconstructing the causal structure that underlies a phenomenon of interest through observation and experimentation. While there exists a plethora of methods capable of learning the equivalence class of causal structures that are compatible with observations, it is less well-understood how to systematically combine observations and experiments to reconstruct the underlying structure. In this paper, we investigate the task of structural learning in non-Markovian systems (i.e., when latent variables affect more than one observable) from a combination of observational and soft experimental data when the interventional targets are unknown. Using causal invariances found across the collection of observational and interventional distributions (not only conditional independences), we define a property called psi-Markov that connects these distributions to a pair consisting of (1) a causal graph D and (2) a set of interventional targets I. Building on this property, our main contributions are two-fold: First, we provide a graphical characterization that allows one to test whether two causal graphs with possibly different sets of interventional targets belong to the same psi-Markov equivalence class. Second, we develop an algorithm capable of harnessing the collection of data to learn the corresponding equivalence class. We then prove that this algorithm is sound and complete, in the sense that it is the most informative in the sample limit, i.e., it discovers as many tails and arrowheads as can be oriented within a psi-Markov equivalence class.

paragraphs: Reconstructing causal structure becomes difficult when hidden variables influence multiple observed quantities and experiments do not reveal which variables they changed. This paper studies that combination, using observational data together with soft interventions whose targets are unknown. Its goal is to characterize and learn the causal structures compatible with these sources of evidence.

The authors introduce a property called psi-Markov that connects the observed distributions to both a causal graph and a set of intervention targets. It uses relationships that remain invariant across observational and experimental conditions, going beyond conditional independences alone. They then give a graphical test for whether two graph-and-target descriptions belong to the same equivalence class.

An accompanying algorithm learns that equivalence class from the combined data. The authors prove soundness and completeness in the sample limit: the method identifies every edge endpoint that can be oriented within the class. This is a maximal-information guarantee relative to the defined equivalence class, rather than a promise that every underlying causal graph or intervention target becomes uniquely identifiable.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes and learns causal equivalence classes from observational data and soft interventions with unknown targets, allowing shared latent causes.

title: Causal Discovery from Soft Interventions with Unknown Targets: Characterization and Learning

abstract: In recent years we see a rapidly growing line of research which shows learnability of various models via common neural network algorithms. Yet, besides a very few outliers, these results show learnability of models that can be learned using linear methods. Namely, such results show that learning neural-networks with gradient-descent is competitive with learning a linear classifier on top of a data-independent representation of the examples. This leaves much to be desired, as neural networks are far more successful than linear methods. Furthermore, on the more conceptual level, linear models don't seem to capture the``deepness" of deep networks. In this paper we make a step towards showing leanability of models that are inherently non-linear. We show that under certain distributions, sparse parities are learnable via gradient decent on depth-two network. On the other hand, under the same distributions, these parities cannot be learned efficiently by linear methods.

paragraphs: Many theoretical results about neural-network learning concern problems that linear methods can also solve. Such results establish useful capabilities but leave open why learning a nonlinear representation can offer a computational advantage. This paper addresses that gap by studying sparse parity functions as a learning problem with an inherently nonlinear aspect.

The authors show that, under certain data distributions, gradient descent can learn sparse parities using a depth-two neural network. Their comparison uses the same distributions: linear methods cannot efficiently learn those parities there. The relevant linear approach is a classifier built on a representation of examples that is fixed independently of the data.

The result provides a theoretical separation between the specified neural-network training procedure and linear methods in this setting. Its force comes from comparing learnability under shared distributions, rather than changing the data between approaches. The distribution condition is essential to the stated result: the paper establishes a particular setting where neural learning goes beyond linear methods, not unrestricted learnability of sparse parities.
summary.tldr: Under certain distributions, gradient descent learns sparse parities with a depth-two network while linear methods cannot learn them efficiently.

title: Learning Parities with Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the Wasserstein distance between the empirical measure and a set of probability measures whose expectations over a class of functions (hypothesis class) are constrained. If this class is sufficiently rich to characterize a particular distribution (e.g., all Lipschitz functions), then our formulation recovers the Wasserstein distance to such a distribution. We establish a strong duality result that generalizes the celebrated Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. We also show that our formulation can be used to beat the curse of dimensionality, which is well known to affect the rates of statistical convergence of the empirical Wasserstein distance. In particular, examples of infinite-dimensional hypothesis classes are presented, informed by a complex correlation structure, for which it is shown that the empirical Wasserstein distance to such classes converges to zero at the standard parametric rate. Our formulation provides insights that help clarify why, despite the curse of dimensionality, the Wasserstein distance enjoys favorable empirical performance across a wide range of statistical applications.

paragraphs: Estimating Wasserstein distance from samples can become statistically difficult in high dimensions. This paper considers distance from an empirical distribution to a set of distributions, where membership is specified by constraints on expected values of a function class. The target therefore encodes selected distributional properties.

If the function class is rich enough to identify one distribution, the formulation recovers distance to that distribution. The authors establish a strong duality theorem extending Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. This gives the set-based formulation a mathematical foundation while connecting it to the familiar single-distribution case.

The paper also presents infinite-dimensional function classes informed by complex correlation structure for which the empirical distance converges to zero at the standard parametric rate. These examples show that the formulation can avoid the usual dimensionality penalty in suitable settings. They do not remove that penalty for every Wasserstein estimation problem. Instead, they help explain how useful empirical performance can coexist with unfavorable general convergence rates by making the target constraints central to the analysis.
summary.tldr: Measuring Wasserstein distance to suitably constrained distribution sets can achieve parametric convergence despite the usual curse of dimensionality.

title: Quantifying the Empirical Wasserstein Distance to a Set of Measures: Beating the Curse of Dimensionality

abstract: The brain solves the credit assignment problem remarkably well. For credit to be assigned across neural networks they must, in principle, wait for specific neural computations to finish. How the brain deals with this inherent locking problem has remained unclear. Deep learning methods suffer from similar locking constraints both on the forward and feedback phase. Recently, decoupled neural interfaces (DNIs) were introduced as a solution to the forward and feedback locking problems in deep networks.Here we propose that a specialised brain region, the cerebellum, helps the cerebral cortex solve similar locking problems akin to DNIs. To demonstrate the potential of this framework we introduce a systems-level model in which a recurrent cortical network receives online temporal feedback predictions from a cerebellar module. We test this cortico-cerebellar recurrent neural network (ccRNN) model on a number of sensorimotor (line and digit drawing) and cognitive tasks (pattern recognition and caption generation) that have been shown to be cerebellar-dependent. In all tasks, we observe that ccRNNs facilitates learning while reducing ataxia-like behaviours, consistent with classical experimental observations. Moreover, our model also explains recent behavioural and neuronal observations while making several testable predictions across multiple levels.Overall, our work offers a novel perspective on the cerebellum as a brain-wide decoupling machine for efficient credit assignment and opens a new avenue between deep learning and neuroscience.

paragraphs: Learning requires assigning credit to the computations that contributed to an outcome. In a network, that can create waiting: one part needs information from another before it can update. This paper proposes that the cerebellum helps the cerebral cortex overcome such dependencies, drawing inspiration from decoupled neural interfaces in deep learning.

The authors build a systems-level model consisting of a recurrent cortical network and a cerebellar module. The cerebellar component supplies online predictions of temporal feedback, offering a way to support learning despite delays in the relevant computations. They test this combined network on line and digit drawing, pattern recognition, and caption generation, tasks described as cerebellar-dependent.

Across the tested tasks, the model facilitates learning and reduces behaviors resembling ataxia, consistent with classical experimental observations. The authors also report explanations for recent behavioral and neuronal observations and derive testable predictions. These results support the potential of the proposed framework; the claim is a computational account of cerebellar function, rather than a direct demonstration that the brain implements this particular mechanism.
summary.tldr: A cortical–cerebellar network model suggests that predicted feedback could reduce learning delays and explain several cerebellar-dependent behaviors.

title: Cortico-cerebellar networks as decoupling neural interfaces

abstract: Understanding why deep nets can classify data in large dimensions remains a challenge. It has been proposed that they do so by becoming stable to diffeomorphisms, yet existing empirical measurements support that it is often not the case. We revisit this question by defining a maximum-entropy distribution on diffeomorphisms, that allows to study typical diffeomorphisms of a given norm. We confirm that stability toward diffeomorphisms does not strongly correlate to performance on benchmark data sets of images. By contrast, we find that the stability toward diffeomorphisms relative to that of generic transformations $R_f$ correlates remarkably with the test error $\epsilon_t$. It is of order unity at initialization but decreases by several decades during training for state-of-the-art architectures. For CIFAR10 and 15 known architectures, we find $\epsilon_t\approx 0.2\sqrt{R_f}$, suggesting that obtaining a small $R_f$ is important to achieve good performance. We study how $R_f$ depends on the size of the training set and compare it to a simple model of invariant learning.

paragraphs: One proposed explanation for image-classification performance is that neural networks become insensitive to smooth, invertible deformations, called diffeomorphisms. Earlier empirical measurements have not consistently supported that explanation. This paper revisits it by defining a maximum-entropy distribution over deformations, allowing typical transformations of a specified magnitude to be studied.

The authors confirm that stability to these deformations alone does not strongly correlate with performance on image benchmarks. A relative measure is much more informative: they compare the network's response to diffeomorphisms with its response to generic transformations. The resulting quantity, R_f, correlates strongly with test error and decreases by several orders of magnitude during training.

For CIFAR10 across 15 architectures, the observed relationship is approximately test error = 0.2 times the square root of R_f. This suggests that small relative sensitivity is important for good performance in the studied setting, without establishing a universal causal law. The paper also examines dependence on training-set size and compares the findings with a simple model of learning invariance.
summary.tldr: Sensitivity to smooth deformations relative to generic transformations correlates with image-classification error much more strongly than deformation stability alone.

title: Relative stability toward diffeomorphisms indicates performance in deep nets

abstract: Social recommendation has shown promising improvements over traditional systems since it leverages social correlation data as an additional input. Most existing work assumes that all data are available to the recommendation platform. However, in practice, user-item interaction data (e.g.,rating) and user-user social data are usually generated by different platforms, and both of which contain sensitive information. Therefore, "How to perform secure and efficient social recommendation across different platforms, where the data are highly-sparse in nature" remains an important challenge. In this work, we bring secure computation techniques into social recommendation, and propose S3Rec, a sparsity-aware secure cross-platform social recommendation framework. As a result, our model can not only improve the recommendation performance of the rating platform by incorporating the sparse social data on the social platform, but also protect data privacy of both platforms. Moreover, to further improve model training efficiency, we propose two secure sparse matrix multiplication protocols based on homomorphic encryption and private information retrieval. Our experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of S3Rec.

paragraphs: Social recommendation uses relationships between users to supplement information such as ratings. In practice, those two kinds of data may belong to different platforms, and both contain sensitive information. The paper addresses how a recommendation platform can benefit from another platform's social data while protecting the information held by each.

The proposed S3Rec framework brings secure computation into cross-platform social recommendation. It explicitly accounts for the high sparsity of the data: user-item interactions and user-user relationships occupy only a small part of their possible combinations. The framework aims to improve the rating platform's recommendations using the social platform's data while maintaining privacy for both parties.

To make training more efficient, the authors develop two secure sparse matrix multiplication protocols based on homomorphic encryption and private information retrieval. These protocols connect the computational design to the sparse structure of the recommendation problem. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate S3Rec's effectiveness. The contribution combines recommendation modeling with secure computation designed around the data structures encountered across the two platforms.
summary.tldr: S3Rec uses sparsity-aware secure computation to combine ratings and social data across platforms while protecting both platforms' data.

title: Exploiting Data Sparsity in Secure Cross-Platform Social Recommendation

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), aiming to obtain the representation of a node by aggregating its neighbors, have demonstrated great power in tackling various analytics tasks on graph (network) data. The remarkable performance of GCNs typically relies on the homophily assumption of networks, while such assumption cannot always be satisfied, since the heterophily or randomness are also widespread in real-world. This gives rise to one fundamental question: whether networks with different structural properties should adopt different propagation mechanisms? In this paper, we first conduct an experimental investigation. Surprisingly, we discover that there are actually segmentation rules for the propagation mechanism, i.e., 1-hop, 2-hop and $k$-nearest neighbor ($k$NN) neighbors are more suitable as neighborhoods of network with complete homophily, complete heterophily and randomness, respectively. However, the real-world networks are complex, and may present diverse structural properties, e.g., the network dominated by homophily may contain a small amount of randomness. So can we reasonably utilize these segmentation rules to design a universal propagation mechanism independent of the network structural assumption? To tackle this challenge, we develop a new universal GCN framework, namely U-GCN. It first introduces a multi-type convolution to extract information from 1-hop, 2-hop and $k$NN networks simultaneously, and then designs a discriminative aggregation to sufficiently fuse them aiming to given learning objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of U-GCN over state-of-the-arts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/jindi-tju.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks form node representations by combining information from neighbors. This often works well when connected nodes resemble one another, a property called homophily. Real networks can instead connect dissimilar nodes or contain substantial randomness, raising the question of whether the same neighborhood definition should serve every graph.

The paper first investigates neighborhood choices experimentally. It finds one-hop neighborhoods more suitable under complete homophily, two-hop neighborhoods under complete heterophily, and nearest-neighbor neighborhoods under randomness. Because actual networks can mix these structural properties, the findings motivate using several information sources together rather than selecting one rule for an entire network.

U-GCN implements that idea through convolution over one-hop, two-hop, and nearest-neighbor networks simultaneously. A discriminative aggregation stage combines their information according to the learning objective. Extensive experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art methods. The framework's contribution is to accommodate multiple neighborhood structures within one model, reducing dependence on a single structural assumption; the experimental neighborhood patterns are not presented as universal mathematical laws.
summary.tldr: U-GCN combines several neighborhood types to handle graphs with mixed homophily, heterophily, and randomness.

title: Universal Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Current SOTA adversarially robust models are mostly based on adversarial training (AT) and differ only by some regularizers either at inner maximization or outer minimization steps. Being repetitive in nature during the inner maximization step, they take a huge time to train. We propose a non-iterative method that enforces the following ideas during training. Attribution maps are more aligned to the actual object in the image for adversarially robust models compared to naturally trained models. Also, the allowed set of pixels to perturb an image (that changes model decision) should be restricted to the object pixels only, which reduces the attack strength by limiting the attack space. Our method achieves significant performance gains with a little extra effort (10-20%) over existing AT models and outperforms all other methods in terms of adversarial as well as natural accuracy. We have performed extensive experimentation with CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet datasets and reported results against many popular strong adversarial attacks to prove the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Adversarial training commonly spends substantial computation repeatedly searching for image perturbations that fool a model. This paper proposes a non-iterative training method motivated by where robust models appear to look. Its starting observation is that attribution maps, which indicate image regions associated with a prediction, align more closely with the actual object in robust models than in naturally trained models.

The method enforces object-focused ideas during training. One concerns aligning attribution with the object; another restricts the pixels available for decision-changing perturbations to the object itself. That restriction makes the attack space smaller and therefore weakens the permitted attack. It is a substantive part of the approach, rather than an equivalent formulation of unrestricted image perturbation.

The authors report experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet against several strong attacks. They report gains over existing adversarial-training models with 10–20% extra effort and better adversarial and natural accuracy than the compared methods. The findings support object-focused training as a route to robustness, with the stated perturbation restriction central to understanding the approach.
summary.tldr: A non-iterative, object-focused training approach reports improved clean and adversarial accuracy while restricting perturbations to object pixels.

title: Adversarial Robustness without Adversarial Training: A Teacher-Guided Curriculum Learning Approach

abstract: Circuit representations are becoming the lingua franca to express and reason about tractable generative and discriminative models. In this paper, we show how complex inference scenarios for these models that commonly arise in machine learning---from computing the expectations of decision tree ensembles to information-theoretic divergences of sum-product networks---can be represented in terms of tractable modular operations over circuits. Specifically, we characterize the tractability of simple transformations---sums, products, quotients, powers, logarithms, and exponentials---in terms of sufficient structural constraints of the circuits they operate on, and present novel hardness results for the cases in which these properties are not satisfied. Building on these operations, we derive a unified framework for reasoning about tractable models that generalizes several results in the literature and opens up novel tractable inference scenarios.

paragraphs: A model can support efficient basic calculations while still making a more complicated inference question difficult. This paper studies that gap for models represented as computational circuits. Its central idea is to express complex questions as combinations of simpler circuit operations, so that their computational feasibility can be understood piece by piece.

The authors analyze sums, products, quotients, powers, logarithms, and exponentials. For each kind of transformation, they identify structural conditions on the circuits that are sufficient for efficient computation. They also establish new hardness results for cases where relevant properties are absent. These results distinguish supported routes to efficient inference from settings where computation becomes provably difficult.

Combining these operations yields a common framework for questions ranging from expectations of decision-tree ensembles to information-theoretic divergences between sum-product networks. The contribution is therefore both organizational and constructive: it brings earlier tractability results together and derives additional tractable inference scenarios. The structural conditions provide sufficient guarantees, rather than a claim that every efficient calculation must satisfy them.
summary.tldr: The paper builds a modular framework for determining when circuit operations can support efficient probabilistic inference.

title: A Compositional Atlas of Tractable Circuit Operations for Probabilistic Inference

abstract: A significant obstacle in the development of robust machine learning models is \emph{covariate shift}, a form of distribution shift that occurs when the input distributions of the training and test sets differ while the conditional label distributions remain the same. Despite the prevalence of covariate shift in real-world applications, a theoretical understanding in the context of modern machine learning has remained lacking. In this work, we examine the exact high-dimensional asymptotics of random feature regression under covariate shift and present a precise characterization of the limiting test error, bias, and variance in this setting. Our results motivate a natural partial order over covariate shifts that provides a sufficient condition for determining when the shift will harm (or even help) test performance. We find that overparameterized models exhibit enhanced robustness to covariate shift, providing one of the first theoretical explanations for this ubiquitous empirical phenomenon. Additionally, our analysis reveals an exact linear relationship between the in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization performance, offering an explanation for this surprising recent observation.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions while the conditional relationship between inputs and labels stays the same. This paper analyzes that problem for random-feature regression in a high-dimensional limit. It derives precise limiting expressions for test error, bias, and variance, allowing the effect of a shift to be examined mathematically.

The analysis motivates a partial ordering of covariate shifts. This ordering gives a sufficient condition for deciding when a shift will worsen or improve test performance. A partial order need not compare every pair of shifts, and a sufficient condition does not claim to characterize every possible case. The result nevertheless gives a structured way to identify the direction of performance changes.

Within the analyzed setting, overparameterized models show greater robustness to covariate shift, supplying a theoretical explanation for an empirically observed pattern. The analysis also produces an exact linear relationship between in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization performance. These conclusions are tied to the random-feature model and high-dimensional asymptotics, where the paper can characterize the relevant errors precisely.
summary.tldr: High-dimensional random-feature theory explains enhanced covariate-shift robustness from overparameterization and a linear relationship between in- and out-of-distribution performance.

title: Overparameterization Improves Robustness to Covariate Shift in High Dimensions

abstract: Molecular property prediction plays a fundamental role in drug discovery to identify candidate molecules with target properties. However, molecular property prediction is essentially a few-shot problem, which makes it hard to use regular machine learning models. In this paper, we propose Property-Aware Relation networks (PAR) to handle this problem. In comparison to existing works, we leverage the fact that both relevant substructures and relationships among molecules change across different molecular properties. We first introduce a property-aware embedding function to transform the generic molecular embeddings to substructure-aware space relevant to the target property. Further, we design an adaptive relation graph learning module to jointly estimate molecular relation graph and refine molecular embeddings w.r.t. the target property, such that the limited labels can be effectively propagated among similar molecules. We adopt a meta-learning strategy where the parameters are selectively updated within tasks in order to model generic and property-aware knowledge separately. Extensive experiments on benchmark molecular property prediction datasets show that PAR consistently outperforms existing methods and can obtain property-aware molecular embeddings and model molecular relation graph properly.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular properties with few labeled examples requires making good use of relationships between molecules. This paper argues that those relationships, and the molecular substructures that matter, change with the property being predicted. Property-Aware Relation networks, or PAR, therefore adapt both molecular representations and their relationships to the target property.

A property-aware embedding function first transforms generic molecular representations into a space emphasizing relevant substructures. An adaptive graph module then jointly estimates relationships among molecules and refines their embeddings. This graph allows the limited label information to propagate among molecules considered similar for the particular property, making the definition of similarity part of the learned solution.

PAR uses meta-learning with selective parameter updates within tasks to separate generic knowledge from property-specific knowledge. On benchmark molecular property datasets, it consistently outperforms the methods included in the evaluation. The experiments also support its ability to learn property-aware embeddings and appropriate relation graphs, connecting the predictive improvements to the intended adaptation of molecular structure and similarity.
summary.tldr: PAR adapts molecular embeddings and relation graphs to each target property, improving prediction from limited labeled examples.

title: Property-Aware Relation Networks for Few-Shot Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: We consider a selection problem where sequentially arrived applicants apply for a limited number of positions/jobs. At each time step, a decision maker accepts or rejects the given applicant using a pre-trained supervised learning model until all the vacant positions are filled. In this paper, we discuss whether the fairness notions (e.g., equal opportunity, statistical parity, etc.) that are commonly used in classification problems are suitable for the sequential selection problems. In particular, we show that even with a pre-trained model that satisfies the common fairness notions, the selection outcomes may still be biased against certain demographic groups. This observation implies that the fairness notions used in classification problems are not suitable for a selection problem where the applicants compete for a limited number of positions. We introduce a new fairness notion, ``Equal Selection (ES),'' suitable for sequential selection problems and propose a post-processing approach to satisfy the ES fairness notion. We also consider a setting where the applicants have privacy concerns, and the decision maker only has access to the noisy version of sensitive attributes. In this setting, we can show that the \textit{perfect} ES fairness can still be attained under certain conditions.

paragraphs: In sequential selection, applicants arrive one at a time and receive an acceptance or rejection decision until a limited set of positions is filled. This paper examines whether fairness properties of a pretrained classification model carry over to that process. The limited capacity makes the final selection outcome a distinct object of study.

The authors show that a model satisfying familiar classification fairness notions, such as equal opportunity or statistical parity, can still produce selection outcomes biased against demographic groups. A fairness property of individual model decisions therefore does not by itself establish fairness of the resulting competition for positions. The paper introduces Equal Selection, or ES, as a fairness notion tailored to sequential selection.

A proposed post-processing method satisfies this new notion. The authors also study a privacy-sensitive setting in which the decision maker sees only noisy versions of applicants' sensitive attributes. They show that perfect ES remains attainable under certain conditions. This conditional result extends the approach to imperfect demographic information while preserving the distinction between model-level fairness and fairness of the selection procedure.
summary.tldr: Fair classifiers can yield biased sequential selections, motivating Equal Selection and a post-processing method that can also handle noisy sensitive attributes conditionally.

title: Fair Sequential Selection Using Supervised Learning Models

abstract: A mixture of multinomial logits (MMNL) generalizes the single logit model, which is commonly used in predicting the probabilities of different outcomes. While extensive algorithms have been developed in the literature to learn MMNL models, theoretical results are limited. Built on the Frank-Wolfe (FW) method, we propose a new algorithm that learns both mixture weights and component-specific logit parameters with provable convergence guarantees for an arbitrary number of mixtures. Our algorithm utilizes historical choice data to generate a set of candidate choice probability vectors, each being close to the ground truth with a high probability. We further provide a sample complexity analysis to show that only a polynomial number of samples is required to secure the performance guarantee of our algorithm. Finally, we conduct simulation studies to evaluate the performance and demonstrate how to apply our algorithm to real-world applications.

While extensive algorithms have been developed in the literature to learn MMNL models, theoretical results are limited. Built on the Frank-Wolfe (FW) method, we propose a new algorithm that learns both mixture weights and component-specific logit parameters with provable convergence guarantees for an arbitrary number of mixtures. Our algorithm utilizes historical choice data to generate a set of candidate choice probability vectors, each being close to the ground truth with a high probability. paragraphs: A mixed multinomial logit model combines several logit components to predict probabilities of different outcomes. Learning such a model involves estimating both the relative weight of each component and its own parameters. Although many algorithms already address this problem, the paper focuses on providing theoretical guarantees for the learning process.

The proposed algorithm builds on the Frank-Wolfe optimization method and handles an arbitrary number of mixture components. From historical choice observations, it constructs candidate vectors of choice probabilities that are close to the true probabilities with high probability. The approach learns mixture weights and component-specific parameters within one algorithm, with provable convergence guarantees.

The authors also analyze the amount of data needed and show that a polynomial number of samples suffices for the stated performance guarantee. This adds a statistical requirement alongside the convergence result, addressing both the learning procedure and its data needs. Simulation studies evaluate the method, and the paper demonstrates its application to real-world problems. Its main contribution is a theoretically supported procedure for a mixture-model learning task with previously limited guarantees.
summary.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe-based algorithm learns mixed multinomial logit models with convergence guarantees and polynomial sample requirements.

title: Learning Mixed Multinomial Logits with Provable Guarantees

abstract: Recent years have witnessed the rise of misinformation campaigns that spread specific narratives on social media to manipulate public opinions on different areas, such as politics and healthcare. Consequently, an effective and efficient automatic methodology to estimate the influence of the misinformation on user beliefs and activities is needed. However, existing works on misinformation impact estimation either rely on small-scale psychological experiments or can only discover the correlation between user behaviour and misinformation. To address these issues, in this paper, we build up a causal framework that model the causal effect of misinformation from the perspective of temporal point process. To adapt the large-scale data, we design an efficient yet precise way to estimate the \textbf{Individual Treatment Effect} (ITE) via neural temporal point process and gaussian mixture models. Extensive experiments on synthetic dataset verify the effectiveness and efficiency of our model. We further apply our model on a real-world dataset of social media posts and engagements about COVID-19 vaccines. The experimental results indicate that our model recognized identifiable causal effect of misinformation that hurts people's subjective emotions toward the vaccines.

paragraphs: Estimating misinformation's influence requires more than observing that people who encounter it behave differently. The paper addresses the distinction between association and causal influence, with particular attention to social media activity unfolding over time. It aims to estimate effects at the individual level while handling data at a larger scale than small psychological experiments.

The authors build a causal framework using temporal point processes, which model the timing of events. Their estimation method combines a neural temporal point process with Gaussian mixture models to estimate individual treatment effects. The temporal formulation makes event sequences central to the analysis, while the proposed combination is designed to make the estimates both efficient and precise on large datasets.

Synthetic-data experiments support the method's effectiveness and efficiency. The authors then apply it to posts and engagement concerning COVID-19 vaccines. In that application, the model identifies a causal effect of misinformation associated with more negative subjective emotions toward vaccines. This is a finding from the model's analysis of that dataset; its stated outcome concerns emotional attitudes rather than a demonstrated change in vaccination behavior.
summary.tldr: A causal model of social media event timing estimates individual misinformation effects and finds negative effects on vaccine-related emotions in its real-data application.

title: Counterfactual Neural Temporal Point Process for Estimating Causal Influence of Misinformation on Social Media

abstract: Graph contrastive learning (GCL) alleviates the heavy reliance on label information for graph representation learning (GRL) via self-supervised learning schemes. The core idea is to learn by maximising mutual information for similar instances, which requires similarity computation between two node instances. However, GCL is inefficient in both time and memory consumption. In addition, GCL normally requires a large number of training epochs to be well-trained on large-scale datasets. Inspired by an observation of a technical defect (i.e., inappropriate usage of Sigmoid function) commonly used in two representative GCL works, DGI and MVGRL, we revisit GCL and introduce a new learning paradigm for self-supervised graph representation learning, namely, Group Discrimination (GD), and propose a novel GD-based method called Graph Group Discrimination (GGD). Instead of similarity computation, GGD directly discriminates two groups of node samples with a very simple binary cross-entropy loss. In addition, GGD requires much fewer training epochs to obtain competitive performance compared with GCL methods on large-scale datasets. These two advantages endow GGD with very efficient property. Extensive experiments show that GGD outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on eight datasets. In particular, GGD can be trained in 0.18 seconds (6.44 seconds including data preprocessing) on ogbn-arxiv, which is orders of magnitude (10,000+) faster than GCL baselines while consuming much less memory. Trained with 9 hours on ogbn-papers100M with billion edges, GGD outperforms its GCL counterparts in both accuracy and efficiency.
