paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning reduces dependence on labels by learning from relationships between samples, but comparing node instances can require substantial time and memory. Large graphs may also demand many training epochs. This paper revisits that approach after identifying what the authors describe as inappropriate sigmoid use in two representative methods, DGI and MVGRL.

The proposed alternative is Graph Group Discrimination, or GGD. It learns by distinguishing two groups of node samples using binary cross entropy, replacing the similarity-computation objective. The method also needs fewer training epochs to reach competitive performance on large datasets. Together, the simpler learning objective and shorter training explain the proposed efficiency advantage.

Experiments report better performance than leading self-supervised methods on eight datasets. On ogbn-arxiv, training takes 0.18 seconds, or 6.44 seconds including preprocessing, with a reported speed advantage exceeding 10,000 times over graph contrastive baselines and substantially lower memory use. On the billion-edge ogbn-papers100M graph, nine hours of training yields better accuracy and efficiency than the compared contrastive methods. These results demonstrate the practical scale of the proposed change in learning objective.
summary.tldr: GGD replaces pairwise similarity learning with group discrimination, achieving strong graph representations with sharply reduced training time and memory in reported experiments.

title: Rethinking and Scaling Up Graph Contrastive Learning: An Extremely Efficient Approach with Group Discrimination

abstract: A powerful category of (invisible) data poisoning attacks modify a subset of training examples by small adversarial perturbations to change the prediction of certain test-time data. Existing defense mechanisms are not desirable to deploy in practice, as they ofteneither drastically harm the generalization performance, or are attack-specific, and prohibitively slow to apply. Here, we propose a simple but highly effective approach that unlike existing methods breaks various types of invisible poisoning attacks with the slightest drop in the generalization performance. We make the key observation that attacks introduce local sharp regions of high training loss, which when minimized, results in learning the adversarial perturbations and makes the attack successful. To break poisoning attacks, our key idea is to alleviate the sharp loss regions introduced by poisons. To do so, our approach comprises two components: an optimized friendly noise that is generated to maximally perturb examples without degrading the performance, and a randomly varying noise component. The combination of both components builds a very light-weight but extremely effective defense against the most powerful triggerless targeted and hidden-trigger backdoor poisoning attacks, including Gradient Matching, Bulls-eye Polytope, and Sleeper Agent. We show that our friendly noise is transferable to other architectures, and adaptive attacks cannot break our defense due to its random noise component.

paragraphs: Invisible data poisoning changes a subset of training examples through small adversarial perturbations, aiming to alter predictions on selected test inputs. This paper connects successful poisoning with sharp local regions of high training loss. Minimizing those regions can lead a model to learn the adversarial perturbations embedded in its training data.

The proposed defense attempts to soften those sharp regions using two forms of noise. An optimized friendly component perturbs examples as much as possible without degrading performance, while a second component varies randomly. Combining them is intended to disrupt the learning of poisoned perturbations while retaining the model’s ability to generalize.

The authors report a lightweight defense against multiple triggerless targeted and hidden-trigger backdoor attacks, including Gradient Matching, Bulls-eye Polytope, and Sleeper Agent, with only a slight generalization drop. They also show that friendly noise transfers across architectures and report that adaptive attacks fail to break the defense because of its random component. These findings support the combined noise design against the attacks examined in the work.
summary.tldr: Optimized friendly noise combined with random noise counters several invisible data-poisoning attacks with a slight generalization cost.

title: Friendly Noise against Adversarial Noise: A Powerful Defense against Data Poisoning Attack

abstract: We present a unified hard-constraint framework for solving geometrically complex PDEs with neural networks, where the most commonly used Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundary conditions (BCs) are considered. Specifically, we first introduce the "extra fields'' from the mixed finite element method to reformulate the PDEs so as to equivalently transform the three types of BCs into linear forms. Based on the reformulation, we derive the general solutions of the BCs analytically, which are employed to construct an ansatz that automatically satisfies the BCs. With such a framework, we can train the neural networks without adding extra loss terms and thus efficiently handle geometrically complex PDEs, alleviating the unbalanced competition between the loss terms corresponding to the BCs and PDEs. We theoretically demonstrate that the "extra fields'' can stabilize the training process. Experimental results on real-world geometrically complex PDEs showcase the effectiveness of our method compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Neural networks used to solve partial differential equations must satisfy both the equation inside a domain and conditions along its boundary. Training with separate penalties for these requirements can create competition between loss terms. This paper develops a unified way to satisfy boundary conditions automatically, including Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions in geometrically complex problems.

The approach introduces additional fields borrowed from mixed finite element methods. These fields reformulate the equations so that all three boundary-condition types take equivalent linear forms. The authors then derive analytical general solutions for those conditions and use them to construct the form of the network's candidate solution. Boundary compliance is therefore built into that construction.

This removes the need for extra boundary-condition loss terms and alleviates their competition with the equation loss. The authors also provide a theoretical argument that the additional fields can stabilize training. Experiments on real-world equations with complex geometry demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the value of combining analytical constraint handling with neural solution methods.
summary.tldr: The framework builds common boundary conditions directly into neural PDE solutions, reducing competing training losses and potentially stabilizing optimization.

title: A Unified Hard-Constraint Framework for Solving Geometrically Complex PDEs

abstract: Extensive literature on backdoor poison attacks has studied attacks and defenses for backdoors using “digital trigger patterns.” In contrast, “physical backdoors” use physical objects as triggers, have only recently been identified, and are qualitatively different enough to resist most defenses targeting digital trigger backdoors. Research on physical backdoors is limited by access to large datasets containing real images of physical objects co-located with misclassification targets. Building these datasets is time- and labor-intensive.This work seeks to address the challenge of accessibility for research on physical backdoor attacks. We hypothesize that there may be naturally occurring physically co-located objects already present in popular datasets such as ImageNet. Once identified, a careful relabeling of these data can transform them into training samples for physical backdoor attacks. We propose a method to scalably identify these subsets of potential triggers in existing datasets, along with the specific classes they can poison. We call these naturally occurring trigger-class subsets natural backdoor datasets. Our techniques successfully identify natural backdoors in widely-available datasets, and produce models behaviorally equivalent to those trained on manually curated datasets. We release our code to allow the research community to create their own datasets for research on physical backdoor attacks.

paragraphs: Physical backdoors use real objects as triggers for a model's misclassification. Studying them requires images where candidate trigger objects appear alongside relevant target objects, and manually collecting these images takes considerable work. The paper asks whether suitable combinations already exist in widely available image datasets.

The authors propose a scalable method for finding subsets containing potential physical triggers and identifying the classes those triggers could poison. Carefully relabeling the selected images turns them into training data for backdoor research. The naturally occurring element is the co-location of objects in existing images; the attack-training dataset is constructed through the subsequent selection and relabeling.

The method successfully identifies such subsets in widely available datasets. Models trained using them exhibit behavior equivalent to models trained on manually curated physical-backdoor datasets in the reported study. This makes existing image collections a useful resource for investigating a type of backdoor that the abstract describes as resistant to most defenses designed for digital trigger patterns.
summary.tldr: The paper finds existing images with useful object co-occurrences and turns selected, relabeled subsets into datasets for physical-backdoor research.

title: Finding Naturally Occurring Physical Backdoors in Image Datasets

abstract: Glass surfaces are omnipresent in our daily lives and often go unnoticed by the majority of us. While humans are generally able to infer their locations and thus avoid collisions, it can be difficult for current object detection systems to handle them due to the transparent nature of glass surfaces. Previous methods approached the problem by extracting global context information to obtain priors such as object boundaries and reflections. However, their performances cannot be guaranteed when these deterministic features are not available. We observe that humans often reason through the semantic context of the environment, which offers insights into the categories of and proximity between entities that are expected to appear in the surrounding. For example, the odds of co-occurrence of glass windows with walls and curtains are generally higher than that with other objects such as cars and trees, which have relatively less semantic relevance. Based on this observation, we propose a model ('GlassSemNet') that integrates the contextual relationship of the scenes for glass surface detection with two novel modules: (1) Scene Aware Activation (SAA) Module to adaptively filter critical channels with respect to spatial and semantic features, and (2) Context Correlation Attention (CCA) Module to progressively learn the contextual correlations among objects both spatially and semantically. In addition, we propose a large-scale glass surface detection dataset named {\it Glass Surface Detection - Semantics} ('GSD-S'), which contains 4,519 real-world RGB glass surface images from diverse real-world scenes with detailed annotations for both glass surface detection and semantic segmentation. Experimental results show that our model outperforms contemporary works, especially with 42.6\% MAE improvement on our proposed GSD-S dataset. Code, dataset, and models are available at https://jiaying.link/neurips2022-gsds/

abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer, a sparsely-activated model controlled by a router, has achieved great success in deep learning. However, the understanding of such architecture remains elusive. In this paper, we formally study how the MoE layer improves the performance of neural network learning and why the mixture model will not collapse into a single model. Our empirical results suggest that the cluster structure of the underlying problem and the non-linearity of the expert are pivotal to the success of MoE. This motivates us to consider a challenging classification problem with intrinsic cluster structures. Theoretically, we proved that this problem is hard to solve by a single expert such as a two-layer convolutional neural network (CNN). Yet with the MoE layer with each expert being a two-layer CNN, the problem can be solved successfully. In particular, our theory shows that the router can learn the cluster-center features, which helps divide the input complex problem into simpler classification sub-problems that individual experts can conquer. To our knowledge, this is the first theoretical result toward formally understanding the mechanism of the MoE layer for deep learning.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts layer uses a router to activate selected expert networks for an input. This paper investigates why that architecture can improve learning and why its experts need not collapse into one effective model. Empirical observations point to two important ingredients: clusters in the underlying problem and nonlinear expert networks.

Motivated by those observations, the authors construct a challenging classification problem with intrinsic cluster structure. They prove that a single expert, such as a two-layer convolutional network, has difficulty solving it. A mixture whose experts are themselves two-layer convolutional networks can solve the problem successfully.

The analysis explains how this advantage arises: the router can learn features representing cluster centers and use them to divide the overall problem into simpler classification subproblems. Individual experts can then handle those subproblems. This provides a theoretical mechanism for useful specialization in the studied setting. The result helps explain how routing and expert nonlinearity can cooperate, with the formal claim tied to the structured classification problem analyzed.
summary.tldr: For a structured classification problem, the paper proves that learned routing lets multiple nonlinear experts solve tasks that challenge a single expert.

title: Towards Understanding the Mixture-of-Experts Layer in Deep Learning

abstract: We study the linear contextual bandit problem where an agent has to select one candidate from a pool and each candidate belongs to a sensitive group. In this setting, candidates' rewards may not be directly comparable between groups, for example when the agent is an employer hiring candidates from different ethnic groups and some groups have a lower reward due to discriminatory bias and/or social injustice. We propose a notion of fairness that states that the agent's policy is fair when it selects a candidate with highest relative rank, which measures how good the reward is when compared to candidates from the same group. This is a very strong notion of fairness, since the relative rank is not directly observed by the agent and depends on the underlying reward model and on the distribution of rewards. Thus we study the problem of learning a policy which approximates a fair policy under the condition that the contexts are independent between groups and the distribution of rewards of each group is absolutely continuous. In particular, we design a greedy policy which at each round constructs a ridge regression estimate from the observed context-reward pairs, and then computes an estimate of the relative rank of each candidate using the empirical cumulative distribution function. We prove that, despite its simplicity and the lack of an initial exploration phase, the greedy policy achieves, up to log factors and with high probability, a fair pseudo-regret of order $\sqrt{dT}$ after $T$ rounds, where $d$ is the dimension of the context vectors. The policy also satisfies demographic parity at each round when averaged over all possible information available before the selection. Finally, we use simulated settings and experiments on the US census data to show that our policy achieves sub-linear fair pseudo-regret also in practice.

paragraphs: This paper considers sequential selection from candidates belonging to sensitive groups, where rewards may not be directly comparable across groups. Its fairness criterion selects the candidate with the highest relative standing within their own group. The motivation is that raw reward differences can reflect discrimination or social injustice rather than comparable merit.

Relative standing is not directly observed, so the algorithm must estimate both rewards and their group-specific distributions. The proposed greedy policy fits ridge regression to observed context-reward pairs and uses empirical cumulative distributions to estimate each candidate's rank. The analysis assumes that contexts are independent between groups and that each group's reward distribution is absolutely continuous.

Under these conditions, the policy achieves fair pseudo-regret of order square root of dT, up to logarithmic factors, with high probability, despite having no initial exploration phase. It also satisfies demographic parity each round when averaged over all possible prior information. Simulations and US census experiments show sublinear fair pseudo-regret in practice, supporting the possibility of learning this relative-rank criterion while making sequential decisions.
summary.tldr: A greedy contextual bandit policy learns to select candidates by within-group reward rank, with conditional fairness and regret guarantees.

title: Group Meritocratic Fairness in Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: Spiking neural network (SNN) has been viewed as a potential candidate for the next generation of artificial intelligence with appealing characteristics such as sparse computation and inherent temporal dynamics. By adopting architectures of deep artificial neural networks (ANNs), SNNs are achieving competitive performances in benchmark tasks such as image classification. However, successful architectures of ANNs are not necessary ideal for SNN and when tasks become more diverse effective architectural variations could be critical. To this end, we develop a spike-based differentiable hierarchical search (SpikeDHS) framework, where spike-based computation is realized on both the cell and the layer level search space. Based on this framework, we find effective SNN architectures under limited computation cost. During the training of SNN, a suboptimal surrogate gradient function could lead to poor approximations of true gradients, making the network enter certain local minima. To address this problem, we extend the differential approach to surrogate gradient search where the SG function is efficiently optimized locally. Our models achieve state-of-the-art performances on classification of CIFAR10/100 and ImageNet with accuracy of 95.50%, 76.25% and 68.64%. On event-based deep stereo, our method finds optimal layer variation and surpasses the accuracy of specially designed ANNs meanwhile with 26$\times$ lower energy cost ($6.7\mathrm{mJ}$), demonstrating the advantage of SNN in processing highly sparse and dynamic signals. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/Huawei-BIC/SpikeDHS}.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation and temporal dynamics, but architectures borrowed from conventional neural networks may not suit them well. This paper introduces SpikeDHS to search for architectures using spike-based computation at both the cell and layer levels. The aim is to find effective designs within limited computational cost as tasks demand different structures.

The method also searches for surrogate gradient functions used during training. A poorly chosen surrogate can approximate the true gradient badly and steer optimization into certain local minima. The resulting models report state-of-the-art classification performance on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, with accuracies of 95.50%, 76.25%, and 68.64%. On event-based deep stereo, the searched model surpasses specially designed conventional networks in accuracy while using 26 times less energy, at 6.7 mJ. These findings support the usefulness of adapting spiking architectures and training functions, particularly for sparse, dynamic inputs.
summary.tldr: SpikeDHS searches spiking-network architectures and surrogate gradients, reporting strong classification results and energy-efficient event-based stereo.

title: Differentiable hierarchical and surrogate gradient search for spiking neural networks

abstract: Large pretrained models can be fine-tuned with differential privacy to achieve performance approaching that of non-private models. A common theme in these results is the surprising observation that high-dimensional models can achieve favorable privacy-utility trade-offs. This seemingly contradicts known results on the model-size dependence of differentially private convex learning and raises the following research question: When does the performance of differentially private learning not degrade with increasing model size? We identify that the magnitudes of gradients projected onto subspaces is a key factor that determines performance. To precisely characterize this for private convex learning, we introduce a condition on the objective that we term restricted Lipschitz continuity and derive improved bounds for the excess empirical and population risks that are dimension- independent under additional conditions. We empirically show that in private fine-tuning of large language models, gradients obtained during fine-tuning are mostly controlled by a few principal components. This behavior is similar to conditions under which we obtain dimension-independent bounds in convex settings. Our theoretical and empirical results together provide a possible explanation for the recent success of large-scale private fine-tuning. Code to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/lxuechen/private-transformers/tree/main/examples/classification/spectral_analysis.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models can sometimes be fine-tuned privately with performance close to non-private models, despite theoretical concerns about growing model size. This paper investigates when high dimensionality need not worsen the privacy–utility tradeoff. Its focus is the size of gradients after projection onto different subspaces.

For convex learning, the authors introduce restricted Lipschitz continuity to describe the relevant structure of the objective. They derive improved bounds on excess empirical and population risk that become independent of dimension under additional conditions. The result identifies circumstances in which parameter count alone does not determine the theoretical cost of private learning.

These gradients are mostly controlled by a few principal components, resembling the structure associated with the convex theory’s dimension-independent guarantees. This provides a possible explanation for successful large-scale private fine-tuning. The connection is suggestive rather than a proof that the convex guarantees directly apply to language-model training.
summary.tldr: Structured gradients can yield dimension-independent private-learning bounds under conditions and may help explain successful private language-model fine-tuning.

title: When Does Differentially Private Learning Not Suffer in High Dimensions?

abstract: We give a simple, generic conformal prediction method for sequential prediction that achieves target empirical coverage guarantees on adversarial data. It is computationally lightweight --- comparable to split conformal prediction --- but does not require having a held-out validation set, and so all data can be used for training models from which to derive a conformal score. Furthermore, it gives stronger than marginal coverage guarantees in two ways. First, it gives threshold-calibrated prediction sets that have correct empirical coverage even conditional on the threshold used to form the prediction set from the conformal score. Second, the user can specify an arbitrary collection of subsets of the feature space --- possibly intersecting --- and the coverage guarantees will also hold conditional on membership in each of these subsets. We call our algorithm MVP, short for MultiValid Prediction. We give both theory and an extensive set of empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with a target coverage level. This paper introduces MultiValid Prediction, or MVP, for sequential prediction on adversarial data. Its guarantees concern empirical coverage, allowing the method to address how often prediction sets contain the outcome over the sequence.

MVP strengthens overall marginal coverage in two ways. Coverage also holds conditional on the threshold used to turn a conformal score into a prediction set. In addition, users can specify a collection of feature-space subsets, including overlapping ones, and obtain coverage guarantees conditional on membership in each subset. This addresses distinctions that an overall coverage figure can conceal.

The method is computationally lightweight, with cost comparable to split conformal prediction. It does not require a held-out validation set, so all available data can be used to train the models supplying conformal scores. The paper provides theoretical results and extensive empirical evaluations. Its contribution combines these richer empirical coverage requirements with a practical sequential procedure.
summary.tldr: MVP provides lightweight sequential prediction sets with empirical coverage guarantees across thresholds and specified groups, even on adversarial data.

title: Practical Adversarial Multivalid Conformal Prediction

abstract: Point cloud completion is an active research topic for 3D vision and has been widelystudied in recent years. Instead of directly predicting missing point cloud fromthe partial input, we introduce a Semantic-Prototype Variational Transformer(SPoVT) in this work, which takes both partial point cloud and their semanticlabels as the inputs for semantic point cloud object completion. By observingand attending at geometry and semantic information as input features, our SPoVTwould derive point cloud features and their semantic prototypes for completionpurposes. As a result, our SPoVT not only performs point cloud completion withvarying resolution, it also allows manipulation of different semantic parts of anobject. Experiments on benchmark datasets would quantitatively and qualitativelyverify the effectiveness and practicality of our proposed model.

paragraphs: Point cloud completion reconstructs an object from an incomplete collection of three-dimensional points. This paper introduces SPoVT, a Semantic-Prototype Variational Transformer that uses both the partial geometry and semantic labels attached to the input. Those labels are a stated part of the method's input, giving completion access to information about what the observed points represent.

The model attends to geometric and semantic information to derive point cloud features and semantic prototypes for completion. This ties reconstruction to the semantic organization of the object. The resulting representation supports completing point clouds at varying resolutions and manipulating different semantic parts of an object, making part-level information relevant to both reconstruction and control.

Experiments on benchmark datasets provide quantitative and qualitative evidence for the model's effectiveness and practicality. The stated contribution is therefore broader than predicting missing points alone: it brings semantic information into the completion process and supports operations on meaningful object parts. Its capabilities are presented in the setting where both partial points and their semantic labels are available.
summary.tldr: SPoVT combines partial point clouds with semantic labels to complete objects at varying resolutions and enable semantic-part manipulation.

title: SPoVT: Semantic-Prototype Variational Transformer for Dense Point Cloud Semantic Completion

abstract: In computer vision, models must be able to adapt to changes in image resolution to effectively carry out tasks such as image segmentation; This is known as scale-equivariance. Recent works have made progress in developing scale-equivariant convolutional neural networks, e.g., through weight-sharing and kernel resizing. However, these networks are not truly scale-equivariant in practice. Specifically, they do not consider anti-aliasing as they formulate the down-scaling operation in the continuous domain. To address this shortcoming, we directly formulate down-scaling in the discrete domain with consideration of anti-aliasing. We then propose a novel architecture based on Fourier layers to achieve truly scale-equivariant deep nets, i.e., absolute zero equivariance-error. Following prior works, we test this model on MNIST-scale and STL-10 datasets. Our proposed model achieves competitive classification performance while maintaining zero equivariance-error.

paragraphs: Scale equivariance means a network’s behavior changes consistently when image resolution changes. This paper argues that earlier scale-equivariant convolutional architectures fail to achieve the property exactly in practice. Their formulations describe downscaling in a continuous domain and omit the anti-aliasing considerations needed for discrete images.

The authors formulate downscaling directly in the discrete domain and incorporate anti-aliasing. They then construct a network architecture based on Fourier layers that achieves zero equivariance error under this formulation. The key change is to build the desired consistency around the actual discrete scaling operation, making the treatment of image resampling part of the architecture’s mathematical foundation.

Experiments on MNIST-scale and STL-10 show competitive classification performance while retaining zero equivariance error. These are separate aspects of the result: the model preserves exact scaling consistency and remains competitive at the evaluated predictive task. The paper demonstrates that carefully accounting for discrete downscaling can close the gap between intended scale equivariance and the behavior of an implemented network.
summary.tldr: Fourier-layer networks achieve zero scale-equivariance error by explicitly incorporating anti-aliasing into a discrete downscaling formulation.

title: Truly Scale-Equivariant Deep Nets with Fourier Layers

abstract: We consider alternating gradient descent (AGD) with fixed step size applied to the asymmetric matrix factorization objective. We show that, for a rank-$r$ matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $T = C ( \frac{\sigma_1(A)}{\sigma_r(A)} )^2 \log(1/\epsilon)$ iterations of alternating gradient descent suffice to reach an $\epsilon$-optimal factorization $\| A - X_{T} Y_{T}' \|^2 \leq \epsilon \| A \|^2$ with high probability starting from an atypical random initialization. The factors have rank $d \geq r$ so that $X_{T}\in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$ and $Y_{T} \in\mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, and mild overparameterization suffices for the constant $C$ in the iteration complexity $T$ to be an absolute constant. Experiments suggest that our proposed initialization is not merely of theoretical benefit, but rather significantly improves the convergence rate of gradient descent in practice. Our proof is conceptually simple: a uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality and uniform Lipschitz smoothness constant are guaranteed for a sufficient number of iterations, starting from our random initialization. Our proof method should be useful for extending and simplifying convergence analyses for a broader class of nonconvex low-rank factorization problems.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization represents a matrix as the product of two smaller factors. This paper studies alternating gradient descent, which updates those factors in turn using a fixed step size. Although the objective is nonconvex, the authors establish a high-probability convergence guarantee from a particular, atypical random initialization.

For a matrix of rank r, the factors may have width d at least r. The number of iterations sufficient to reach a specified relative squared reconstruction error scales with the squared ratio of the largest to smallest nonzero singular values, multiplied by the logarithm of inverse accuracy. Mild overparameterization makes the remaining constant absolute. Thus, the guarantee explicitly connects convergence to the matrix's conditioning and the requested precision.

The proof establishes a uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality and a uniform smoothness bound for enough iterations after initialization. Together, these properties support sustained optimization progress. Experiments suggest that the initialization also substantially accelerates gradient descent in practice. The authors further propose that this proof strategy could simplify or extend analyses of other nonconvex low-rank factorization problems.
summary.tldr: A specialized random initialization enables a high-probability convergence guarantee for fixed-step alternating gradient descent in matrix factorization.

title: Convergence of Alternating Gradient Descent for Matrix Factorization

abstract: Topological data analysis (TDA) is an area of data science that focuses on using invariants from algebraic topology to provide multiscale shape descriptors for geometric data sets such as point clouds. One of the most important such descriptors is persistent homology, which encodes the change in shape as a filtration parameter changes; a typical parameter is the feature scale. For many data sets, it is useful to simultaneously vary multiple filtration parameters, for example feature scale and density. While the theoretical properties of single parameter persistent homology are well understood, less is known about the multiparameter case. A central question is the problem of representing multiparameter persistent homology by elements of a vector space for integration with standard machine learning algorithms. Existing approaches to this problem either ignore most of the multiparameter information to reduce to the one-parameter case or are heuristic and potentially unstable in the face of noise. In this article, we introduce a new general representation framework that leverages recent results on decompositions of multiparameter persistent homology. This framework is rich in information, fast to compute, and encompasses previous approaches. Moreover, we establish theoretical stability guarantees under this framework as well as efficient algorithms for practical computation, making this framework an applicable and versatile tool for analyzing geometric and point cloud data. We validate our stability results and algorithms with numerical experiments that demonstrate statistical convergence, prediction accuracy, and fast running times on several real data sets.

paragraphs: Topological data analysis describes the shape of data across different scales. Persistent homology tracks how that shape changes as a parameter varies. For some datasets, however, several parameters matter together, such as feature scale and density. The paper addresses how to turn this richer description into vectors that standard machine learning methods can use.

Existing representations can discard much of the information by reducing the problem to one parameter, or rely on heuristics that may react unpredictably to noise. The proposed framework uses mathematical decompositions of multiparameter persistent homology to construct informative representations. It includes previous approaches within a broader framework and provides efficient algorithms for computing the resulting descriptors.

The authors establish theoretical stability guarantees, connecting the representations to a principled treatment of perturbations. Numerical experiments on several real datasets examine statistical convergence, prediction accuracy, and running time. Together, these contributions make the framework useful for bringing multiscale geometric information into machine learning while addressing both computational cost and sensitivity to noise.
summary.tldr: A general framework turns multiparameter topological descriptions into efficiently computed machine learning representations with theoretical stability guarantees.

title: A Framework for Fast and Stable Representations of Multiparameter Persistent Homology Decompositions

abstract: In this paper, we derive norm-based generalization bounds for sparse ReLU neural networks, including convolutional neural networks. These bounds differ from previous ones because they consider the sparse structure of the neural network architecture and the norms of the convolutional filters, rather than the norms of the (Toeplitz) matrices associated with the convolutional layers. Theoretically, we demonstrate that these bounds are significantly tighter than standard norm-based generalization bounds. Empirically, they offer relatively tight estimations of generalization for various simple classification problems. Collectively, these findings suggest that the sparsity of the underlying target function and the model's architecture plays a crucial role in the success of deep learning.

paragraphs: Generalisation bounds aim to relate a model's properties to how well it performs beyond its training examples. This paper develops norm-based bounds for sparse ReLU networks, including convolutional networks. Its central idea is that the network's pattern of connections should enter the analysis, rather than being obscured by a less structured mathematical representation.

For convolutional layers, the authors use the norms of the filters themselves instead of the norms of the associated Toeplitz matrices. This lets the bounds account for sparse architectural structure more directly. They theoretically show that the resulting bounds are significantly tighter than standard norm-based bounds, offering a more informative estimate within this style of analysis.

On several simple classification problems, the bounds also give relatively tight empirical estimates of generalisation. Together, the theoretical and experimental results suggest that sparsity in both the target function and the model architecture helps explain deep learning's success. The empirical evidence is specifically about the simple classification settings evaluated, while the theoretical contribution concerns the improved bounds.
summary.tldr: Generalisation bounds that account for sparse connections and convolutional filter norms are theoretically tighter and empirically informative on simple classification tasks.

title: Norm-based Generalization Bounds for Sparse Neural Networks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in solving various natural language processing tasks due to emergent reasoning abilities. However, LLMs have inherent limitations as they are incapable of accessing up-to-date information (stored on the Web or in task-specific knowledge bases), using external tools, and performing precise mathematical and logical reasoning. In this paper, we present Chameleon, an AI system that mitigates these limitations by augmenting LLMs with plug-and-play modules for compositional reasoning. Chameleon synthesizes programs by composing various tools (e.g., LLMs, off-the-shelf vision models, web search engines, Python functions, and heuristic-based modules) for accomplishing complex reasoning tasks. At the heart of Chameleon is an LLM-based planner that assembles a sequence of tools to execute to generate the final response. We showcase the effectiveness of Chameleon on two multi-modal knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks: ScienceQA and TabMWP. Chameleon, powered by GPT-4, achieves an 86.54% overall accuracy on ScienceQA, improving the best published few-shot result by 11.37%. On TabMWP, GPT-4-powered Chameleon improves the accuracy by 17.0%, lifting the state of the art to 98.78%. Our analysis also shows that the GPT-4-powered planner exhibits more consistent and rational tool selection via inferring potential constraints from instructions, compared to a ChatGPT-powered planner.

Its motivation is that answering some questions requires current external information, visual processing, or precise computation. The system combines language models with tools including vision models, search engines, Python functions, and heuristic modules.

An LLM-based planner assembles these components into a sequence of operations that produces the final response. This approach matters because a complex question can require several kinds of processing that are supplied by different modules.

Their analysis also finds that the GPT-4 planner makes more consistent and rational tool selections than a ChatGPT-powered planner by inferring potential constraints from instructions. The findings support both modular reasoning and the importance of the planner choosing the modules.
summary.tldr: Chameleon uses an LLM planner to compose external tools into reasoning programs, improving results on ScienceQA and TabMWP.

title: Chameleon: Plug-and-Play Compositional Reasoning with Large Language Models

abstract: Deep sparse networks are widely investigated as a neural network architecture for prediction tasks with high-dimensional sparse features, with which feature interaction selection is a critical component. While previous methods primarily focus on how to search feature interaction in a coarse-grained space, less attention has been given to a finer granularity. In this work, we introduce a hybrid-grained feature interaction selection approach that targets both feature field and feature value for deep sparse networks. To explore such expansive space, we propose a decomposed space which is calculated on the fly. We then develop a selection algorithm called OptFeature, which efficiently selects the feature interaction from both the feature field and the feature value simultaneously. Results from experiments on three large real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that OptFeature performs well in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Additional studies support the feasibility of our method. All source code are publicly available\footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OptFeature-Anonymous}.

paragraphs: Prediction problems with many sparse features often depend on interactions between features, making the choice of interactions an important part of deep sparse networks. Previous approaches have mainly searched at a coarse level. This paper asks how interaction selection can also account for finer distinctions within the features.

The proposed approach selects interactions at both the feature-field and feature-value levels. Combining these levels creates a large search space, so the authors introduce a decomposed representation of that space that is calculated as needed. Their OptFeature algorithm uses this construction to select field-level and value-level interactions simultaneously.

The design addresses the practical challenge of exploring finer interactions without losing the ability to search efficiently. Experiments on three large real-world benchmark datasets report good accuracy and efficiency, while additional studies support the method’s feasibility. These findings provide empirical support for hybrid-grained selection: considering both broad feature groupings and individual values can be practical within the evaluated deep sparse networks.
summary.tldr: OptFeature efficiently selects feature interactions at both field and value levels using an on-demand decomposed search space.

title: Towards Hybrid-grained Feature Interaction Selection for Deep Sparse Network

abstract: Simulation of autonomous vehicle systems requires that simulated traffic participants exhibit diverse and realistic behaviors. The use of prerecorded real-world traffic scenarios in simulation ensures realism but the rarity of safety critical events makes large scale collection of driving scenarios expensive. In this paper, we present DJINN -- a diffusion based method of generating traffic scenarios. Our approach jointly diffuses the trajectories of all agents, conditioned on a flexible set of state observations from the past, present, or future. On popular trajectory forecasting datasets, we report state of the art performance on joint trajectory metrics. In addition, we demonstrate how DJINN flexibly enables direct test-time sampling from a variety of valuable conditional distributions including goal-based sampling, behavior-class sampling, and scenario editing.

paragraphs: Testing autonomous vehicles in simulation requires traffic participants whose behavior is both realistic and varied. Recorded driving scenarios provide realism, but collecting enough examples of rare, safety-critical events is expensive. This paper introduces DJINN, a diffusion-based method for generating traffic scenarios, offering a way to produce scenarios beyond a fixed collection of recordings.

DJINN generates the trajectories of all agents jointly. This makes the combined traffic situation the object being modeled, so its output concerns how multiple participants move together. Generation can be conditioned on a flexible collection of state observations drawn from the past, present, or future. That flexibility allows users to specify different kinds of constraints on the scenario.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on joint trajectory metrics using established forecasting datasets. They also demonstrate conditional generation at test time, including sampling toward goals, requesting behavior classes, and editing scenarios. These findings support DJINN as both a joint forecasting method and a flexible tool for constructing traffic simulations.
summary.tldr: DJINN jointly generates traffic participants’ trajectories with diffusion, supporting flexible constraints and scenario editing.

title: A Diffusion-Model of Joint Interactive Navigation

abstract: Weight decay is a standard technique to improve generalization performance in modern deep neural network optimization, and is also widely adopted in federated learning (FL) to prevent overfitting in local clients. In this paper, we first explore the choices of weight decay and identify that weight decay value appreciably influences the convergence of existing FL algorithms. While preventing overfitting is crucial, weight decay can introduce a different optimization goal towards the global objective, which is further amplified in FL due to multiple local updates and heterogeneous data distribution.To address this challenge, we develop {\it Federated optimization with Normalized Annealing Regularization} (FedNAR), a simple yet effective and versatile algorithmic plug-in that can be seamlessly integrated into any existing FL algorithms. Essentially, we regulate the magnitude of each update by performing co-clipping of the gradient and weight decay.We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of FedNAR's convergence rate and conduct extensive experiments on both vision and language datasets with different backbone federated optimization algorithms. Our experimental results consistently demonstrate that incorporating FedNAR into existing FL algorithms leads to accelerated convergence and heightened model accuracy. Moreover, FedNAR exhibits resilience in the face of various hyperparameter configurations. Specifically, FedNAR has the ability to self-adjust the weight decay when the initial specification is not optimal, while the accuracy of traditional FL algorithms would markedly decline. Our codes are released at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fednar-BE8F}{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fednar-BE8F}.

paragraphs: Weight decay helps prevent overfitting, but its value can also substantially affect convergence in federated learning. The paper identifies a tension: regularizing local models can shift optimization away from the global objective. Multiple local updates and differences between clients' data amplify this effect, making weight decay an important part of federated optimization.

FedNAR is a plug-in designed for integration with existing federated learning algorithms. It controls update magnitudes by jointly clipping the gradient and weight decay. This treats the two contributions together when regulating a local update. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the resulting convergence rate.

The method also remains resilient across tested hyperparameter configurations and can adjust weight decay when its initial value is poorly chosen. These findings suggest that controlling regularization within the update process can improve both optimization and tolerance to imperfect parameter choices.
summary.tldr: FedNAR jointly regulates gradients and weight decay to improve federated learning convergence, accuracy, and resilience to imperfect hyperparameter choices.

title: FedNAR: Federated Optimization with Normalized Annealing Regularization

abstract: Vision and Language (VL) models offer an effective method for aligning representation spaces of images and text allowing for numerous applications such as cross-modal retrieval, visual and multi-hop question answering, captioning, and many more. However, the aligned image-text spaces learned by all the popular VL models are still suffering from the so-called 'object bias' - their representations behave as 'bags of nouns' mostly ignoring or downsizing the attributes, relations, and states of objects described/appearing in texts/images. Although some great attempts at fixing these `compositional reasoning' issues were proposed in the recent literature, the problem is still far from being solved. In this paper, we uncover two factors limiting the VL models' compositional reasoning performance. These two factors are properties of the paired VL dataset used for finetuning (or pre-training) the VL model: (i) the caption quality, or in other words 'image-alignment', of the texts; and (ii) the 'density' of the captions in the sense of mentioning all the details appearing on the image. We propose a fine-tuning approach for automatically treating these factors on a standard collection of paired VL data (CC3M). Applied to CLIP, we demonstrate its significant compositional reasoning performance increase of up to $\sim27$\% over the base model, up to $\sim20$\% over the strongest baseline, and by $6.7$\% on average. Our code is provided in the Supplementary and would be released upon acceptance.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can align images with text while paying too little attention to attributes, relations, and object states. The paper describes this as an object bias: representations emphasize which objects appear but underrepresent how those objects are described or related. This weakens compositional reasoning even when image-text matching is useful for many other tasks.

The authors identify two properties of paired training data that limit this reasoning. Captions need to match the image accurately, which they call alignment, and mention its details comprehensively, which they call density. They propose an automatic fine-tuning approach that addresses both properties using the CC3M collection, then apply it to CLIP. The approach makes caption content a direct target for improving learned representations.

The reported compositional-reasoning gains reach approximately 27% over the base model and approximately 20% over the strongest baseline, with a reported average improvement of 6.7%. The largest gains are therefore not presented as uniform improvements across every evaluation. The results support the role of detailed, image-aligned captions in improving how models represent more than object identity.
summary.tldr: Automatically improving caption detail and image alignment strengthens CLIP's compositional reasoning, with gains varying across evaluations.

title: Dense and Aligned Captions (DAC) Promote Compositional Reasoning in VL Models

abstract: Some of the most successful knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models for link prediction – CP, RESCAL, TuckER, ComplEx – can be interpreted as energy-based models. Under this perspective they are not amenable for exact maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE), sampling and struggle to integrate logical constraints. This work re-interprets the score functions of these KGEs as circuits – constrained computational graphs allowing efficient marginalisation. Then, we design two recipes to obtain efficient generative circuit models by either restricting their activations to be non-negative or squaring their outputs. Our interpretation comes with little or no loss of performance for link prediction, while the circuits framework unlocks exact learning by MLE, efficient sampling of new triples, and guarantee that logical constraints are satisfied by design. Furthermore, our models scale more gracefully than the original KGEs on graphs with millions of entities.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embedding models assign scores to possible relationships between entities, making them useful for predicting missing links. This paper examines CP, RESCAL, TuckER, and ComplEx. Interpreting these models as energy-based systems creates difficulties for exact maximum-likelihood learning, sampling new relationships, and enforcing logical constraints.

The authors reinterpret their scoring functions as computational circuits with structural restrictions that permit efficient marginalization. They then provide two ways to construct generative models: constrain activations to be nonnegative or square the circuit outputs. These transformations connect familiar link-prediction models to a framework that supports additional probabilistic operations.

The resulting models support exact maximum-likelihood learning, efficient generation of new triples, and logical constraints that hold by construction. The authors report little or no loss in link-prediction performance and more favorable scaling on graphs containing millions of entities. The contribution is therefore a change in model formulation that expands what knowledge graph embeddings can do while largely preserving their demonstrated predictive usefulness.
summary.tldr: Recasting knowledge graph embeddings as probabilistic circuits enables exact learning, efficient generation, and logical constraints with little or no predictive loss.

title: How to Turn Your Knowledge Graph Embeddings into Generative Models

abstract: In recent years, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) techniques have made significant strides in achieving high asymptotic performance in single task. However, there has been limited exploration of model transferability across tasks. Training a model from scratch for each task can be time-consuming and expensive, especially for large-scale Multi-Agent Systems. Therefore, it is crucial to develop methods for generalizing the model across tasks. Considering that there exist task-independent subtasks across MARL tasks, a model that can decompose such subtasks from the source task could generalize to target tasks. However, ensuring true task-independence of subtasks poses a challenge. In this paper, we propose to \textbf{d}ecompose a \textbf{t}ask in\textbf{to} a series of \textbf{g}eneralizable \textbf{s}ubtasks (DT2GS), a novel framework that addresses this challenge by utilizing a scalable subtask encoder and an adaptive subtask semantic module. We show that these components endow subtasks with two properties critical for task-independence: avoiding overfitting to the source task and maintaining consistent yet scalable semantics across tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that DT2GS possesses sound zero-shot generalization capability across tasks, exhibits sufficient transferability, and outperforms existing methods in both multi-task and single-task problems.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning can achieve strong performance on individual tasks, yet retraining a system for every new task can be costly. This paper explores transferring knowledge through subtasks shared across tasks. The difficulty is making those subtasks genuinely independent of the source task, so that their usefulness survives a change in the overall problem.

DT2GS decomposes a task using a scalable subtask encoder and an adaptive subtask semantic module. The authors show that these components support two properties needed for task independence: avoiding overfitting to the source task and retaining consistent meanings that can scale across tasks. The decomposition is therefore intended to create reusable components with stable interpretations.

Empirical results show zero-shot generalization across tasks and transferability, along with better performance than existing methods on both single-task and multi-task problems. These findings support subtask decomposition as a route to reuse in multi-agent learning. The key idea is to shape both how subtasks are represented and how their meanings carry over, rather than assuming any decomposition will transfer.
summary.tldr: DT2GS learns reusable subtasks with consistent, scalable meanings, improving multi-agent transfer and zero-shot generalization in empirical evaluations.

title: Decompose a Task into Generalizable Subtasks in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Differentially private (stochastic) gradient descent is the workhorse of DP private machine learning in both the convex and non-convex settings. Without privacy constraints, second-order methods, like Newton's method, converge faster than first-order methods like gradient descent. In this work, we investigate the prospect of using the second-order information from the loss function to accelerate DP convex optimization. We first develop a private variant of the regularized cubic Newton method of Nesterov and Polyak, and show that for the class of strongly convex loss functions, our algorithm has quadratic convergence and achieves the optimal excess loss. We then design a practical second-order DP algorithm for the unconstrained logistic regression problem. We theoretically and empirically study the performance of our algorithm. Empirical results show our algorithm consistently achieves the best excess loss compared to other baselines and is 10-40x faster than DP-GD/DP-SGD for challenging datasets.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning commonly relies on gradient descent, which uses first-order information about a loss function. Second-order methods also use information about its curvature and can converge faster without privacy constraints. This paper investigates whether those advantages can be retained when the optimization procedure must provide differential privacy.

The theoretical contribution is a private version of a regularized cubic Newton method. For strongly convex loss functions, the authors establish quadratic convergence and optimal excess loss. These guarantees are tied to that stated function class, giving a specific setting in which second-order information can accelerate private optimization while retaining a strong accuracy guarantee.

The authors also design a practical second-order private algorithm for unconstrained logistic regression and analyze it theoretically and empirically. In their experiments, it consistently achieves the best excess loss among the compared baselines and runs 10–40 times faster than private gradient-descent methods on challenging datasets. The work connects a formal result for strongly convex objectives with evidence of substantial practical gains in logistic regression.
summary.tldr: Private second-order optimization achieves strong guarantees for strongly convex losses and substantial reported speedups for unconstrained logistic regression.

title: Faster Differentially Private Convex Optimization via Second-Order Methods

abstract: With the rapid development of multimedia technology, audio-visual learning has emerged as a promising research topic within the field of multimodal analysis. In this paper, we explore parameter-efficient transfer learning for audio-visual learning and propose the Audio-Visual Mixture of Experts (\ourmethodname) to inject adapters into pre-trained models flexibly. Specifically, we introduce unimodal and cross-modal adapters as multiple experts to specialize in intra-modal and inter-modal information, respectively, and employ a lightweight router to dynamically allocate the weights of each expert according to the specific demands of each task. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed approach \ourmethodname achieves superior performance across multiple audio-visual tasks, including AVE, AVVP, AVS, and AVQA. Furthermore, visual-only experimental results also indicate that our approach can tackle challenging scenes where modality information is missing.The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/yingchengy/AVMOE}.

paragraphs: Audio-visual tasks need information from sound, images, and the relationships between them, but those needs can vary by task. This paper studies parameter-efficient transfer learning: adapting pretrained models through added components. Its Audio-Visual Mixture of Experts provides multiple kinds of adapters and lets the model adjust their contributions.

Unimodal adapters specialize in information within an individual modality, while cross-modal adapters specialize in interactions between modalities. A lightweight router dynamically assigns weights to these experts according to the task’s demands. This provides a flexible mechanism for combining within-modality processing and cross-modal integration rather than using one fixed combination for every task.

Experiments report superior performance across the audio-visual tasks AVE, AVVP, AVS, and AVQA. Visual-only experiments also indicate that the approach can handle challenging situations in which modality information is missing. The findings support the use of specialized adapters with dynamic weighting across several tasks. The missing-modality evidence specifically comes from visual-only evaluations, rather than establishing equivalent behavior for every possible pattern of absent inputs.
summary.tldr: Dynamically weighted unimodal and cross-modal adapters improve parameter-efficient transfer across several audio-visual tasks.

title: Mixtures of Experts for Audio-Visual Learning

abstract: Backdoor attacks aim to inject a backdoor into a classifier such that it predicts any input with an attacker-chosen backdoor trigger as an attacker-chosen target class. Existing backdoor attacks require either retraining the classifier with some clean data or modifying the model's architecture.As a result, they are 1) not applicable when clean data is unavailable, 2) less efficient when the model is large, and 3) less stealthy due to architecture changes. In this work, we propose DFBA, a novel retraining-free and data-free backdoor attack without changing the model architecture. Technically, our proposed method modifies a few parameters of a classifier to inject a backdoor. Through theoretical analysis, we verify that our injected backdoor is provably undetectable and unremovable by various state-of-the-art defenses under mild assumptions. Our evaluation on multiple datasets further demonstrates that our injected backdoor: 1) incurs negligible classification loss, 2) achieves 100\% attack success rates, and 3) bypasses six existing state-of-the-art defenses. Moreover, our comparison with a state-of-the-art non-data-free backdoor attack shows our attack is more stealthy and effective against various defenses while achieving less classification accuracy loss.We will release our code upon paper acceptance.
originalAbstract: Backdoor attacks aim to inject a backdoor into a classifier such that it predicts any input with an attacker-chosen backdoor trigger as an attacker-chosen target class. Existing backdoor attacks require either retraining the classifier with some clean data or modifying the model's architecture.As a result, they are 1) not applicable when clean data is unavailable, 2) less efficient when the model is large, and 3) less stealthy due to architecture changes. In this work, we propose DFBA, a novel retraining-free and data-free backdoor attack without changing the model architecture. Technically, our proposed method modifies a few parameters of a classifier to inject a backdoor. Through theoretical analysis, we verify that our injected backdoor is provably undetectable and unremovable by various state-of-the-art defenses under mild assumptions. Our evaluation on multiple datasets further demonstrates that our injected backdoor: 1) incurs negligible classification loss, 2) achieves 100\% attack success rates, and 3) bypasses six existing state-of-the-art defenses. Moreover, our comparison with a state-of-the-art non-data-free backdoor attack shows our attack is more stealthy and effective against various defenses while achieving less classification accuracy loss.We will release our code upon paper acceptance.

paragraphs: A classifier backdoor makes inputs containing a particular trigger receive an attacker-selected label. Existing approaches described in this paper require clean training data for retraining or changes to the model architecture. DFBA investigates whether a backdoor can be introduced without either requirement, reducing the resources and visible structural changes associated with the attack.

The method modifies a small number of classifier parameters while leaving the architecture intact and avoiding retraining. The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under mild assumptions, the inserted backdoor cannot be detected or removed by various defenses considered in their analysis. That guarantee is conditional on those assumptions and concerns the specified defenses.

Across multiple evaluated datasets, the authors report negligible classification loss, a 100% attack success rate, and successful evasion of six existing defenses. A comparison with a non-data-free attack also finds better stealth and effectiveness against defenses, with less classification accuracy loss. The findings expose a vulnerability in which ordinary predictive performance can remain largely intact despite malicious trigger behavior.
summary.tldr: DFBA inserts classifier backdoors through a few parameter changes without training data, retraining, or architecture changes.

title: Data Free Backdoor Attacks

abstract: This paper considers the distributed convex-concave minimax optimization under the second-order similarity.We propose stochastic variance-reduced optimistic gradient sliding (SVOGS) method, which takes the advantage of the finite-sum structure in the objective by involving the mini-batch client sampling and variance reduction.We prove SVOGS can achieve the $\varepsilon$-duality gap within communication rounds of ${\mathcal O}(\delta D^2/\varepsilon)$, communication complexity of ${\mathcal O}(n+\sqrt{n}\delta D^2/\varepsilon)$,and local gradient calls of $\tilde{\mathcal O}(n+(\sqrt{n}\delta+L)D^2/\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))$, where $n$ is the number of nodes, $\delta$ is the degree of the second-order similarity, $L$ is the smoothness parameter and $D$ is the diameter of the constraint set.We can verify that all of above complexity (nearly) matches the corresponding lower bounds.For the specific $\mu$-strongly-convex-$\mu$-strongly-convex case, our algorithm has the upper bounds on communication rounds, communication complexity, and local gradient calls of $\mathcal O(\delta/\mu\log(1/\varepsilon))$, ${\mathcal O}((n+\sqrt{n}\delta/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))$, and $\tilde{\mathcal O}(n+(\sqrt{n}\delta+L)/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ respectively, which are also nearly tight.Furthermore, we conduct the numerical experiments to show the empirical advantages of proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper studies distributed convex-concave minimax optimization when objectives across nodes satisfy a second-order similarity condition. The challenge involves several costs at once: synchronization rounds, total communication, and local gradient computations. Its proposed method, SVOGS, uses the objective’s finite-sum structure to improve these costs together.

SVOGS combines optimistic gradient sliding with variance reduction and mini-batch client sampling. For an epsilon duality gap, the authors prove a communication-round bound of O(delta D²/epsilon) and total communication of O(n + √n delta D²/epsilon). Here, n counts nodes, delta measures second-order similarity, and D is the constraint-set diameter. The local gradient bound additionally depends on the smoothness parameter.

The reported bounds match or nearly match corresponding lower bounds, making the theoretical efficiency claim specific to this problem setting. The authors also derive nearly tight bounds for a stronger special case involving a parameter mu, with logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy in communication rounds. Numerical experiments support empirical advantages, complementing the analysis of communication and computation.
summary.tldr: SVOGS exploits second-order similarity, client sampling, and variance reduction to achieve nearly optimal distributed minimax communication and computation bounds.

title: Near-Optimal Distributed Minimax Optimization under the Second-Order Similarity

abstract: Trustworthiness of generative language models (GLMs) is crucial in their deployment to critical decision making systems. Hence, certified risk control methods such as selective prediction and conformal prediction have been applied to mitigating the hallucination problem in various supervised downstream tasks. However, the lack of appropriate correctness metric hinders applying such principled methods to language generation tasks. In this paper, we circumvent this problem by leveraging the concept of textual entailment to evaluate the correctness of the generated sequence, and propose two selective generation algorithms which control the false discovery rate with respect to the textual entailment relation (FDR-E) with a theoretical guarantee: $\texttt{SGen}^{\texttt{Sup}}$ and $\texttt{SGen}^{\texttt{Semi}}$. $\texttt{SGen}^{\texttt{Sup}}$, a direct modification of the selective prediction, is a supervised learning algorithm which exploits entailment-labeled data, annotated by humans. Since human annotation is costly, we further propose a semi-supervised version, $\texttt{SGen}^{\texttt{Semi}}$, which fully utilizes the unlabeled data by pseudo-labeling, leveraging an entailment set function learned via conformal prediction. Furthermore, $\texttt{SGen}^{\texttt{Semi}}$ enables to use more general class of selection functions, neuro-selection functions, and provides users with an optimal selection function class given multiple candidates. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of the $\texttt{SGen}$ family in achieving a desired FDR-E level with comparable selection efficiency to those from baselines on both open and closed source GLMs. Code and datasets are provided at https://github.com/ml-postech/selective-generation.

paragraphs: Applying statistical risk control to generated language requires a usable definition of correctness. This paper uses textual entailment, judging correctness through whether the relevant text supports a generated sequence. It proposes two selective generation algorithms with theoretical control of the false discovery rate defined relative to that entailment relation, called FDR-E.

The supervised algorithm, SGenSup, learns from human-annotated entailment labels. To reduce dependence on costly annotation, SGenSemi also uses unlabeled data with pseudo-labels produced through an entailment set function learned using conformal prediction. The semi-supervised method further supports a broader family of neural selection functions and selection of an optimal function class among supplied candidates.

Experiments on both open-source and closed-source generative language models show that the methods achieve desired FDR-E levels with selection efficiency comparable to baselines. This supports controlled selection of generated outputs while retaining a useful amount of output. The guarantee is specifically about errors measured through textual entailment, which is the paper’s chosen basis for making generation risk mathematically controllable.
summary.tldr: Two selective generation methods provide theoretical false-discovery control measured through textual entailment, with supervised and semi-supervised training options.

title: Selective Generation for Controllable Language Models

abstract: Biological motion perception (BMP) refers to humans' ability to perceive and recognize the actions of living beings solely from their motion patterns, sometimes as minimal as those depicted on point-light displays. While humans excel at these tasks \textit{without any prior training}, current AI models struggle with poor generalization performance. To close this research gap, we propose the Motion Perceiver (MP). MP solely relies on patch-level optical flows from video clips as inputs. During training, it learns prototypical flow snapshots through a competitive binding mechanism and integrates invariant motion representations to predict action labels for the given video. During inference, we evaluate the generalization ability of all AI models and humans on 62,656 video stimuli spanning 24 BMP conditions using point-light displays in neuroscience. Remarkably, MP outperforms all existing AI models with a maximum improvement of 29\% in top-1 action recognition accuracy on these conditions. Moreover, we benchmark all AI models in point-light displays of two standard video datasets in computer vision. MP also demonstrates superior performance in these cases. More interestingly, via psychophysics experiments, we found that MP recognizes biological movements in a way that aligns with human behaviors. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/ZhangLab-DeepNeuroCogLab/MotionPerceiver.

paragraphs: People can recognize actions from very sparse motion cues, including point-light displays. The paper studies why this kind of biological motion perception remains difficult for AI models to generalize to. Its proposed Motion Perceiver uses only optical flow from local video patches, making motion patterns the input from which it predicts actions.

During training, the model learns representative flow snapshots through a competitive binding mechanism. It then integrates invariant motion representations to classify the action in a video. The authors evaluate generalization using 62,656 video stimuli across 24 biological-motion conditions, drawing on point-light displays used in neuroscience and comparisons with human observers.

Motion Perceiver outperforms the other AI models evaluated on these conditions, with a maximum reported improvement of 29% in top-1 action recognition accuracy. It also performs better on point-light versions of two standard video datasets. Psychophysics experiments reveal behavior aligned with human recognition of biological movement. These findings support the proposed motion representation as a route toward better generalization under sparse visual cues.
summary.tldr: Motion Perceiver learns from local optical flow to improve action recognition in point-light displays and exhibits recognition behavior aligned with humans.

title: Flow Snapshot Neurons in Action: Deep Neural Networks Generalize to Biological Motion Perception

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on web-scale datasets raise substantial concerns regarding permissible data usage. One major question is whether these models "memorize" all their training data or they integrate many data sources in some way more akin to how a human would learn and synthesize information. The answer hinges, to a large degree, on \emph{how we define memorization.} In this work, we propose the Adversarial Compression Ratio (ACR) as a metric for assessing memorization in LLMs. A given string from the training data is considered memorized if it can be elicited by a prompt (much) shorter than the string itself---in other words, if these strings can be ``compressed'' with the model by computing adversarial prompts of fewer tokens. The ACR overcomes the limitations of existing notions of memorization by (i) offering an adversarial view of measuring memorization, especially for monitoring unlearning and compliance; and (ii) allowing for the flexibility to measure memorization for arbitrary strings at a reasonably low compute. Our definition serves as a practical tool for determining when model owners may be violating terms around data usage, providing a potential legal tool and a critical lens through which to address such scenarios.
