paragraphs: Whether a language model has memorized training text depends partly on what counts as memorization. This paper proposes measuring it through adversarial compression: asking whether a short prompt can make the model produce a much longer target string. Under this definition, the model helps compress the string when the eliciting prompt requires substantially fewer tokens.

The proposed Adversarial Compression Ratio turns that relationship into a metric. It uses adversarially constructed prompts to assess how compactly a target can be elicited, giving memorization an operational meaning based on model behavior. The authors describe the approach as flexible enough to assess arbitrary strings at reasonably low computational cost.

This perspective is intended to support monitoring unlearning and compliance with data-use requirements. It shifts the assessment toward how much prompting is needed to recover specific text, rather than leaving memorization as an informal claim about the model’s training. The authors also present it as a potential legal tool for identifying problematic data use. That proposed application is a possible use of the definition, rather than a determination that any particular model violates legal obligations.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Compression Ratio measures memorization by how much shorter an eliciting prompt can be than the text a language model reproduces.

title: Rethinking LLM Memorization through the Lens of Adversarial Compression

abstract: Existing perception models achieve great success by learning from large amounts of labeled data, but they still struggle with open-world scenarios. To alleviate this issue, researchers introduce open-set perception tasks to detect or segment unseen objects in the training set. However, these models require predefined object categories as inputs during inference, which are not available in real-world scenarios. Recently, researchers pose a new and more practical problem, i.e., open-ended object detection, which discovers unseen objects without any object categories as inputs. In this paper, we present VL-SAM, a training-free framework that combines the generalized object recognition model (i.e., Vision-Language Model) with the generalized object localization model (i.e., Segment-Anything Model), to address the open-ended object detection and segmentation task. Without additional training, we connect these two generalized models with attention maps as the prompts. Specifically, we design an attention map generation module by employing head aggregation and a regularized attention flow to aggregate and propagate attention maps across all heads and layers in VLM, yielding high-quality attention maps. Then, we iteratively sample positive and negative points from the attention maps with a prompt generation module and send the sampled points to SAM to segment corresponding objects. Experimental results on the long-tail instance segmentation dataset (LVIS) show that our method surpasses the previous open-ended method on the object detection task and can provide additional instance segmentation masks. Besides, VL-SAM achieves favorable performance on the corner case object detection dataset (CODA), demonstrating the effectiveness of VL-SAM in real-world applications. Moreover, VL-SAM exhibits good model generalization that can incorporate various VLMs and SAMs.

paragraphs: Open-ended object detection asks a system to discover objects without being given a list of categories at inference time. VL-SAM addresses this task by combining a vision-language model's recognition capabilities with the Segment Anything Model's localization capabilities. The framework connects these existing models without additional training and also produces object segmentation masks.

The connection uses attention maps as an intermediate signal. First, a module aggregates attention across the vision-language model's heads and propagates it across layers using regularized attention flow. A second module repeatedly selects positive and negative points from the resulting maps. These points become prompts that guide SAM toward the corresponding objects.

On LVIS, the method surpasses the previous open-ended approach in object detection while additionally providing instance masks. It also performs favorably on CODA, which tests difficult object-detection cases, and can incorporate different vision-language models and SAM variants. The findings support attention as a practical bridge between recognition and segmentation. Here, training-free refers to the combination requiring no further training, while the framework draws on capabilities already present in its component models.
summary.tldr: VL-SAM turns vision-language attention into segmentation prompts to detect and segment objects without category lists or additional training.

title: Training-Free Open-Ended Object Detection and Segmentation via Attention as Prompts

abstract: We study a class of optimization problems motivated by automating the design and update of AI systems like coding assistants, robots, and copilots. AutoDiff frameworks, like PyTorch, enable efficient end-to-end optimization of differentiable systems. However, general computational workflows can be non-differentiable and involve rich feedback (e.g. console output or user’s responses), heterogeneous parameters (e.g. prompts, codes), and intricate objectives (beyond maximizing a score). We investigate end-to-end generative optimization – using generative models such as LLMs within the optimizer for automatic updating of general computational workflows. We discover that workflow execution traces are akin to back-propagated gradients in AutoDiff and can provide key information to interpret feedback for efficient optimization. Formally, we frame a new mathematical setup, Optimization with Trace Oracle (OPTO). In OPTO, an optimizer receives an execution trace along with feedback on the computed output and updates parameters iteratively. We provide a Python library, Trace, that efficiently converts a workflow optimization problem into an OPTO instance using PyTorch-like syntax. Using Trace, we develop a general LLM-based generative optimizer called OptoPrime. In empirical studies, we find that OptoPrime is capable of first-order numerical optimization, prompt optimization, hyper-parameter tuning, robot controller design, code debugging, etc., and is often competitive with specialized optimizers for each domain. We envision Trace as an open research platform for devising novel generative optimizers and developing the next generation of interactive learning agents. Website: https://microsoft.github.io/Trace/.

paragraphs: AI workflows can contain prompts, code, and other components that cannot be optimized through ordinary differentiation. Their feedback may also consist of console messages or user responses instead of a single numerical score. This paper studies how generative models can iteratively update such workflows using both feedback and information about their execution.

The authors formalize Optimization with Trace Oracle, where an optimizer receives an execution trace alongside feedback on the output. The trace helps relate that feedback to the computations and parameters that produced the result. Their Python library, Trace, expresses workflow optimization in this form using PyTorch-like syntax. They then build OptoPrime, a general optimizer that uses a language model to propose updates.

Experiments demonstrate applications including numerical optimization, prompt improvement, hyperparameter tuning, robot-controller design, and code debugging. OptoPrime is often competitive with specialized optimizers in these domains. The central contribution is the use of execution traces as structured optimization information, playing a role analogous to gradients without requiring the workflow itself to be differentiable.
summary.tldr: Trace uses workflow execution records and rich feedback to support language-model-driven optimization of diverse computational systems.

title: Trace is the Next AutoDiff: Generative Optimization with Rich Feedback, Execution Traces, and LLMs

abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have shown impressive capabilities as a general-purpose interface for various visual and linguistic tasks. However, building a unified MLLM for multi-task learning in the medical field remains a thorny challenge. To mitigate the tug-of-war problem of multi-modal multi-task optimization in MLLMs, recent advances primarily focus on improving the LLM components, while neglecting the connector that bridges the gap between modalities. In this paper, we introduce Uni-Med, a novel medical generalist foundation model which consists of a universal visual feature extraction module, a connector mixture-of-experts (CMoE) module, and an LLM. Benefiting from the proposed CMoE that leverages a well-designed router with a mixture of projection experts at the connector, Uni-Med achieves efficient solution to the tug-of-war problem and can perform six different medical tasks including question answering, visual question answering, report generation, referring expression comprehension, referring expression generation and image classification. To the best of our knowledge, Uni-Med is the first effort to tackle multi-task interference at the connector in MLLMs. Extensive ablation experiments validate the effectiveness of introducing CMoE under any configuration, with up to an average 8% performance gains. We further provide interpretation analysis of the tug-of-war problem from the perspective of gradient optimization and parameter statistics. Compared to previous state-of-the-art medical MLLMs, Uni-Med achieves competitive or superior evaluation metrics on diverse tasks. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/MSIIP/Uni-Med.

paragraphs: A medical multimodal model must coordinate several tasks whose training objectives can interfere with one another. Uni-Med addresses this interference in the connector that transfers visual information to the language model. Its architecture combines a universal visual feature extractor, a connector mixture of experts, and a large language model.

The connector uses a router and multiple projection experts to manage the visual-to-language mapping. This gives the model a way to handle competing task demands at the point where modalities meet. The model supports medical question answering, visual question answering, report generation, referring-expression comprehension and generation, and image classification.

Ablation experiments support the connector's effectiveness across the tested configurations, with reported average performance gains reaching 8%. The authors also analyze task interference through gradients and parameter statistics. Comparisons show competitive or superior metrics against previous medical multimodal models across diverse tasks. These findings identify the connector as a useful place to address multitask interference within a unified medical model.
summary.tldr: Uni-Med uses a mixture of experts in its visual-language connector to reduce interference across six medical tasks.

title: Uni-Med: A Unified Medical Generalist Foundation Model For Multi-Task Learning Via Connector-MoE

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited impressive performance in language comprehension and various reasoning tasks. However, their abilities in spatial reasoning, a crucial aspect of human cognition, remain relatively unexplored. Human possess a remarkable ability to create mental images of unseen objects and actions through a process known as the Mind's Eye, enabling the imagination of the unseen world. Inspired by this cognitive capacity, we propose Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) prompting. VoT aims to elicit spatial reasoning of LLMs by visualizing their reasoning traces, thereby guiding subsequent reasoning steps. We employed VoT for multi-hop spatial reasoning tasks, including natural language navigation, visual navigation, and visual tiling in 2D grid worlds. Experimental results demonstrated that VoT significantly enhances the spatial reasoning abilities of LLMs. Notably, VoT outperformed existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in these tasks. While VoT works surprisingly well on LLMs, the ability to generate mental images to facilitate spatial reasoning resembles the mind's eye process, suggesting its potential viability in MLLMs. Please find the dataset and codes in our [project page](https://microsoft.github.io/visualization-of-thought).

paragraphs: Visualization-of-Thought is a prompting method intended to improve spatial reasoning in language models. It draws inspiration from the human ability to imagine objects and actions that are not directly visible. The method asks models to visualize their reasoning traces so that these representations can guide later steps in the same problem.

The authors evaluate this approach on tasks requiring several connected spatial reasoning steps in two-dimensional grid worlds. These include navigation described through natural language, visual navigation, and visual tiling. The shared idea is that making intermediate spatial relationships explicit can provide useful context as reasoning proceeds through a sequence of decisions.

Experiments show significant improvements in the language models’ spatial reasoning, and the prompted models outperform existing multimodal language models on the evaluated tasks. The authors suggest that a similar approach may also be viable for multimodal models. The connection to a human mind’s eye serves as an inspiration and analogy for the prompting strategy, while the demonstrated findings concern performance on the grid-world tasks.
summary.tldr: Visualization-of-Thought prompting improves reported spatial reasoning by having language models visualize intermediate reasoning to guide subsequent steps.

title: Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Among approaches for provably safe reinforcement learning, Model Predictive Shielding (MPS) has proven effective at complex tasks in continuous, high-dimensional state spaces, by leveraging a *backup policy* to ensure safety when the learned policy attempts to take risky actions. However, while MPS can ensure safety both during and after training, it often hinders task progress due to the conservative and task-oblivious nature of backup policies.This paper introduces *Dynamic Model Predictive Shielding* (DMPS), which optimizes reinforcement learning objectives while maintaining provable safety. DMPS employs a local planner to dynamically select safe recovery actions that maximize both short-term progress as well as long-term rewards. Crucially, the planner and the neural policy play a synergistic role in DMPS. When planning recovery actions for ensuring safety, the planner utilizes the neural policy to estimate long-term rewards, allowing it to *observe* beyond its short-term planning horizon. Conversely, the neural policy under training learns from the recovery plans proposed by the planner, converging to policies that are both *high-performing* and *safe* in practice.This approach guarantees safety during and after training, with bounded recovery regret that decreases exponentially with planning horizon depth. Experimental results demonstrate that DMPS converges to policies that rarely require shield interventions after training and achieve higher rewards compared to several state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Model Predictive Shielding protects a reinforcement learning agent by using a backup policy when its proposed actions are risky. Experiments find that trained policies rarely need the shield and achieve higher rewards than several state-of-the-art baselines. The theoretical and empirical results address complementary goals: preserving safety guarantees and reducing how much recovery behavior obstructs useful progress.
summary.tldr: DMPS combines local planning and policy learning to choose productive recovery actions while maintaining provable safety.

title: Dynamic Model Predictive Shielding for Provably Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study online classification with general hypothesis classes where the true labels are determined by some function within the class, but are corrupted by *unknown* stochastic noise, and the features are generated adversarially. Predictions are made using observed *noisy* labels and noiseless features, while the performance is measured via minimax risk when comparing against *true* labels. The noisy mechanism is modeled via a general noisy kernel that specifies, for any individual data point, a set of distributions from which the actual noisy label distribution is chosen. We show that minimax risk is *tightly* characterized (up to a logarithmic factor of the hypothesis class size) by the *Hellinger gap* of the noisy label distributions induced by the kernel, *independent* of other properties such as the means and variances of the noise. Our main technique is based on a novel reduction to an online comparison scheme of two hypotheses, along with a new *conditional* version of Le Cam-Birgé testing suitable for online settings. Our work provides the first comprehensive characterization of noisy online classification with guarantees that apply to the *ground truth* while addressing *general* noisy observations.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential classification when observed labels are corrupted by unknown stochastic noise. Crucially, prediction quality is judged against those true labels even though the learner only sees their noisy versions.

The noise model allows a set of possible label distributions for each data point. The authors show that worst-case optimal risk is tightly characterized, up to a logarithmic factor in hypothesis-class size, by the Hellinger gap between the relevant noisy distributions. This gap measures distributional separation, making distinguishability the governing quantity rather than noise means or variances.

The proof reduces the learning problem to online comparisons between two hypotheses and develops a conditional version of Le Cam–Birgé testing suited to sequential observations. The result provides a general characterization within the stated setting, linking what can be learned about ground truth to how clearly competing hypotheses remain distinguishable after label corruption. Its guarantees explicitly concern underlying truth despite the learner’s noisy feedback.
summary.tldr: The Hellinger separation of noisy label distributions characterizes minimax online classification risk up to a logarithmic hypothesis-class factor.

title: Information-theoretic Limits of Online Classification with Noisy Labels

abstract: Semi-structured networks (SSNs) merge the structures familiar from additive models with deep neural networks, allowing the modeling of interpretable partial feature effects while capturing higher-order non-linearities at the same time. A significant challenge in this integration is maintaining the interpretability of the additive model component. Inspired by large-scale biomechanics datasets, this paper explores extending SSNs to functional data. Existing methods in functional data analysis are promising but often not expressive enough to account for all interactions and non-linearities and do not scale well to large datasets. Although the SSN approach presents a compelling potential solution, its adaptation to functional data remains complex. In this work, we propose a functional SSN method that retains the advantageous properties of classical functional regression approaches while also improving scalability. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach accurately recovers underlying signals, enhances predictive performance, and performs favorably compared to competing methods.

paragraphs: Semi-structured networks combine an interpretable additive component with a neural network that captures more complicated relationships. The attraction is that a model can describe individual feature effects while also learning interactions and nonlinear patterns. This paper extends that combination to functional data, where the objects being analyzed have a structured, function-like form.

The work is motivated by large biomechanics datasets. Existing functional analysis methods offer useful modeling properties, but the authors describe limitations in their ability to represent complex interactions and handle large datasets. Simply adding a neural network creates another challenge: the additive component must remain interpretable within the combined model.

The proposed functional semi-structured network aims to retain the useful properties of classical functional regression while improving scalability. Numerical experiments show recovery of underlying signals, stronger predictive performance, and favorable comparisons with competing methods. These findings support combining interpretable functional modeling with neural flexibility, with the reported evidence covering both prediction and recovery of the modeled signal.
summary.tldr: The paper extends semi-structured networks to functional data, combining interpretable feature effects with flexible neural modeling and improved scalability.

title: A Functional Extension of Semi-Structured Networks

abstract: The key challenge of multi-view indoor 3D object detection is to infer accurate geometry information from images for precise 3D detection. Previous method relies on NeRF for geometry reasoning. However, the geometry extracted from NeRF is generally inaccurate, which leads to sub-optimal detection performance. In this paper, we propose MVSDet which utilizes plane sweep for geometry-aware 3D object detection. To circumvent the requirement for a large number of depth planes for accurate depth prediction, we design a probabilistic sampling and soft weighting mechanism to decide the placement of pixel features on the 3D volume. We select multiple locations that score top in the probability volume for each pixel and use their probability score to indicate the confidence. We further apply recent pixel-aligned Gaussian Splatting to regularize depth prediction and improve detection performance with little computation overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes datasets are conducted to show the superiority of our model. Our code is available at https://github.com/Pixie8888/MVSDet.

paragraphs: Detecting indoor objects in three dimensions from multiple images depends on recovering accurate geometry. MVSDet instead uses plane sweeps to make image features useful for geometry-aware three-dimensional object detection.

For each pixel, it chooses several locations with high scores in a probability volume. Those scores express confidence and determine how the pixel's features contribute to the three-dimensional volume, retaining multiple promising placements rather than depending on only one.

The method also uses pixel-aligned Gaussian Splatting to regularize depth prediction, improving detection with little additional computation. Experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes demonstrate the model's superiority in the reported comparisons. The approach connects depth uncertainty directly to feature placement, making geometry estimation part of the detection process while reducing the need for a large collection of depth planes.
summary.tldr: MVSDet improves multi-view indoor 3D detection using probabilistic plane sweeps and Gaussian Splatting to guide geometry estimation.

title: MVSDet: Multi-View Indoor 3D Object Detection via Efficient Plane Sweeps

abstract: We consider how to construct state abstractions compatible with a given set of abstract actions, to obtain a well-formed abstract Markov decision process (MDP). We show that the Bellman equation suggests that abstract states should represent distributions over states in the ground MDP; we characterize the conditions under which the resulting process is Markov and approximately model-preserving, derive algorithms for constructing and planning with the abstract MDP, and apply them to a visual maze task. We generalize these results to the factored actions case, characterizing the conditions that result in factored abstract states and apply the resulting algorithm to Montezuma's Revenge. These results provide a powerful and principled framework for constructing neurosymbolic abstract Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: Planning with abstract actions requires a compatible description of the world. This paper asks how to construct abstract states when the available high-level actions are already given. The objective is a well-formed abstract Markov decision process, so that planning over the simplified representation remains connected to the underlying environment.

The authors use the Bellman equation to motivate representing each abstract state as a distribution over underlying states. They characterize conditions under which this construction is Markov and approximately preserves the underlying model. In practical terms, the abstraction must support predictions from its current state and retain enough of the original process for planning.

The paper derives algorithms for constructing the abstract process and planning within it, then applies them to a visual maze. It also extends the analysis to factored actions, identifying conditions that yield factored abstract states and applying the resulting algorithm to Montezuma’s Revenge. The contribution is a principled connection between available skills and state representations, with theoretical conditions specifying when the resulting abstraction has the desired properties.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs state abstractions around available skills and identifies conditions that make the resulting abstract decision process suitable for planning.

title: Skill-Driven Neurosymbolic State Abstractions

abstract: We consider the problem of conformal prediction under covariate shift. Given labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from a covariate shifted target domain, we seek to construct prediction sets with valid marginal coverage in the target domain. Most existing methods require estimating the unknown likelihood ratio function, which can be prohibitive for high-dimensional data such as images. To address this challenge, we introduce the likelihood ratio regularized quantile regression (LR-QR) algorithm, which combines the pinball loss with a novel choice of regularization in order to construct a threshold function without directly estimating the unknown likelihood ratio. We show that the LR-QR method has coverage at the desired level in the target domain, up to a small error term that we can control. Our proofs draw on a novel analysis of coverage via stability bounds from learning theory. Our experiments demonstrate that the LR-QR algorithm outperforms existing methods on high-dimensional prediction tasks, including a regression task for the Communities and Crime dataset, an image classification task from the WILDS repository, and an LLM question-answering task on the MMLU benchmark.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction sets when labeled training data and unlabeled deployment data come from domains with different covariate distributions. Its goal is valid marginal coverage in the target domain: the sets should include the correct answer at the desired overall frequency. This matters when uncertainty estimates must transfer across domains.

Many existing approaches require estimating a likelihood ratio between source and target distributions, which can become difficult for high-dimensional inputs. The proposed likelihood ratio regularized quantile regression method, LR-QR, instead constructs a threshold function using pinball loss and a new regularization choice. It avoids directly estimating that unknown ratio as a separate function.

The authors prove target-domain coverage at the desired level up to a small, controllable error, using stability bounds from learning theory. Experiments report improvements over existing methods on regression with Communities and Crime data, image classification from WILDS, and MMLU question answering. Together, the findings connect a qualified coverage guarantee with empirical performance across several kinds of prediction task.
summary.tldr: LR-QR constructs prediction sets under covariate shift without directly estimating likelihood ratios, with target coverage guaranteed up to controllable error.

title: Conformal Inference under High-Dimensional Covariate Shifts via Likelihood-Ratio Regularization

abstract: The multi-armed bandit (MAB) is a fundamental online decision-making framework that has been extensively studied over the past two decades. To mitigate the high cost and slow convergence of purely online learning, modern MAB approaches have explored _hybrid_ paradigms that leverage offline data to warm-start online learning. However, existing approaches face a significant limitation by assuming that the offline and online data are homogeneous—they share the same feedback structure and are drawn from the same underlying distribution. This assumption is often violated in practice, where offline data often originate from diverse sources and evolving environments, resulting in feedback heterogeneity and distributional shifts. In this work, we tackle the challenge of learning across this offline-online gap by developing a general hybrid bandit framework that incorporates heterogeneous offline data to improve online performance. We study two hybrid settings: (1) using reward-based offline data to accelerate online learning in preference-based bandits (i.e., dueling bandits), and (2) using preference-based offline data to improve online standard MAB algorithms. For both settings, we design novel algorithms and derive tight regret bounds that match or improve upon existing benchmarks despite heterogeneity. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our proposed methods significantly outperform baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-armed bandit methods learn which choices work best through repeated interaction. Historical data can help start that process, reducing the cost of learning entirely online. However, many hybrid methods assume that historical and live data have the same feedback structure and underlying distribution, even though data from different sources or changing environments may violate that assumption.

This paper develops a hybrid framework for heterogeneous offline and online data. It studies two directions of transfer: using historical numerical rewards to improve online preference-based learning, and using historical preferences to improve standard online bandits. The distinction matters because a reward for one choice and a comparison between two choices provide different forms of evidence.

For both settings, the authors design algorithms and establish tight regret bounds that match or improve existing benchmarks despite heterogeneity. Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning rather than consistently making the best choices. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also show significant improvements over baseline algorithms, supporting the value of using historical feedback even when its form differs from live feedback.
summary.tldr: The paper develops hybrid bandit algorithms that transfer between historical rewards and preferences, with tight regret guarantees and improved empirical performance.

title: Learning Across the Gap: Hybrid Multi-armed Bandits with Heterogeneous Offline and Online Data

abstract: Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as a promising approach for scaling Transformer models. While initial works primarily incorporated MoE into feed-forward network (FFN) layers, recent studies have explored extending the MoE paradigm to attention layers to enhance model performance. However, existing attention-based MoE layers require specialized implementations and demonstrate suboptimal performance compared to their FFN-based counterparts. In this paper, we aim to unify MoE designs in attention and FFN layers by introducing a novel reformulation of the attention mechanism, that reveals an underlying FFN-like structure within attention modules. Our proposed architecture, UMoE, achieves superior performance through attention-based MoE layers while enabling efficient parameter sharing between FFN and attention components.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts architectures offer a way to scale transformers through expert components. Most early designs placed those experts in feed-forward layers. Extending the same idea to attention has been harder: existing attention-based expert layers require specialized implementations and, according to the authors, perform less well than their feed-forward counterparts.

UMoE approaches this mismatch by reformulating attention to expose an underlying structure resembling a feed-forward network. That connection provides a common basis for designing expert layers in both parts of the transformer. It also enables parameters to be shared efficiently between attention and feed-forward components, linking two places where earlier designs treated expert computation differently.

The authors report superior performance through UMoE’s attention-based expert layers. The significance of the result is architectural: a different mathematical view of attention makes it possible to unify expert designs and support parameter sharing within the same system. The stated contribution therefore combines improved attention-based MoE performance with a more coordinated use of parameters across transformer components.
summary.tldr: UMoE reformulates attention to unify attention and feed-forward expert layers while enabling efficient parameter sharing.

title: UMoE: Unifying Attention and FFN with Shared Experts

abstract: Foundation models (FMs) are pre-trained on large-scale datasets and then fine-tuned for a specific downstream task. The most common fine-tuning method is to update pretrained weights via low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Existing initialization strategies for LoRA often rely on singular value decompositions (SVD) of gradients or weight matrices. However, they do not provably maximize the expected gradient signal, which is critical for fast adaptation. To this end, we introduce **E**xplained **V**ariance **A**daptation (EVA), an initialization scheme that uses the directions capturing the most activation variance, provably maximizing the expected gradient signal and accelerating fine-tuning. EVA performs incremental SVD on minibatches of activation vectors and selects the right-singular vectors for initialization once they converged. Further, by selecting the directions that capture the most activation-variance for a given rank budget, EVA accommodates adaptive ranks that reduce the number of trainable parameters. We apply EVA to a variety of fine-tuning tasks as language generation and understanding, image classification, and reinforcement learning. EVA exhibits faster convergence than competitors and achieves the highest average score across a multitude of tasks per domain while reducing the number of trainable parameters through rank redistribution. In summary, EVA establishes a new Pareto frontier compared to existing LoRA initialization schemes in both accuracy and efficiency.

EVA instead selects directions that capture the most variation in the model's activations.

summary.tldr: EVA initializes and allocates LoRA directions using activation variance, improving fine-tuning speed, accuracy, and parameter efficiency.

title: Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning via Explained Variance Adaptation

abstract: In the incentivized exploration model, a principal aims to explore and learn over time by interacting with a sequence of self-interested agents. It has been recently understood that the main challenge in designing incentive-compatible algorithms for this problem is to gather a moderate amount of initial data, after which one can obtain near-optimal regret via posterior sampling. With high-dimensional contexts, however, this \emph{initial exploration} phase requires exponential sample complexity in some cases, which prevents efficient learning unless initial data can be acquired exogenously. We show that these barriers to exploration disappear under mild geometric conditions on the set of available actions, in which case incentive-compatibility does not preclude regret-optimality. Namely, we consider the linear bandit model with actions in the Euclidean unit ball, and give an incentive-compatible exploration algorithm with sample complexity that scales polynomially with the dimension and other parameters.

paragraphs: In incentivized exploration, a principal learns by interacting with successive agents who pursue their own interests. The learning strategy must give those agents reasons to follow its recommendations. A central difficulty is collecting enough initial information: once a moderate amount is available, posterior sampling can achieve near-optimal regret, measuring losses relative to better choices.

With high-dimensional contexts, this initial exploration can require exponentially many samples in some settings. The paper shows that this obstacle disappears under mild geometric conditions on the available actions. It studies a linear bandit setting whose actions lie in the Euclidean unit ball, making the geometry of the choices central to the result.

For this setting, the authors construct an incentive-compatible exploration algorithm whose sample requirement grows polynomially with dimension and other parameters. The finding establishes that respecting agents’ incentives need not prevent regret-optimal learning under the stated geometric conditions. It also identifies action-space structure as a reason some initial exploration problems can be tractable despite the difficulties found in other high-dimensional settings.
summary.tldr: Under suitable action-space geometry, incentive-compatible linear-bandit exploration needs polynomially many initial samples rather than facing exponential barriers.

title: Geometry Meets Incentives: Sample-Efficient Incentivized Exploration with Linear Contexts

abstract: Reasoning models have demonstrated impressive performance in self-reflection and chain-of-thought reasoning. However, they often produce excessively long outputs, leading to prohibitively large key-value (KV) caches during inference. While chain-of-thought inference significantly improves performance on complex reasoning tasks, it can also lead to reasoning failures when deployed with existing KV cache compression approaches. To address this, we propose Redundancy-aware KV Cache Compression for Reasoning models (R-KV), a novel method specifically targeting redundant tokens in reasoning models. Our method preserves nearly 100% of the full KV cache performance using only 10% of the KV cache, substantially outperforming existing KV cache baselines, which reach only 60% of the performance. Remarkably, R-KV even achieves 105% of full KV cache performance with 38% of the KV cache. This KV-cache reduction also leads to a 50% memory saving and a 2x speedup over standard chain-of-thought reasoning inference. Experimental results show that R-KV consistently outperforms existing KV cache compression baselines across two mathematical reasoning datasets.

paragraphs: Reasoning models often generate long chains of thought, increasing the size of the key-value cache used during inference. Compressing that cache can reduce resource use, but existing compression approaches can also disrupt reasoning. R-KV addresses this problem by specifically targeting redundant tokens in reasoning models.

The reported results retain nearly all full-cache performance while using only 10% of the cache. Existing cache-compression baselines reach about 60% of full-cache performance in the stated comparison. With 38% of the cache, R-KV reaches 105% of the full-cache performance, showing that the tested compression setting can even improve the measured result.

The cache reduction also produces reported total memory savings of 50% and a twofold speedup over standard chain-of-thought inference. Those resource measurements are distinct from the percentage of cache retained. Across two mathematical reasoning datasets, R-KV consistently outperforms existing compression baselines. The findings support redundancy-aware cache management as a way to preserve reasoning quality while reducing the cost of long generations.
summary.tldr: R-KV targets redundant reasoning tokens to shrink inference caches substantially while retaining nearly all full-cache performance in reported tests.

title: R-KV: Redundancy-aware KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Models

abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning demands adaptation to unseen environmental conditions without costly retraining. Contextual Markov Decision Processes (cMDP) model this challenge, but existing methods often require explicit context variables (e.g., friction, gravity), limiting their use when contexts are latent or hard to measure. We introduce Dynamics-Aligned Latent Imagination (DALI), a framework integrated within the Dreamer architecture that infers latent context representations from agent-environment interactions. By training a self-supervised encoder to predict forward dynamics, DALI generates actionable representations conditioning the world model and policy, bridging perception and control. We theoretically prove this encoder is essential for efficient context inference and robust generalization. DALI’s latent space enables counterfactual consistency: Perturbing a gravity-encoding dimension alters imagined rollouts in physically plausible ways. On challenging cMDP benchmarks, DALI achieves significant gains over context-unaware baselines, often surpassing context-aware baselines in extrapolation tasks, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen contextual variations.

DALI addresses this problem within the Dreamer architecture by inferring hidden context from interactions. Its goal is to support adaptation to unseen conditions without costly retraining.

A self-supervised encoder learns representations by predicting forward dynamics: how the environment changes following actions. These representations condition both the world model and the policy, linking context inference to prediction and control. The paper provides a theoretical argument for the encoder’s essential role in efficient inference and robust generalization within its framework. It also demonstrates counterfactual consistency: changing a dimension encoding gravity changes imagined trajectories in physically plausible ways.

On contextual decision-process benchmarks, DALI significantly improves over methods that ignore context and often exceeds context-aware methods when extrapolating. These findings support using interaction-derived context for zero-shot generalization. The representations are useful because they influence imagined behavior and decisions, beyond merely describing observations.
summary.tldr: DALI infers hidden environmental context from dynamics and uses it to improve zero-shot control under unseen contextual changes.

title: Dynamics-Aligned Latent Imagination in Contextual World Models for Zero-Shot Generalization

abstract: Video generative models can be regarded as world simulators due to their ability to capture dynamic, continuous changes inherent in real-world environments. These models integrate high-dimensional information across visual, temporal, spatial, and causal dimensions, enabling predictions of subjects in various status. A natural and valuable research direction is to explore whether a fully trained video generative model in high-dimensional space can effectively support lower-dimensional tasks such as controllable image generation. In this work, we propose a paradigm for video-to-image knowledge compression and task adaptation, termed \textit{Dimension-Reduction Attack} (\texttt{DRA-Ctrl}), which utilizes the strengths of video models, including long-range context modeling and flatten full-attention, to perform various generation tasks. Specially, to address the challenging gap between continuous video frames and discrete image generation, we introduce a mixup-based transition strategy that ensures smooth adaptation. Moreover, we redesign the attention structure with a tailored masking mechanism to better align text prompts with image-level control. Experiments across diverse image generation tasks, such as subject-driven and spatially conditioned generation, show that repurposed video models outperform those trained directly on images. These results highlight the untapped potential of large-scale video generators for broader visual applications. \texttt{DRA-Ctrl} provides new insights into reusing resource-intensive video models and lays foundation for future unified generative models across visual modalities. The project page is \url{https://dra-ctrl-2025.github.io/DRA-Ctrl/}.

This paper asks whether knowledge acquired for that richer task can help with controlled image generation. DRA-Ctrl provides a method for transferring a trained video generator into image tasks, making use of its ability to model long-range context and broad attention relationships.

The transfer must bridge a mismatch: video frames form a continuous sequence, while controlled image generation works with separate image outputs. DRA-Ctrl introduces a mixup-based transition strategy to smooth that adaptation. It also changes the attention structure through a tailored mask, intended to align textual instructions more closely with controls applied at the image level.

Experiments cover several image-generation tasks, including subject-driven generation and generation conditioned on spatial information. In these evaluations, the adapted video models outperform models trained directly on images. The findings support reusing expensive video generators for a wider range of visual tasks. title: Dimension-Reduction Attack! Video Generative Models are Experts on Controllable Image Synthesis

abstract: Consistency Models (CMs) have shown promise for efficient one-step generation. However, most existing CMs rely on manually designed discretization schemes, which can cause repeated adjustments for different noise schedules and datasets. To address this, we propose a unified framework for the automatic and adaptive discretization of CMs, formulating it as an optimization problem with respect to the discretization step. Concretely, during the consistency training process, we propose using local consistency as the optimization objective to ensure trainability by avoiding excessive discretization, and taking global consistency as a constraint to ensure stability by controlling the denoising error in the training target. We establish the trade-off between local and global consistency with a Lagrange multiplier. Building on this framework, we achieve adaptive discretization for CMs using the Gauss-Newton method. We refer to our approach as ADCMs. Experiments demonstrate that ADCMs significantly improve the training efficiency of CMs, achieving superior generative performance with minimal training overhead on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Moreover, ADCMs exhibit strong adaptability to more advanced DM variants. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/rainstonee/ADCM}.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to generate samples in a single step, but their training still depends on choices about how to divide the noise process into discrete steps. Those choices are often designed manually and adjusted for different datasets or noise schedules. This paper makes the discretization step an optimization variable so that training can adapt it automatically.

The method balances two requirements. Local consistency serves as the optimization objective, helping keep the model trainable by avoiding excessive discretization. Global consistency acts as a constraint that controls denoising error in the training target and supports stability. A Lagrange multiplier connects these competing requirements, and a Gauss–Newton method performs the adaptive optimization. The resulting approach is called ADCMs.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet report improved training efficiency and better generative performance with little additional training overhead. The authors also report adaptability to more advanced diffusion-model variants. These findings suggest that choosing the training discretization automatically can improve both the learning process and its generated outputs, while reducing dependence on manually selected discretization schemes.
summary.tldr: ADCMs automatically optimize consistency-model discretization by balancing trainability and stability, improving training efficiency and generation in reported experiments.

title: Adaptive Discretization for Consistency Models

abstract: Advances in large-scale recording technologies now enable simultaneous measurements from multiple brain areas, offering new opportunities to study signal transmission across interacting components of neural circuits. However, neural responses exhibit substantial trial-to-trial variability, often driven by unobserved factors such as subtle changes in animal behavior or internal states. To prevent evolving background dynamics from contaminating identification of functional coupling, we developed a hybrid neural spike train model, GLM-Transformer, that incorporates flexible, deep latent variable models into a point process generalized linear model (GLM) having an interpretable component for cross-population interactions. A Transformer-based variational autoencoder captures nonstationary individual-neuron dynamics that vary across trials, while standard nonparametric regression GLM coupling terms provide estimates of directed interactions between neural populations. We incorporate a low-rank structure on population-to-population coupling effects to improve scalability. Across synthetic datasets and mechanistic simulations, GLM-Transformer recovers known coupling structure and remains robust to shared background fluctuations. When applied to the Allen Institute Visual Coding dataset, it identifies feedforward pathways consistent with established visual hierarchies. This work offers a step toward improved identification of neural population interactions, and contributes to ongoing efforts aimed at achieving interpretable results while harvesting the benefits of deep learning.

title: Identifying interactions across brain areas while accounting for individual-neuron dynamics with a Transformer-based variational autoencoder

abstract: Transformer-based algorithms, such as LoRAT, have significantly enhanced object-tracking performance. However, these approaches rely on a standard attention mechanism, which incurs quadratic token complexity, making real-time inference computationally expensive. In this paper, we introduce LoRATv2, a novel tracking framework that addresses these limitations with three main contributions. First, LoRATv2 integrates frame-wise causal attention, which ensures full self-attention within each frame while enabling causal dependencies across frames, significantly reducing computational overhead. Moreover, key-value (KV) caching is employed to efficiently reuse past embeddings for further speedup. Second, building on LoRAT's parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we propose Stream-Specific LoRA Adapters (SSLA). As frame-wise causal attention introduces asymmetry in how streams access temporal information, SSLA assigns dedicated LoRA modules to the template and each search stream, with the main ViT backbone remaining frozen. This allows specialized adaptation for each stream's role in temporal tracking. Third, we introduce a two-phase progressive training strategy, which first trains a single-search-frame tracker and then gradually extends it to multi-search-frame inputs by introducing additional LoRA modules. This curriculum-based learning paradigm improves long-term tracking while maintaining training efficiency. In extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks, LoRATv2 achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially improved efficiency, and a superior performance-to-FLOPs ratio over state-of-the-art trackers. The code is available at https://github.com/LitingLin/LoRATv2.

The framework uses frame-wise causal attention: tokens within a frame retain full self-attention, while dependencies between frames follow temporal order. Key-value caching reuses past embeddings to further reduce repeated computation.

This attention structure gives different streams unequal access to temporal information. Each stream can therefore specialize for its role without updating the entire backbone.

This curriculum supports longer-term tracking while retaining training efficiency. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art tracking performance, substantially improved efficiency, and a better performance-to-FLOPs ratio than the compared trackers. The method links temporal reuse, specialized adaptation, and progressive training in one tracking framework.
summary.tldr: LoRATv2 combines causal frame attention, cached embeddings, and stream-specific LoRA adapters for efficient temporal object tracking.

title: LoRATv2: Enabling Low-Cost Temporal Modeling in One-Stream Trackers

abstract: Rectified Flows learn ODE vector fields whose trajectories are straight between source and target distributions, enabling near one-step inference. We show that this straight-path objective reveals fundamental failure modes: under deterministic training, low gradient variance drives memorization of arbitrary training pairings, even when interpolant lines between training pairs intersect. To analyze this mechanism, we study Gaussian-to-Gaussian transport and use the loss gradient variance across stochastic and deterministic regimes to characterize which vector fields optimization favors in each setting. We then show that, in a setting where all interpolating lines intersect, applying Rectified Flow yields the same specific pairings at inference as during training. More generally, we prove that a memorizing vector field exists even when training interpolants intersect, and that optimizing the straight-path objective converges to this ill-defined field. At inference, deterministic integration reproduces the exact training pairings. We validate our findings empirically on the CelebA dataset, confirming that deterministic interpolants induce memorization, while the injection of small noise restores generalization.

paragraphs: Rectified Flows learn vector fields intended to move samples along straight paths between source and target distributions, supporting very few inference steps. This paper examines a failure mode of that objective under deterministic training: the model can memorize arbitrary source-target training pairings instead of learning a transport rule that generalizes.

The authors analyze Gaussian-to-Gaussian transport and compare loss-gradient variance in stochastic and deterministic regimes. Low gradient variance in deterministic training favors memorization. They show that intersecting training paths do not prevent this behavior: a memorizing vector field can exist even at such intersections, and optimization can converge to that ill-defined field. Deterministic integration then reproduces the training pairings.

A particularly direct construction makes every interpolating line intersect, yet inference still recovers the specific pairings used in training. Experiments on CelebA support the analysis: deterministic interpolants induce memorization, while adding small amounts of noise restores generalization in the reported evaluation. The work links a concrete optimization signal, gradient variance, to the distinction between learning transferable transport and reproducing training associations.
summary.tldr: The paper links deterministic Rectified Flow training to memorized source-target pairings and shows that small noise restores generalization in its empirical evaluation.

title: Gradient Variance Reveals Failure Modes in Flow-Based Generative Models

abstract: The dynamic nature of information necessitates continuously updating large vision-language models (LVLMs). While recent knowledge editing techniques hint at promising directions, they often focus on editing a single modality (vision or language) in isolation. This prevalent practice neglects the inherent multimodality of LVLMs and the continuous nature of knowledge updates, potentially leading to suboptimal editing outcomes when considering the interplay between modalities and the need for ongoing knowledge refinement. To address these limitations, we propose MemEIC, a novel method for Continual and Compositional Knowledge Editing (CCKE) in LVLMs. MemEIC enables compositional editing of both visual and textual knowledge sequentially. Our approach employs a hybrid external-internal editor featuring a dual external memory for cross-modal evidence retrieval and dual LoRA adapters that facilitate disentangled parameter updates for each modality. A key component is a brain-inspired knowledge connector, activated selectively for compositional reasoning, that integrates information across different modalities. Experiments demonstrate that MemEIC significantly improves performance on complex multimodal questions and effectively preserves prior edits, setting a new benchmark for CCKE in LVLMs. Our project is available at https://github.com/MemEIC/MemEIC.

paragraphs: Updating a vision-language model involves knowledge expressed through both images and text. Editing only one modality in isolation can overlook how the two interact, especially when updates arrive repeatedly. MemEIC addresses continual and compositional knowledge editing: making sequential updates that can also be used together in multimodal reasoning.

The method combines external retrieval with internal parameter changes. Dual external memories retrieve evidence across modalities, while two LoRA adapters support separate parameter updates for visual and textual knowledge. A brain-inspired knowledge connector is selectively activated for compositional reasoning, integrating information across modalities when the task calls for it.

This design distinguishes storing and updating knowledge from combining it to answer a question. Experiments report significant improvements on complex multimodal questions while effectively preserving earlier edits. Both outcomes matter for continual editing: newly updated information must remain usable alongside information changed previously. The results support MemEIC as a way to handle repeated visual and textual edits within a shared model.
summary.tldr: MemEIC combines external memories, modality-specific adapters, and a selective connector to support repeated, compositional vision-language knowledge edits.

title: MemEIC: A Step Toward Continual and Compositional Knowledge Editing

abstract: Natural images often exhibit underlying sparse structures, with information density varying significantly across different spatial locations. However, most generative models rely on dense grid-based pixels or latents, neglecting this inherent sparsity. In this paper, we explore modeling visual generation paradigm via sparse non-grid latent representations. Specifically, we design a sparse autoencoder that represents an image as a small number of latents with their positional properties (i.e., regions of interest, RoIs) with high reconstruction quality. We then explore training flow-matching transformers jointly on non-grid latents and RoI values. To the best knowledge, we are the first to address spatial sparsity using RoIs in generative process. Experimental results show that our sparse flow-based transformers have competitive performance compared with dense grid-based counterparts with significantly reduced lower compute, and reaches a competitive 2.76 FID with just 64 latents on class-conditional ImageNet $256\times 256$ generation.

paragraphs: Visual information is not distributed evenly across an image, but many generators represent every image through a dense grid of pixels or latent features. This paper explores a sparse alternative in which a small collection of latent representations carries both image content and information about the regions associated with that content.

The authors first design a sparse autoencoder that reconstructs images with high quality using a small number of latents and their regions of interest, or RoIs. They then train flow-matching transformers jointly on the latent values and RoI values. Generation thus models both the visual representation and its spatial properties without relying on a fixed latent grid.

Experiments show competitive performance relative to dense-grid counterparts with substantially lower computation. On class-conditioned ImageNet generation at 256-by-256 resolution, the method reaches an FID of 2.76 using only 64 latents. The finding supports sparse, spatially located representations as a practical approach to image synthesis, with competitive quality in the evaluated setting despite using far fewer latent elements.
summary.tldr: Jointly generating sparse image latents and their regions of interest delivers competitive image quality with reduced computation.

title: Sparse Image Synthesis via Joint Latent and RoI Flow

abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) systems typically employ maximum *a posteriori* (MAP) decoding to select the highest-scoring translation from the distribution. However, recent evidence highlights the inadequacy of MAP decoding, often resulting in low-quality or even pathological hypotheses as the decoding objective is only weakly aligned with real-world translation quality. This paper proposes to directly calibrate hypothesis likelihood with translation quality from a distributional view by directly optimizing their Pearson correlation, thereby enhancing decoding effectiveness. With our method, translation with large language models (LLMs) improves substantially after limited training (2K instances per direction). This improvement is orthogonal to those achieved through supervised fine-tuning, leading to substantial gains across a broad range of metrics and human evaluations. This holds even when applied to top-performing translation-specialized LLMs fine-tuned on high-quality translation data, such as Tower, or when compared to recent preference optimization methods, like CPO. Moreover, the calibrated translation likelihood can directly serve as a strong proxy for translation quality, closely approximating or even surpassing some state-of-the-art translation quality estimation models, like CometKiwi. Lastly, our in-depth analysis demonstrates that calibration enhances the effectiveness of MAP decoding, thereby enabling greater efficiency in real-world deployment. The resulting state-of-the-art translation model, which covers 10 languages, along with the accompanying code and human evaluation data, has been released: https://github.com/moore3930/calibrating-llm-mt.

summary.tldr: Aligning translation likelihood with estimated quality improves translation selection and makes likelihood a useful quality signal.

title: Calibrating Translation Decoding with Quality Estimation on LLMs

abstract: Dense and versatile image representations underpin the success of virtually all computer vision applications. However, state-of-the-art networks, such as transformers, produce low-resolution feature grids, which are suboptimal for dense prediction tasks. To address this limitation, we present *FlowFeat*, a high-resolution and multi-task feature representation. The key ingredient behind FlowFeat is a novel distillation technique that embeds a distribution of plausible apparent motions, or *motion profiles*. By leveraging optical flow networks and diverse video data, we develop an effective self-supervised training framework that statistically approximates the apparent motion. With its remarkable level of spatial detail, FlowFeat encodes a compelling degree of geometric and semantic cues while exhibiting high temporal consistency. Empirically, FlowFeat significantly enhances the representational power of five state-of-the-art encoders and alternative upsampling strategies across three dense tasks: video object segmentation, monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation. Training FlowFeat is computationally inexpensive and robust to inaccurate flow estimation, remaining highly effective even when using unsupervised flow networks. Our work takes a step forward towards reliable and versatile dense image representations.

paragraphs: Tasks such as segmentation and depth estimation need detailed information at individual image locations. Yet strong visual encoders often produce coarse feature grids. FlowFeat addresses this mismatch by learning a high-resolution representation that captures distributions of plausible apparent motion, which the authors call motion profiles.

The method distills information from optical flow networks using diverse video data in a self-supervised training framework. Instead of relying only on coarse image features, it statistically approximates apparent motion to build spatially detailed representations. The resulting features contain geometric and semantic information and remain highly consistent over time, properties relevant to both image-level interpretation and following content through video.

The authors report improvements involving five state-of-the-art encoders and alternative upsampling strategies across video object segmentation, monocular depth estimation, and semantic segmentation. They also find training computationally inexpensive and robust to inaccurate flow estimates, including those from unsupervised flow networks. These results suggest that motion-derived supervision can enrich dense visual features without requiring especially accurate flow estimates to remain effective.
summary.tldr: FlowFeat distills motion profiles from video into detailed visual features that improve segmentation and depth estimation.

title: FlowFeat: Pixel-Dense Embedding of Motion Profiles

abstract: In the theory of compressed sensing (CS), the sparsity \|x\|_0 of the unknown signal x∈\R^p is commonly assumed to be a known parameter. However, it is typically unknown in practice. Due to the fact that many aspects of CS depend on knowing \|x\|_0, it is important to estimate this parameter in a data-driven way. A second practical concern is that \|x\|_0 is a highly unstable function of x. In particular, for real signals with entries not exactly equal to 0, the value \|x\|_0=p is not a useful description of the effective number of coordinates. In this paper, we propose to estimate a stable measure of sparsity s(x):=\|x\|_1^2/\|x\|_2^2, which is a sharp lower bound on \|x\|_0. Our estimation procedure uses only a small number of linear measurements, does not rely on any sparsity assumptions, and requires very little computation. A confidence interval for s(x) is provided, and its width is shown to have no dependence on the signal dimension p. Moreover, this result extends naturally to the matrix recovery setting, where a soft version of matrix rank can be estimated with analogous guarantees. Finally, we show that the use of randomized measurements is essential to estimating s(x). This is accomplished by proving that the minimax risk for estimating s(x) with deterministic measurements is large when n≪p.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing often treats the number of nonzero signal entries as known, although that quantity is usually unavailable in practice. Exact counting is also unstable: tiny nonzero entries count just as much as large ones. The paper therefore estimates an effective sparsity measure, defined as the squared L1 norm divided by the squared L2 norm.

This measure is a sharp lower bound on the number of nonzero coordinates and provides a more stable description of how spread out a signal is. The proposed estimator uses a small number of linear measurements, requires little computation, and does not assume the signal is sparse. Its confidence interval has a width that does not depend on the signal’s dimension.

The framework also extends to estimating a soft version of matrix rank with analogous guarantees. A further theoretical result explains the role of randomness: when measurements are far fewer than coordinates, deterministic measurements have large minimax estimation risk. Thus the paper combines a practical uncertainty-aware estimator with a specific justification for randomized measurement design.
summary.tldr: A lightweight randomized estimator measures effective signal sparsity with confidence-interval width independent of signal dimension.

title: Estimating Unknown Sparsity in Compressed Sensing

abstract: The parameters of temporal models, such as dynamic Bayesian networks, may be modelled in a Bayesian context as static or atemporal variables that influence transition probabilities at every time step. Particle filters fail for models that include such variables, while methods that use Gibbs sampling of parameter variables may incur a per-sample cost that grows linearly with the length of the observation sequence. Storvik devised a method for incremental computation of exact sufficient statistics that, for some cases, reduces the per-sample cost to a constant. In this paper, we demonstrate a connection between Storvik’s filter and a Kalman filter in parameter space and establish more general conditions under which Storvik’s filter works. Drawing on an analogy to the extended Kalman filter, we develop and analyze, both theoretically and experimentally, a Taylor approximation to the parameter posterior that allows Storvik’s method to be applied to a broader class of models. Our experiments on both synthetic examples and real applications show improvement over existing methods.

Storvik devised a method for incremental computation of exact sufficient statistics that, for some cases, reduces the per-sample cost to a constant. In this paper, we demonstrate a connection between Storvik’s filter and a Kalman filter in parameter space and establish more general conditions under which Storvik’s filter works. Drawing on an analogy to the extended Kalman filter, we develop and analyze, both theoretically and experimentally, a Taylor approximation to the parameter posterior that allows Storvik’s method to be applied to a broader class of models. Our experiments on both synthetic examples and real applications show improvement over existing methods.

paragraphs: Temporal models can include fixed parameters that affect transitions at every time step. Bayesian inference must learn those parameters alongside the evolving system. The paper describes difficulties with particle filters in this setting and notes that Gibbs-based parameter sampling can become more expensive as the observation sequence grows.

Storvik's filter can avoid that growing per-sample cost in some cases by incrementally updating exact sufficient statistics. The authors connect this method to a Kalman filter operating in parameter space and establish more general conditions for its applicability. This connection supplies a basis for extending the approach beyond the cases handled by exact updates.

Drawing on the extended Kalman filter analogy, the paper develops a Taylor approximation to the parameter posterior. The approximation makes Storvik's method applicable to a broader class of models and receives both theoretical and experimental analysis. Experiments on synthetic examples and real applications show improvements over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of this extension for sequential parameter inference.
summary.tldr: A Kalman-filter connection and Taylor posterior approximation extend Storvik's parameter filtering method to a broader class of temporal models.

title: The Extended Parameter Filter

abstract: Recently, researchers have made significant progress combining the advances in deep learning for learning feature representations with reinforcement learning. Some notable examples include training agents to play Atari games based on raw pixel data and to acquire advanced manipulation skills using raw sensory inputs. However, it has been difficult to quantify progress in the domain of continuous control due to the lack of a commonly adopted benchmark. In this work, we present a benchmark suite of continuous control tasks, including classic tasks like cart-pole swing-up, tasks with very high state and action dimensionality such as 3D humanoid locomotion, tasks with partial observations, and tasks with hierarchical structure. We report novel findings based on the systematic evaluation of a range of implemented reinforcement learning algorithms. Both the benchmark and reference implementations are released at https://github.com/rllab/rllab in order to facilitate experimental reproducibility and to encourage adoption by other researchers.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a measurement problem in reinforcement learning: progress in continuous control was difficult to assess without a commonly adopted benchmark. Continuous control involves choosing actions from a range of possible values. The contribution is a shared collection of tasks and algorithm implementations that makes systematic evaluation easier.

The suite deliberately includes different sources of difficulty. It covers familiar tasks such as cart-pole swing-up and problems with large state and action spaces, including three-dimensional humanoid locomotion. It also includes tasks with partial observations and hierarchical structure. Together, these settings allow evaluation to extend beyond a single kind of control problem.

The authors systematically evaluate a range of implemented reinforcement learning algorithms and report findings from those comparisons. They release both the benchmark and reference implementations to support reproducibility and broader adoption. The stated contribution therefore combines experimental evaluation with reusable research infrastructure: other researchers can work from shared tasks and implementations when assessing their own methods.
summary.tldr: A shared continuous-control benchmark and reference implementations support more systematic, reproducible reinforcement learning comparisons.

title: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Continuous Control

abstract: A data-driven identification of dynamical systems requiring only minimal prior knowledge is promising whenever no analytically derived model structure is available, e.g., from first principles in physics. However, meta-knowledge on the system’s behavior is often given and should be exploited: Stability as fundamental property is essential when the model is used for controller design or movement generation. Therefore, this paper proposes a framework for learning stable stochastic systems from data. We focus on identifying a state-dependent coefficient form of the nonlinear stochastic model which is globally asymptotically stable according to probabilistic Lyapunov methods. We compare our approach to other state of the art methods on real-world datasets in terms of flexibility and stability.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamical system from data is useful when no model derived from physical principles is available. Yet an absence of detailed equations does not mean an absence of useful knowledge. This paper focuses on stability as a known behavioral property that should inform the learned model, especially for controller design or movement generation.

The proposed framework learns nonlinear stochastic systems in a state-dependent coefficient form. In this representation, coefficients vary with the system's state. The targeted models are globally asymptotically stable according to probabilistic Lyapunov methods, bringing a stability requirement into the identification problem while accounting for the stochastic nature of the dynamics.

The authors compare their approach with other methods on real-world datasets in terms of flexibility and stability. The stated contribution is a framework that incorporates behavioral knowledge into data-driven system identification. It connects learning from observations with a formal stability property relevant to how the resulting model will be used.
summary.tldr: A learning framework incorporates probabilistic stability requirements into the identification of nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems.

title: Learning Stable Stochastic Nonlinear Dynamical Systems

abstract: Multi-Rate Multivariate Time Series (MR-MTS) are the multivariate time series observations which come with various sampling rates and encode multiple temporal dependencies. State-space models such as Kalman filters and deep learning models such as deep Markov models are mainly designed for time series data with the same sampling rate and cannot capture all the dependencies present in the MR-MTS data. To address this challenge, we propose the Multi-Rate Hierarchical Deep Markov Model (MR-HDMM), a novel deep generative model which uses the latent hierarchical structure with a learnable switch mechanism to capture the temporal dependencies of MR-MTS. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our MR-HDMM model outperforms the existing state-of-the-art deep learning and state-space models on forecasting and interpolation tasks. In addition, the latent hierarchies in our model provide a way to show and interpret the multiple temporal dependencies.
