paragraphs: Multivariate time series can contain variables observed at different sampling rates, with dependencies operating across multiple temporal scales. Models mainly designed around a common sampling rate may fail to capture all of that structure. This paper treats the mixture of sampling rates as a central modeling issue.

The proposed Multi-Rate Hierarchical Deep Markov Model uses a hierarchy of latent variables together with a learnable switching mechanism. These components are intended to capture the multiple temporal dependencies present in the observations. The hidden hierarchy provides a structured representation of the time series rather than treating all temporal relationships at one level.

Experiments on two real-world datasets show better forecasting and interpolation performance than the evaluated state-of-the-art deep learning and state-space models. Forecasting concerns future observations, while interpolation concerns values within the observed span. The hierarchy also offers a way to display and interpret temporal dependencies. The reported contribution therefore combines improved predictions in those evaluations with a representation that can help explain the data's temporal structure.
summary.tldr: MR-HDMM uses latent hierarchies and learned switching to model differently sampled time series, improving reported forecasting and interpolation.

title: Hierarchical Deep Generative Models for Multi-Rate Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Modern reinforcement learning algorithms reach super-human performance on many board and video games, but they are sample inefficient, i.e. they typically require significantly more playing experience than humans to reach an equal performance level. To improve sample efficiency, an agent may build a model of the environment and use planning methods to update its policy. In this article we introduce Variational State Tabulation (VaST), which maps an environment with a high-dimensional state space (e.g. the space of visual inputs) to an abstract tabular model. Prioritized sweeping with small backups, a highly efficient planning method, can then be used to update state-action values. We show how VaST can rapidly learn to maximize reward in tasks like 3D navigation and efficiently adapt to sudden changes in rewards or transition probabilities.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can achieve strong performance while still requiring large amounts of experience. Building an environment model offers a way to make more use of what has already been observed, because planning can update decisions without relying only on new interactions. This paper introduces Variational State Tabulation, or VaST, to connect that strategy with high-dimensional observations.

VaST maps an environment’s large state space, such as visual inputs, into an abstract tabular model. That representation allows the agent to use prioritized sweeping with small backups to update state-action values. The approach connects learned state abstraction to an efficient planning method that operates on the resulting table.

The authors show that VaST can rapidly learn reward-maximizing behavior in tasks including 3D navigation. They also demonstrate efficient adaptation when rewards or transition probabilities change suddenly. These findings highlight two uses of the abstract model: learning from limited experience and revising behavior when previously learned environmental relationships or rewards change.
summary.tldr: VaST converts high-dimensional observations into a tabular model that supports efficient planning and adaptation to environmental changes.

title: Efficient Model-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning with Variational State Tabulation

abstract: Robust subspace tracking (RST) can be simply understood as a dynamic (time-varying) extension of robust PCA. More precisely, it is the problem of tracking data lying in a fixed or slowly-changing low-dimensional subspace while being robust to sparse outliers. This work develops a recursive projected compressive sensing algorithm called “Nearly Optimal RST (NORST)”, and obtains one of the first guarantees for it. We show that NORST provably solves RST under weakened standard RPCA assumptions, slow subspace change, and a lower bound on (most) outlier magnitudes. Our guarantee shows that (i) NORST is online (after initialization) and enjoys near-optimal values of tracking delay, lower bound on required delay between subspace change times, and of memory complexity; and (ii) it has a significantly improved worst-case outlier tolerance compared with all previous robust PCA or RST methods without requiring any model on how the outlier support is generated.

paragraphs: Robust subspace tracking seeks a low-dimensional structure in incoming data even when some entries are corrupted by sparse outliers. Unlike a static robust PCA problem, the structure may change over time. This paper introduces NORST, a recursive projected compressive sensing algorithm, and establishes guarantees for tracking fixed or slowly changing subspaces.

The guarantees depend on weakened standard robust PCA assumptions, slow subspace changes, and a lower bound on the magnitude of most outliers. Under those conditions, NORST operates online after initialization. Its tracking delay, required spacing between subspace changes, and memory use are near optimal, according to the paper's theoretical results.

The analysis also gives significantly better worst-case tolerance to outliers than previous robust PCA or subspace-tracking methods. It does so without requiring a model for how corrupted positions are generated. This matters because the guarantee controls how much corruption the algorithm can withstand while allowing flexibility in where it occurs. The contribution joins efficient ongoing tracking with explicit conditions for reliable recovery.
summary.tldr: NORST provides conditional guarantees for online robust subspace tracking with near-optimal delay and memory use and improved worst-case outlier tolerance.

title: Nearly Optimal Robust Subspace Tracking

abstract: The recently-developed WaveNet architecture is the current state of the art in realistic speech synthesis, consistently rated as more natural sounding for many different languages than any previous system. However, because WaveNet relies on sequential generation of one audio sample at a time, it is poorly suited to today’s massively parallel computers, and therefore hard to deploy in a real-time production setting. This paper introduces Probability Density Distillation, a new method for training a parallel feed-forward network from a trained WaveNet with no significant difference in quality. The resulting system is capable of generating high-fidelity speech samples at more than 20 times faster than real-time, a 1000x speed up relative to the original WaveNet, and capable of serving multiple English and Japanese voices in a production setting.

paragraphs: WaveNet produces highly natural speech, but its original generation process creates one audio sample after another. This sequential dependency makes it difficult to exploit massively parallel computers and complicates real-time deployment. The paper addresses that generation bottleneck while aiming to retain the speech quality of an already trained WaveNet.

The authors introduce Probability Density Distillation, a method that trains a parallel feed-forward network from the trained WaveNet. The resulting generator can use parallel computation instead of relying on the original sample-by-sample generation process. The reported quality shows no significant difference from the source model, making the transfer useful for accelerating synthesis.

The resulting system generates high-fidelity speech at more than twenty times real-time speed and achieves a thousandfold speedup relative to the original WaveNet. It also supports multiple English and Japanese voices in a production setting. These findings connect the training method to a concrete deployment outcome: retaining high speech quality while making generation fast enough for practical, real-time use.
summary.tldr: Probability Density Distillation trains a parallel WaveNet-derived generator with no significant quality difference and a reported thousandfold synthesis speedup.

title: Parallel WaveNet: Fast High-Fidelity Speech Synthesis

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks have shown remarkable success in learning a distribution that faithfully recovers a reference distribution in its entirety. However, in some cases, we may want to only learn some aspects (e.g., cluster or manifold structure), while modifying others (e.g., style, orientation or dimension). In this work, we propose an approach to learn generative models across such incomparable spaces, and demonstrate how to steer the learned distribution towards target properties. A key component of our model is the Gromov-Wasserstein distance, a notion of discrepancy that compares distributions relationally rather than absolutely. While this framework subsumes current generative models in identically reproducing distributions, its inherent flexibility allows application to tasks in manifold learning, relational learning and cross-domain learning.

However, in some cases, we may want to only learn some aspects (e.g., cluster or manifold structure), while modifying others (e.g., style, orientation or dimension). While this framework subsumes current generative models in identically reproducing distributions, its inherent flexibility allows application to tasks in manifold learning, relational learning and cross-domain learning.

paragraphs: Generative modeling often aims to reproduce a reference distribution as faithfully as possible. This paper considers a different goal: preserving selected aspects of a distribution while deliberately changing others. For example, a model may retain cluster or manifold structure while changing style, orientation, or even the dimension of the space containing the data.

The proposed approach uses Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which compares distributions through relationships within them rather than direct comparisons between their coordinates. This relational perspective makes it possible to connect spaces that are not directly comparable. The model can therefore use structural agreement as its guide while allowing other properties of the generated distribution to change.

The authors demonstrate how to steer generated distributions toward target properties. Their framework also includes ordinary distribution reproduction as a special case, so structural transfer and faithful copying fit within the same formulation. Its flexibility supports applications to manifold learning, relational learning, and cross-domain learning. The contribution is a way to specify what should remain similar when matching an entire distribution would be unnecessarily restrictive.
summary.tldr: Gromov-Wasserstein distance enables generators to preserve relational structure while changing properties such as style, orientation, or dimensionality.

title: Learning Generative Models across Incomparable Spaces

abstract: We improve the efficiency of algorithms for stochastic combinatorial semi-bandits. In most interesting problems, state-of-the-art algorithms take advantage of structural properties of rewards, such as independence. However, while being minimax optimal in terms of regret, these algorithms are intractable. In our paper, we first reduce their implementation to a specific submodular maximization. Then, in case of matroid constraints, we design adapted approximation routines, thereby providing the first efficient algorithms that exploit the reward structure. In particular, we improve the state-of-the-art efficient gap-free regret bound by a factor sqrt(k), where k is the maximum action size. Finally, we show how our improvement translates to more general budgeted combinatorial semi-bandits.

In most interesting problems, state-of-the-art algorithms take advantage of structural properties of rewards, such as independence. However, while being minimax optimal in terms of regret, these algorithms are intractable. In our paper, we first reduce their implementation to a specific submodular maximization. paragraphs: Combinatorial semi-bandit problems involve repeatedly selecting combinations of items while learning about their uncertain rewards. Reward structure, such as independence, can help an algorithm make better decisions. The paper addresses a computational obstacle: existing algorithms that exploit such structure can achieve optimal worst-case regret while being intractable to implement.

The authors first express the implementation problem as a particular submodular maximization problem. They then develop approximation routines adapted to matroid constraints, which restrict the combinations that an action may contain. This connects a difficult learning procedure to an optimization problem for which tailored approximations make efficient execution possible.

The resulting algorithms are presented as the first efficient methods that exploit the reward structure in this setting. Their gap-free regret bound improves the previous efficient bound by a factor of the square root of k, where k is the maximum action size. Thus, the theoretical improvement grows with the size of allowable actions. The authors also show how the gain extends to more general budget-constrained combinatorial semi-bandit problems.
summary.tldr: Tailored submodular approximations make reward-structure-aware matroid semi-bandits efficient and improve their gap-free regret bound by a factor of √k.

title: Exploiting structure of uncertainty for efficient matroid semi-bandits

abstract: Nonconvex regularizers have been successfully used in low-rank matrix learning. In this paper, we extend this to the more challenging problem of low-rank tensor completion. Based on the proximal average algorithm, we develop an efficient solver that avoids expensive tensor folding and unfolding. A special “sparse plus low-rank" structure, which is essential for fast computation of individual proximal steps, is maintained throughout the iterations. We also incorporate adaptive momentum to further speed up empirical convergence. Convergence results to critical points are provided under smoothness and Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz conditions. Experimental results on a number of synthetic and real-world data sets show that the proposed algorithm is more efficient in both time and space, and is also more accurate than existing approaches.

Based on the proximal average algorithm, we develop an efficient solver that avoids expensive tensor folding and unfolding. A special “sparse plus low-rank" structure, which is essential for fast computation of individual proximal steps, is maintained throughout the iterations. We also incorporate adaptive momentum to further speed up empirical convergence. Convergence results to critical points are provided under smoothness and Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz conditions. Experimental results on a number of synthetic and real-world data sets show that the proposed algorithm is more efficient in both time and space, and is also more accurate than existing approaches.

paragraphs: Low-rank tensor completion fills missing entries in multiway data by exploiting a compact underlying structure. This paper brings nonconvex regularizers, previously successful in low-rank matrix learning, to the more challenging tensor setting. Its central concern is making the resulting optimization efficient enough to benefit from that modeling choice.

The solver builds on the proximal average algorithm and preserves a sparse-plus-low-rank representation throughout its iterations. Maintaining this structure makes individual proximal updates faster and avoids expensive folding and unfolding of tensors. Adaptive momentum is added to accelerate empirical convergence, so both the data representation and the update process contribute to the computational approach.

The authors provide convergence results to critical points under smoothness and Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz conditions. These results concern critical points rather than a guaranteed global optimum. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the method is reported to use less time and space and achieve higher accuracy than existing approaches. Together, the results support combining nonconvex regularization with an implementation that explicitly preserves useful tensor structure.
summary.tldr: A tensor-completion solver preserves sparse-plus-low-rank structure to improve efficiency and accuracy, with conditional convergence guarantees to critical points.

title: Efficient Nonconvex Regularized Tensor Completion with Structure-aware Proximal Iterations

abstract: There is a growing amount of literature on the relationship between wide neural networks (NNs) and Gaussian processes (GPs), identifying an equivalence between the two for a variety of NN architectures. This equivalence enables, for instance, accurate approximation of the behaviour of wide Bayesian NNs without MCMC or variational approximations, or characterisation of the distribution of randomly initialised wide NNs optimised by gradient descent without ever running an optimiser. We provide a rigorous extension of these results to NNs involving attention layers, showing that unlike single-head attention, which induces non-Gaussian behaviour, multi-head attention architectures behave as GPs as the number of heads tends to infinity. We further discuss the effects of positional encodings and layer normalisation, and propose modifications of the attention mechanism which lead to improved results for both finite and infinitely wide NNs. We evaluate attention kernels empirically, leading to a moderate improvement upon the previous state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10 for GPs without trainable kernels and advanced data preprocessing. Finally, we introduce new features to the Neural Tangents library (Novak et al.,2020) allowing applications of NNGP/NTK models, with and without attention, to variable-length sequences, with an example on the IMDb reviews dataset.

This paper extends that theory to networks containing attention layers. A central finding is that attention’s structure matters: single-head attention produces non-Gaussian behavior, while multi-head attention approaches Gaussian-process behavior as the number of heads grows without bound.

The authors also examine how positional encodings and layer normalization affect these models. They propose attention modifications that improve results for both finite networks and their infinite-width counterparts. This connects the limiting theory to architectural choices that also matter in networks with finite computational resources.

Empirical evaluation of attention kernels yields a moderate CIFAR-10 improvement over the previous best results within the stated category of Gaussian processes without trainable kernels or advanced preprocessing. The work also extends the Neural Tangents library to support variable-length sequences for NNGP and NTK models, including attention-based versions, and demonstrates that capability on IMDb reviews.
summary.tldr: Multi-head attention has a Gaussian-process limit as head count grows, enabling theoretical analysis and practical attention-kernel models.

title: Infinite attention: NNGP and NTK for deep attention networks

abstract: Uncertainty quantification is a fundamental yet unsolved problem for deep learning. The Bayesian framework provides a principled way of uncertainty estimation but is often not scalable to modern deep neural nets (DNNs) that have a large number of parameters. Non-Bayesian methods are simple to implement but often conflate different sources of uncertainties and require huge computing resources. We propose a new method for quantifying uncertainties of DNNs from a dynamical system perspective. The core of our method is to view DNN transformations as state evolution of a stochastic dynamical system and introduce a Brownian motion term for capturing epistemic uncertainty. Based on this perspective, we propose a neural stochastic differential equation model (SDE-Net) which consists of (1) a drift net that controls the system to fit the predictive function; and (2) a diffusion net that captures epistemic uncertainty. We theoretically analyze the existence and uniqueness of the solution to SDE-Net. Our experiments demonstrate that the SDE-Net model can outperform existing uncertainty estimation methods across a series of tasks where uncertainty plays a fundamental role.

This paper approaches that problem through dynamical systems, viewing the network's transformations as the evolution of a state. It introduces stochastic evolution to represent epistemic uncertainty, the uncertainty associated with what the model has learned.

The resulting SDE-Net contains two networks with distinct responsibilities. A drift network controls the evolution needed to fit the predictive function, while a diffusion network captures epistemic uncertainty through a Brownian motion term. This gives uncertainty an explicit role in the model's dynamics, alongside the component responsible for prediction.

The authors theoretically analyze whether the SDE-Net solution exists and is unique. Experiments across tasks where uncertainty matters show that SDE-Net can outperform existing uncertainty estimation methods. The contribution combines a structured dynamical formulation, analysis of its mathematical behavior, and empirical evidence of usefulness. The reported comparisons establish that improvements are possible on the evaluated tasks rather than claiming universal superiority.
summary.tldr: SDE-Net separates predictive dynamics from stochastic uncertainty modeling and can outperform existing uncertainty methods on the evaluated tasks.

title: SDE-Net: Equipping Deep Neural Networks with Uncertainty Estimates

abstract: We present an explicit deep neural network construction that transforms uniformly distributed one-dimensional noise into an arbitrarily close approximation of any two-dimensional Lipschitz-continuous target distribution. The key ingredient of our design is a generalization of the "space-filling" property of sawtooth functions discovered in (Bailey & Telgarsky, 2018). We elicit the importance of depth - in our neural network construction - in driving the Wasserstein distance between the target distribution and the approximation realized by the network to zero. An extension to output distributions of arbitrary dimension is outlined. Finally, we show that the proposed construction does not incur a cost - in terms of error measured in Wasserstein-distance - relative to generating $d$-dimensional target distributions from $d$ independent random variables.

It gives an explicit construction that starts with a single uniformly distributed noise variable and produces an arbitrarily close approximation to any two-dimensional target distribution satisfying the stated Lipschitz-continuity condition. Approximation quality is measured using Wasserstein distance.

The construction builds on a generalized space-filling property of sawtooth functions. This provides a concrete mechanism for transforming one-dimensional noise into a distribution that approximates a higher-dimensional target. The analysis highlights network depth as an important ingredient in making the Wasserstein error approach zero.

The authors also outline an extension to output distributions of arbitrary dimension. They show that the proposed construction incurs no additional Wasserstein-error cost relative to generating a d-dimensional target from d independent random variables. The comparison concerns approximation error in this distance. The result establishes a constructive representational capability: under the stated target conditions, low-dimensional input noise can support increasingly accurate distribution generation through a deep network.
summary.tldr: An explicit deep ReLU construction transforms one-dimensional uniform noise into arbitrarily accurate Wasserstein approximations of Lipschitz-continuous two-dimensional distributions.

title: Constructive Universal High-Dimensional Distribution Generation through Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: Gaussian noise injections (GNIs) are a family of simple and widely-used regularisation methods for training neural networks, where one injects additive or multiplicative Gaussian noise to the network activations at every iteration of the optimisation algorithm, which is typically chosen as stochastic gradient descent (SGD). In this paper, we focus on the so-called ‘implicit effect’ of GNIs, which is the effect of the injected noise on the dynamics of SGD. We show that this effect induces an \emph{asymmetric heavy-tailed noise} on SGD gradient updates. In order to model this modified dynamics, we first develop a Langevin-like stochastic differential equation that is driven by a general family of \emph{asymmetric} heavy-tailed noise. Using this model we then formally prove that GNIs induce an ‘implicit bias’, which varies depending on the heaviness of the tails and the level of asymmetry. Our empirical results confirm that different types of neural networks trained with GNIs are well-modelled by the proposed dynamics and that the implicit effect of these injections induces a bias that degrades the performance of networks.

paragraphs: Adding Gaussian noise to neural-network activations is a common regularization technique. The noise can be additive or multiplicative and is introduced during training. This paper examines its implicit effect: how those injections change the behavior of stochastic gradient descent, beyond their role as a regularization procedure.

The authors show that Gaussian activation noise induces asymmetric, heavy-tailed noise in gradient updates. Thus, the distribution of the injected noise does not directly describe the distribution of its consequences for optimization. To study those consequences, they develop a Langevin-like stochastic differential equation driven by a general family of asymmetric heavy-tailed noise.

Within that model, they prove that the injections create an implicit bias whose form depends on both tail heaviness and asymmetry. Experiments across different network types support the proposed description of the training dynamics and find that this implicit effect degrades performance. The findings identify a specific adverse mechanism in the studied settings, rather than establishing that every use of Gaussian noise must reduce overall performance.
summary.tldr: Gaussian activation noise can produce asymmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise, creating an implicit optimization bias that degraded performance in the reported experiments.

title: Asymmetric Heavy Tails and Implicit Bias in Gaussian Noise Injections

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) is a widely used technique for distribution alignment, with applications throughout the machine learning, graphics, and vision communities. Without any additional structural assumptions on transport, however, OT can be fragile to outliers or noise, especially in high dimensions. Here, we introduce Latent Optimal Transport (LOT), a new approach for OT that simultaneously learns low-dimensional structure in data while leveraging this structure to solve the alignment task. The idea behind our approach is to learn two sets of “anchors” that constrain the flow of transport between a source and target distribution. In both theoretical and empirical studies, we show that LOT regularizes the rank of transport and makes it more robust to outliers and the sampling density. We show that by allowing the source and target to have different anchors, and using LOT to align the latent spaces between anchors, the resulting transport plan has better structural interpretability and highlights connections between both the individual data points and the local geometry of the datasets.

paragraphs: Optimal transport aligns distributions by describing how data mass should move from a source to a target. Without added structural assumptions, this alignment can be sensitive to noise and outliers, especially in high dimensions. Latent Optimal Transport, or LOT, addresses this by learning low-dimensional structure alongside the alignment.

LOT learns two sets of anchor points that constrain the transport flow. The source and target can have different anchors, and the method aligns the latent spaces between those anchors. This gives the transport plan an intermediate structure that reflects how points relate to their respective datasets, rather than relying only on direct point-level connections.

Theoretical and empirical studies show that LOT regularizes transport rank and improves robustness to outliers and sampling density. The authors also report better structural interpretability: the plan exposes relationships among individual points and the local geometry of the datasets. The anchors therefore serve both a statistical role in constraining transport and an explanatory role in making the alignment easier to understand.
summary.tldr: Latent Optimal Transport routes alignment through learned anchors to improve robustness and reveal the datasets’ local structure.

title: Making transport more robust and interpretable by moving data through a small number of anchor points

abstract: We show that the error of iteratively magnitude-pruned networks empirically follows a scaling law with interpretable coefficients that depend on the architecture and task. We functionally approximate the error of the pruned networks, showing it is predictable in terms of an invariant tying width, depth, and pruning level, such that networks of vastly different pruned densities are interchangeable. We demonstrate the accuracy of this approximation over orders of magnitude in depth, width, dataset size, and density. We show that the functional form holds (generalizes) for large scale data (e.g., ImageNet) and architectures (e.g., ResNets). As neural networks become ever larger and costlier to train, our findings suggest a framework for reasoning conceptually and analytically about a standard method for unstructured pruning.

paragraphs: Pruning removes network parameters, raising the question of how much predictive performance changes as the remaining network becomes sparse. This paper finds that the error of iteratively magnitude-pruned networks empirically follows a scaling law. Its coefficients have interpretations and depend on the architecture and task, giving the relationship a structured form.

The authors approximate prediction error using an invariant that combines network width, depth, and pruning level. Within this approximation, networks with very different remaining parameter densities can be interchangeable in terms of error. This connects several design choices through one relationship instead of examining the effect of each choice separately.

The approximation is accurate across orders of magnitude in depth, width, dataset size, and density. The authors also show that its functional form generalizes to large-scale settings, including ImageNet and ResNets. These are empirical findings about the studied pruning process. They suggest a framework for reasoning about the performance consequences of unstructured pruning as network size and training cost continue to grow.
summary.tldr: An empirical scaling law predicts magnitude-pruned network error through a relationship among width, depth, and pruning level.

title: On the Predictability of Pruning Across Scales

abstract: The Euclidean projection onto a convex set is an important problem that arises in numerous constrained optimization tasks. Unfortunately, in many cases, computing projections is computationally demanding. In this work, we focus on projection problems where the constraints are smooth and the number of constraints is significantly smaller than the dimension. The runtime of existing approaches to solving such problems is either cubic in the dimension or polynomial in the inverse of the target accuracy. Conversely, we propose a simple and efficient primal-dual approach, with a runtime that scales only linearly with the dimension, and only logarithmically in the inverse of the target accuracy. We empirically demonstrate its performance, and compare it with standard baselines.

paragraphs: Euclidean projection finds the point in a permitted convex set that is closest to a given point. It appears in many constrained optimization procedures, but computing the projection can itself be expensive. This paper focuses on problems with smooth constraints and substantially fewer constraints than dimensions.

The authors propose a primal-dual method for this setting. Its runtime scales linearly with the dimension and logarithmically with the inverse of the requested accuracy. The abstract contrasts this with existing approaches whose runtime is either cubic in dimension or polynomial in inverse accuracy. Those dependencies matter because both high dimension and a demand for greater precision can otherwise make projection costly.

The contribution is therefore a more favorable computational scaling for a particular class of projection problems. The assumptions about smoothness and the relatively small number of constraints define the setting of the result. The paper also presents empirical performance comparisons with standard baselines, adding an experimental assessment to its runtime analysis.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual method accelerates projection with smooth convex constraints when the number of constraints is much smaller than the dimension.

title: Fast Projection Onto Convex Smooth Constraints

abstract: While normalizing flows for continuous data have been extensively researched, flows for discrete data have only recently been explored. These prior models, however, suffer from limitations that are distinct from those of continuous flows. Most notably, discrete flow-based models cannot be straightforwardly optimized with conventional deep learning methods because gradients of discrete functions are undefined or zero. Previous works approximate pseudo-gradients of the discrete functions but do not solve the problem on a fundamental level. In addition to that, backpropagation can be computationally burdensome compared to alternative discrete algorithms such as decision tree algorithms. Our approach seeks to reduce computational burden and remove the need for pseudo-gradients by developing a discrete flow based on decision trees—building upon the success of efficient tree-based methods for classification and regression for discrete data. We first define a tree-structured permutation (TSP) that compactly encodes a permutation of discrete data where the inverse is easy to compute; thus, we can efficiently compute the density value and sample new data. We then propose a decision tree algorithm to build TSPs that learns the tree structure and permutations at each node via novel criteria. We empirically demonstrate the feasibility of our method on multiple datasets.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows for discrete data face a training obstacle: discrete operations can have gradients that are zero or undefined. Earlier approaches use approximate pseudo-gradients, while backpropagation itself can add computational burden. This paper develops a decision-tree-based flow that avoids needing those pseudo-gradients and seeks a less burdensome training procedure.

Its basic building block is a tree-structured permutation. This compactly represents a rearrangement of discrete data and makes the inverse transformation easy to compute. Efficient inversion matters because the model must support both assigning density values to observations and generating new samples. The tree structure provides a way to organize these reversible transformations.

The authors then design a decision tree algorithm that learns both the tree's structure and the permutations stored at its nodes using new criteria. Learning therefore proceeds through a discrete tree-building procedure. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the method's feasibility. The stated result establishes that this alternative can work in practice, while the methodological contribution is a discrete flow whose training does not depend on pseudo-gradient approximations.
summary.tldr: Tree-structured permutations enable discrete normalizing flows that learn through decision-tree algorithms without pseudo-gradients.

title: Discrete Tree Flows via Tree-Structured Permutations

abstract: To obtain higher sample efficiency and superior final performance simultaneously has been one of the major challenges for deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Previous work could handle one of these challenges but typically failed to address them concurrently. In this paper, we try to tackle these two challenges simultaneously. To achieve this, we firstly decouple these challenges into two classic RL problems: data richness and exploration-exploitation trade-off. Then, we cast these two problems into the training data distribution optimization problem, namely to obtain desired training data within limited interactions, and address them concurrently via i) explicit modeling and control of the capacity and diversity of behavior policy and ii) more fine-grained and adaptive control of selective/sampling distribution of the behavior policy using a monotonic data distribution optimization. Finally, we integrate this process into Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI) and obtain a more general framework called Generalized Data Distribution Iteration (GDI). We use the GDI framework to introduce operator-based versions of well-known RL methods from DQN to Agent57. Theoretical guarantee of the superiority of GDI compared with GPI is concluded. We also demonstrate our state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), wherein our algorithm has achieved 9620.98% mean human normalized score (HNS), 1146.39% median HNS, and surpassed 22 human world records using only 200M training frames. Our performance is comparable to Agent57’s while we consume 500 times less data. We argue that there is still a long way to go before obtaining real superhuman agents in ALE.

summary.tldr: GDI optimizes behavior-policy diversity and data sampling together, delivering strong Atari performance with substantially fewer training frames than Agent57.

title: Generalized Data Distribution Iteration

abstract: We propose a fully unsupervised method to detect bias in contextualized embeddings. The method leverages the assortative information latently encoded by social networks and combines orthogonality regularization, structured sparsity learning, and graph neural networks to find the embedding subspace capturing this information. As a concrete example, we focus on the phenomenon of ideological bias: we introduce the concept of an ideological subspace, show how it can be found by applying our method to online discussion forums, and present techniques to probe it. Our experiments suggest that the ideological subspace encodes abstract evaluative semantics and reflects changes in the political left-right spectrum during the presidency of Donald Trump.

paragraphs: Contextualized embeddings represent language in ways that depend on its surrounding text. This paper proposes a fully unsupervised method for detecting bias within those representations. Its source of information is the structure of social networks, specifically the assortative patterns they implicitly encode. The method seeks an embedding subspace that captures information associated with those patterns.

The approach combines graph neural networks, orthogonality regularization, and structured sparsity learning. Together, these components support identifying the relevant portion of the embedding space. The authors develop ideological bias as a concrete application, introduce an ideological subspace, and show how to recover and probe it using online discussion forums.

The experiments suggest that this subspace contains abstract evaluative semantics and reflects changes in the political left–right spectrum during Donald Trump’s presidency. These are qualified empirical interpretations of the recovered representation. The contribution is a way to investigate socially associated information inside contextualized embeddings without supervised bias labels, using network structure to guide the discovery.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised method uses social-network structure to identify embedding subspaces associated with bias, demonstrated through ideological information in discussion forums.

title: Unsupervised Detection of Contextualized Embedding Bias with Application to Ideology

abstract: We introduce a method for policy improvement that interpolates between the greedy approach of value-based reinforcement learning (RL) and the full planning approach typical of model-based RL. The new method builds on the concept of a geometric horizon model (GHM, also known as a \gamma-model), which models the discounted state-visitation distribution of a given policy. We show that we can evaluate any non-Markov policy that switches between a set of base Markov policies with fixed probability by a careful composition of the base policy GHMs, without any additional learning. We can then apply generalised policy improvement (GPI) to collections of such non-Markov policies to obtain a new Markov policy that will in general outperform its precursors. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis of this approach, develop applications to transfer and standard RL, and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness over standard GPI on a challenging deep RL continuous control task. We also provide an analysis of GHM training methods, proving a novel convergence result regarding previously proposed methods and showing how to train these models stably in deep RL settings.

paragraphs: The paper develops policy improvement between two familiar approaches: greedy value-based decisions and full model-based planning. It builds on geometric horizon models, which describe the discounted distribution of states visited under a policy. These models provide information about a policy's future behavior that can be reused when evaluating combinations of policies.

The authors show how to compose models of base Markov policies to evaluate non-Markov policies that switch among those bases with fixed probability. This evaluation requires no additional learning. Generalised policy improvement can then use a collection of these switching policies to produce a new Markov policy that will generally outperform its precursors.

The work includes theoretical analysis and applications to both transfer and standard reinforcement learning. On a challenging deep continuous-control task, the method improves empirically over standard generalised policy improvement. The authors also analyze how geometric horizon models are trained, proving a new convergence result for previously proposed methods and showing how to train the models stably in deep reinforcement-learning settings.
summary.tldr: Composing geometric horizon models evaluates switching policies without additional learning and enables a richer form of generalised policy improvement.

title: Generalised Policy Improvement with Geometric Policy Composition

abstract: Commonsense causality reasoning (CCR) aims at identifying plausible causes and effects in natural language descriptions that are deemed reasonable by an average person. Although being of great academic and practical interest, this problem is still shadowed by the lack of a well-posed theoretical framework; existing work usually relies on deep language models wholeheartedly, and is potentially susceptible to confounding co-occurrences. Motivated by classical causal principles, we articulate the central question of CCR and draw parallels between human subjects in observational studies and natural languages to adopt CCR to the potential-outcomes framework, which is the first such attempt for commonsense tasks. We propose a novel framework, ROCK, to Reason O(A)bout Commonsense K(C)ausality, which utilizes temporal signals as incidental supervision, and balances confounding effects using temporal propensities that are analogous to propensity scores. The ROCK implementation is modular and zero-shot, and demonstrates good CCR capabilities.

paragraphs: Commonsense causal reasoning asks which causes and effects seem plausible in natural-language descriptions. Language models can help with this task, but recurring associations may reflect confounding rather than causation. This paper develops a causal-inference framing to make the question more precise and reduce reliance on uncorrected co-occurrence patterns.

The authors draw an analogy between subjects in observational studies and natural-language descriptions, adapting the potential-outcomes framework to commonsense reasoning. Their method, ROCK, uses temporal signals as incidental supervision. It then balances confounding effects through temporal propensities, which play a role analogous to propensity scores in observational causal analysis.

The implementation is modular and zero-shot, and the authors report good commonsense causal reasoning capabilities. The contribution is both conceptual and methodological: it supplies a framework for articulating the causal question and a mechanism for addressing confounding within the reasoning process. Temporal information therefore supports both supervision and adjustment, connecting familiar causal principles to reasoning over language.
summary.tldr: ROCK adapts potential-outcomes reasoning and temporal propensity adjustment to zero-shot commonsense causal reasoning in language.

title: ROCK: Causal Inference Principles for Reasoning about Commonsense Causality

abstract: Recently, random feature attentions (RFAs) are proposed to approximate the softmax attention in linear time and space complexity by linearizing the exponential kernel. In this paper, we first propose a novel perspective to understand the bias in such approximation by recasting RFAs as self-normalized importance samplers. This perspective further sheds light on an unbiased estimator for the whole softmax attention, called randomized attention (RA). RA constructs positive random features via query-specific distributions and enjoys greatly improved approximation fidelity, albeit exhibiting quadratic complexity. By combining the expressiveness in RA and the efficiency in RFA, we develop a novel linear complexity self-attention mechanism called linear randomized attention (LARA). Extensive experiments across various domains demonstrate that RA and LARA significantly improve the performance of RFAs by a substantial margin.

RA constructs positive random features via query-specific distributions and enjoys greatly improved approximation fidelity, albeit exhibiting quadratic complexity. By combining the expressiveness in RA and the efficiency in RFA, we develop a novel linear complexity self-attention mechanism called linear randomized attention (LARA). Extensive experiments across various domains demonstrate that RA and LARA significantly improve the performance of RFAs by a substantial margin.

paragraphs: Random-feature attention approximates softmax attention while reducing time and memory requirements to linear complexity. This paper examines why that approximation is biased by interpreting it as self-normalized importance sampling. The interpretation connects the attention approximation to a statistical estimation problem and guides the design of alternative estimators.

The authors first introduce randomized attention, or RA, an unbiased estimator of the complete softmax attention operation. RA constructs positive random features from distributions tailored to individual queries, substantially improving approximation fidelity. Its cost remains quadratic, however, so the more faithful estimator alone does not retain the efficiency advantage of conventional random-feature attention.

The paper then develops linear randomized attention, or LARA, combining RA's expressive approach with the efficiency of random-feature attention. LARA has linear complexity, while the unbiasedness claim in the abstract specifically belongs to RA. Experiments across multiple domains show substantial performance improvements over random-feature attention for both methods. The contribution thus connects an explanation of approximation bias to a more accurate estimator and a separate efficient attention mechanism.
summary.tldr: A sampling-based analysis leads to unbiased randomized attention and to LARA, a linear-complexity mechanism that improves on random-feature attention.

title: Linear Complexity Randomized Self-attention Mechanism

abstract: In this work we focus our attention on distributed optimization problems in the context where the communication time between the server and the workers is non-negligible. We obtain novel methods supporting bidirectional compression (both from the server to the workers and vice versa) that enjoy new state-of-the-art theoretical communication complexity for convex and nonconvex problems. Our bounds are the first that manage to decouple the variance/error coming from the workers-to-server and server-to-workers compression, transforming a multiplicative dependence to an additive one. Moreover, in the convex regime, we obtain the first bounds that match the theoretical communication complexity of gradient descent. Even in this convex regime, our algorithms work with biased gradient estimators, which is non-standard and requires new proof techniques that may be of independent interest. Finally, our theoretical results are corroborated through suitable experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides work between a server and multiple workers, but exchanging information can consume substantial time. Compression reduces what must be sent while introducing error into the optimization process. This paper develops methods that support compression in both directions and analyzes the resulting communication requirements for convex and nonconvex problems.

The central theoretical improvement separates the effects of worker-to-server and server-to-worker compression. Earlier bounds combined these error or variance contributions multiplicatively; the new bounds combine them additively. This changes how the two communication bottlenecks interact in the analysis and yields improved theoretical communication complexity.

The contribution therefore includes both communication-efficient algorithms and an analysis showing how bidirectional compression can be controlled without the previously multiplicative dependence between its two sources of error.
summary.tldr: New distributed optimization methods improve communication bounds by separating the errors introduced by compression in each direction.

title: EF21-P and Friends: Improved Theoretical Communication Complexity for Distributed Optimization with Bidirectional Compression

abstract: The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is a seminal approach in deep generative modeling with latent variables. Interpreting its reconstruction process as a nonlinear transformation of samples from the latent posterior distribution, we apply the Unscented Transform (UT) – a well-known distribution approximation used in the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) from the field of filtering. A finite set of statistics called sigma points, sampled deterministically, provides a more informative and lower-variance posterior representation than the ubiquitous noise-scaling of the reparameterization trick, while ensuring higher-quality reconstruction. We further boost the performance by replacing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence with the Wasserstein distribution metric that allows for a sharper posterior. Inspired by the two components, we derive a novel, deterministic-sampling flavor of the VAE, the Unscented Autoencoder (UAE), trained purely with regularization-like terms on the per-sample posterior. We empirically show competitive performance in Fréchet Inception Distance scores over closely-related models, in addition to a lower training variance than the VAE.

summary.tldr: The Unscented Autoencoder combines deterministic sigma-point sampling with Wasserstein regularization, reporting competitive generation scores and lower training variance than a VAE.

title: Unscented Autoencoder

abstract: The success of graph neural networks (GNNs) provokes the question about explainability: “Which fraction of the input graph is the most determinant of the prediction?” Particularly, parametric explainers prevail in existing approaches because of their more robust capability to decipher the black-box (i.e., target GNNs). In this paper, based on the observation that graphs typically share some common motif patterns, we propose a novel non-parametric subgraph matching framework, dubbed MatchExplainer, to explore explanatory subgraphs. It couples the target graph with other counterpart instances and identifies the most crucial joint substructure by minimizing the node corresponding-based distance. Moreover, we note that present graph sampling or node-dropping methods usually suffer from the false positive sampling problem. To alleviate this issue, we design a new augmentation paradigm named MatchDrop. It takes advantage of MatchExplainer to fix the most informative portion of the graph and merely operates graph augmentations on the rest less informative part. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show the effectiveness of our MatchExplainer by outperforming all state-of-the-art parametric baselines with significant margins. Results also demonstrate that MatchDrop is a general scheme to be equipped with GNNs for enhanced performance. The code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/MatchExplainer.

This paper builds on the observation that graphs commonly share recurring motifs. It proposes using those shared structures to find explanatory subgraphs through non-parametric matching, offering an alternative to prevailing parametric explainers.

MatchExplainer pairs a target graph with counterpart instances and searches for a crucial shared substructure. It does so by minimizing a distance based on node correspondences. The comparison between instances is central: recurring structure provides the basis for identifying the graph portion that serves as the explanation.

The authors also introduce MatchDrop to address false positive sampling in graph sampling or node-dropping approaches. MatchDrop preserves the portion identified as most informative and applies augmentation to the less informative remainder. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over the compared state-of-the-art parametric explainers. They also show that MatchDrop can enhance GNN performance, connecting explanation-derived structure to a practical graph augmentation strategy.
summary.tldr: MatchExplainer finds explanatory graph structures by matching instances, and MatchDrop preserves those structures during augmentation.

title: Rethinking Explaining Graph Neural Networks via Non-parametric Subgraph Matching

abstract: Does the dominant approach to learn representations (as a side effect of optimizing an expected cost for a single training distribution) remain a good approach when we are dealing with multiple distributions? Our thesis is that such scenarios are better served by representations that are richer than those obtained with a single optimization episode. We support this thesis with simple theoretical arguments and with experiments utilizing an apparently näive ensembling technique: concatenating the representations obtained from multiple training episodes using the same data, model, algorithm, and hyper-parameters, but different random seeds. These independently trained networks perform similarly. Yet, in a number of scenarios involving new distributions, the concatenated representation performs substantially better than an equivalently sized network trained with a single training run. This proves that the representations constructed by multiple training episodes are in fact different. Although their concatenation carries little additional information about the training task under the training distribution, it becomes substantially more informative when tasks or distributions change. Meanwhile, a single training episode is unlikely to yield such a redundant representation because the optimization process has no reason to accumulate features that do not incrementally improve the training performance.

paragraphs: A representation learned for one task and distribution may omit features that become useful elsewhere. This paper argues that preparing for changing tasks or distributions calls for richer representations than a single training run tends to produce. It supports that argument with simple theory and an experiment based on combining independently learned features.

The authors train networks using identical data, models, algorithms, and hyperparameters, changing only the random seed. They then concatenate the resulting representations. Although the individual networks perform similarly, their combined representation substantially outperforms an equivalently sized network trained once in a number of scenarios involving new distributions.

The findings show that similar training performance can conceal meaningful differences in learned representations. Features from separate runs add little information for the original task under its original distribution, yet can become much more informative after a shift. The proposed explanation is that one optimization run has little incentive to collect features that do not incrementally improve its training objective, even if those features could help later.
summary.tldr: Combining representations from different random-seed training runs improves transfer in several settings where tasks or distributions change.

title: Learning useful representations for shifting tasks and distributions

abstract: Multi-task learning, which optimizes performance across multiple tasks, is inherently a multi-objective optimization problem. Various algorithms are developed to provide discrete trade-off solutions on the Pareto front. Recently, continuous Pareto front approximations using a linear combination of base networks have emerged as a compelling strategy. However, it suffers from scalability issues when the number of tasks is large. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that integrates a main network with several low-rank matrices to efficiently learn the Pareto manifold. It significantly reduces the number of parameters and facilitates the extraction of shared features. We also introduce orthogonal regularization to further bolster performance. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, especially on datasets with a large number of tasks.

paragraphs: Learning several tasks together requires choosing how to balance their objectives. A Pareto front describes trade-offs where improving one objective comes at a cost to another. Instead of producing only a few separate solutions, recent methods approximate a continuous range of trade-offs by combining base networks. The paper addresses the difficulty of scaling that strategy to many tasks.

The proposed architecture combines a main network with several low-rank matrices. This reduces the number of parameters needed to represent the Pareto manifold and helps extract features shared across tasks. The authors also introduce orthogonal regularization as an additional component intended to improve performance. Together, these choices provide a more compact way to learn a family of task balances.

Extensive experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, especially on datasets containing many tasks. This pattern directly supports the method’s scaling motivation: a compact representation of task variation becomes particularly useful as the number of objectives grows. The contribution concerns both parameter efficiency and the quality of the learned trade-off solutions.
summary.tldr: A shared network with low-rank matrices learns task trade-offs more compactly and improves reported performance, especially when many tasks are involved.

title: Efficient Pareto Manifold Learning with Low-Rank Structure

abstract: Many computational factors limit broader deployment of large language models. In this paper, we focus on a memory bottleneck imposed by the key-value (KV) cache, a computational shortcut that requires storing previous KV pairs during decoding. While existing KV cache methods approach this problem by pruning or evicting large swaths of relatively less important KV pairs to dramatically reduce the memory footprint of the cache, they can have limited success in tasks that require recollecting a majority of previous tokens. To alleviate this issue, we propose LESS, a simple integration of a (nearly free) constant sized cache with eviction-based cache methods, such that all tokens can be queried at later decoding steps. Its ability to retain information throughout time shows merit on a variety of tasks where we demonstrate LESS can help reduce the performance gap from caching everything, sometimes even matching it, all while being efficient. Relevant code can be found at https://github.com/hdong920/LESS.

paragraphs: A language model’s key-value cache stores information from earlier tokens so decoding can reuse previous computation. That shortcut creates a memory bottleneck as more information accumulates. Existing compression methods reduce memory by dropping many cached entries, but this can hurt tasks that require recalling information spread across much of the earlier text.

LESS supplements eviction-based methods with a constant-sized cache described as nearly free. The additional cache retains information over time so that all tokens can still be queried at later decoding steps. Its purpose is to preserve a route to earlier information while continuing to benefit from the memory savings of removing individual cache entries.

Across a variety of tasks, the reported results show that LESS narrows the performance gap between compressed caching and retaining the full cache. In some cases it matches full-cache performance while remaining efficient. The finding supports this combination of selective retention and a compact persistent memory, particularly for tasks where discarding earlier information would otherwise reduce performance.
summary.tldr: LESS adds a constant-sized memory to cache-eviction methods, helping preserve earlier-token information and sometimes matching full-cache performance.

title: Get More with LESS: Synthesizing Recurrence with KV Cache Compression for Efficient LLM Inference

abstract: This study designs an adaptive experiment for efficiently estimating average treatment effects (ATEs). In each round of our adaptive experiment, an experimenter sequentially samples an experimental unit, assigns a treatment, and observes the corresponding outcome immediately. At the end of the experiment, the experimenter estimates an ATE using the gathered samples. The objective is to estimate the ATE with a smaller asymptotic variance. Existing studies have designed experiments that adaptively optimize the propensity score (treatment-assignment probability). As a generalization of such an approach, we propose optimizing the covariate density as well as the propensity score. First, we derive the efficient covariate density and propensity score that minimize the semiparametric efficiency bound and find that optimizing both covariate density and propensity score minimizes the semiparametric efficiency bound more effectively than optimizing only the propensity score. Next, we design an adaptive experiment using the efficient covariate density and propensity score sequentially estimated during the experiment. Lastly, we propose an ATE estimator whose asymptotic variance aligns with the minimized semiparametric efficiency bound.

paragraphs: This paper designs experiments to estimate an average treatment effect more precisely. The experiment proceeds sequentially: an experimental unit is sampled, a treatment is assigned, and the outcome is observed immediately. These observations guide later decisions, and the collected data ultimately support an estimate of the treatment’s average effect.

Previous approaches adapt the probability of assigning a treatment. The authors expand the design choices to include the covariate density, meaning the distribution of observed characteristics among sampled units. They derive a joint choice of sampling distribution and treatment-assignment probability that minimizes the semiparametric efficiency bound, a theoretical benchmark for estimation variance. Optimizing both improves this bound more effectively than optimizing treatment assignment alone.

The proposed procedure estimates those efficient choices as the experiment unfolds and uses them to guide subsequent sampling and assignments. The authors also construct an estimator whose asymptotic variance reaches the minimized bound. The result concerns precision in the large-sample limit and shows the value of jointly choosing whom to sample and which treatment to assign.
summary.tldr: Jointly adapting participant sampling and treatment assignment yields an average treatment effect estimator that attains a minimized asymptotic variance bound.

title: Active Adaptive Experimental Design for Treatment Effect Estimation with Covariate Choice

abstract: The reasoning capabilities of the recent LLMs enable them to execute external function calls to overcome their inherent limitations, such as knowledge cutoffs, poor arithmetic skills, or lack of access to private data. This development has allowed LLMs to select and coordinate multiple functions based on the context to tackle more complex problems. However, current methods for function calling often require sequential reasoning and acting for each function which can result in high latency, cost, and sometimes inaccurate behavior. To address this, we introduce LLMCompiler, which executes functions in parallel to efficiently orchestrate multiple function calls. Drawing inspiration from the principles of classical compilers, LLMCompiler enables parallel function calling with three components: (i) a Function Calling Planner, formulating execution plans for function calling; (ii) a Task Fetching Unit, dispatching function calling tasks; and (iii) an Executor, executing these tasks in parallel. LLMCompiler automatically generates an optimized orchestration for the function calls and can be used with both open-source and closed-source models. We have benchmarked LLMCompiler on a range of tasks with different patterns of function calling. We observe consistent latency speedup of up to $3.7 \times$, cost savings of up to $6.7 \times$, and accuracy improvement of up to $\sim 9 %$ compared to ReAct.Our code is available at https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler.

The results suggest that organizing tool execution can improve efficiency and answer quality together.
summary.tldr: LLMCompiler plans and executes parallel function calls, reporting lower latency and cost and improved accuracy compared with ReAct.

title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling

abstract: Differential privacy is often studied under two different models of neighboring datasets: the add-remove model and the swap model. While the swap model is frequently used in the academic literature to simplify analysis, many practical applications rely on the more conservative add-remove model, where obtaining tight results can be difficult. Here, we study the problem of one-dimensional mean estimation under the add-remove model. We propose a new algorithm and show that it is min-max optimal, achieving the best possible constant in the leading term of the mean squared error for all $\epsilon$, and that this constant is the same as the optimal algorithm under the swap model. These results show that the add-remove and swap models give nearly identical errors for mean estimation, even though the add-remove model cannot treat the size of the dataset as public information. We also demonstrate empirically that our proposed algorithm yields at least a factor of two improvement in mean squared error over algorithms frequently used in practice. One of our main technical contributions is a new hourglass mechanism, which might be of independent interest in other scenarios.

paragraphs: Differential privacy can define neighboring datasets through adding or removing one record, or through swapping a record. These choices affect what an algorithm must protect. In the add-remove model, even dataset size cannot be treated as public information, making sharp accuracy guarantees more difficult to obtain.

The paper develops an algorithm for one-dimensional mean estimation under add-remove privacy. It proves minimax optimality, including the best possible constant in the leading mean-squared-error term for every privacy parameter epsilon. That constant matches the optimum under swap privacy. The result shows that these two privacy models can achieve nearly identical errors for this estimation problem despite their different treatment of dataset size.

The authors also report empirical mean-squared-error improvements of at least a factor of two over algorithms commonly used in practice. Their construction introduces an hourglass mechanism as a central technical contribution. They suggest that this mechanism might be useful elsewhere, while the optimality and empirical findings presented here concern the mean-estimation setting.
summary.tldr: An optimal private one-dimensional mean estimator matches the swap model's leading error constant while protecting dataset size under add-remove privacy.

title: Mean Estimation in the Add-Remove Model of Differential Privacy

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular method to optimize costly black-box functions, and meta-learning has emerged as a way to leverage knowledge from related tasks to optimize new tasks faster. However, existing meta-learning methods for BO rely on surrogate models that are not scalable or are sensitive to varying input scales and noise types across tasks. Moreover, they often overlook the uncertainty associated with task similarity, leading to unreliable task adaptation when a new task differs significantly or has not been sufficiently explored yet. We propose a novel meta-learning BO approach that bypasses the surrogate model and directly learns the utility of queries across tasks. It explicitly models task uncertainty and includes an auxiliary model to enable robust adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves strong performance and outperforms multiple meta-learning BO methods across various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization helps search for good settings when evaluating each candidate is expensive. Knowledge from related tasks can accelerate this search, but transferring it is difficult when tasks differ in scale or noise. Another problem is uncertainty about whether a new task actually resembles the tasks used to learn that knowledge.

MALIBO bypasses the surrogate model used by existing meta-learning approaches and instead learns the utility of candidate queries across tasks. This shifts the learned prediction toward which evaluations are useful to make. The method explicitly represents task uncertainty and adds an auxiliary model to support adaptation when a new task differs or has received little exploration.

The authors report strong results across multiple benchmarks, outperforming several meta-learning methods for Bayesian optimization. The approach matters because it treats transfer as uncertain rather than assuming that previous tasks are reliably informative. Its combination of query utility learning and adaptation mechanisms addresses both how to reuse experience and how to respond when that experience fits poorly.
summary.tldr: MALIBO learns query utility across tasks while modeling task uncertainty, improving adaptation and benchmark performance in Bayesian optimization.

title: MALIBO: Meta-learning for Likelihood-free Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Federated learning is widely used in medical applications for training global models without needing local data access, but varying computational capabilities and network architectures (system heterogeneity) across clients pose significant challenges in effectively aggregating information from non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) data (statistic heterogeneity). Current federated learning methods using knowledge distillation require public datasets, raising privacy and data collection issues. Additionally, these datasets require additional local computing and storage resources, which is a burden for medical institutions with limited hardware conditions. In this paper, we introduce a novel federated learning paradigm, named Model Heterogeneous personalized Federated Learning via Injection and Distillation (MH-pFLID). Our framework leverages a lightweight messenger model, eliminating the need for public datasets and reducing the training cost for each client. We also develops receiver and transmitter modules for each client to separate local biases from generalizable information, reducing biased data collection and mitigating client drift. Our experiments on various medical tasks including image classification, image segmentation, and time-series classification, show MH-pFLID outperforms state-of-the-art methods in all these areas and has good generalizability.

Our experiments on various medical tasks including image classification, image segmentation, and time-series classification, show MH-pFLID outperforms state-of-the-art methods in all these areas and has good generalizability.

paragraphs: Medical institutions participating in federated learning may have different hardware, network architectures, and patient-data distributions. These differences complicate sharing useful knowledge without accessing local data. Distillation-based approaches can additionally require public datasets, adding data-collection, storage, and computing burdens for institutions with limited resources.

MH-pFLID uses a lightweight messenger model to support personalized learning across heterogeneous client models. The framework removes the requirement for public datasets and reduces training costs for each participant. Receiver and transmitter modules aim to separate local biases from information that generalizes across clients, helping mitigate client drift and the effects of biased data collection.

The method is evaluated on medical image classification, image segmentation, and time-series classification. The authors report that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in all these evaluated task areas and shows good generalizability. The findings suggest that a compact communication mechanism and explicit handling of local differences can support effective collaboration across institutions, while allowing their models and data distributions to remain heterogeneous.
summary.tldr: MH-pFLID shares knowledge across heterogeneous medical models through a lightweight messenger, avoiding public datasets and improving results on the evaluated tasks.

title: MH-pFLID: Model Heterogeneous personalized Federated Learning via Injection and Distillation for Medical Data Analysis

abstract: Predicting the binding sites of target proteins plays a fundamental role in drug discovery. Most existing deep-learning methods consider a protein as a 3D image by spatially clustering its atoms into voxels and then feed the voxelized protein into a 3D CNN for prediction. However, the CNN-based methods encounter several critical issues: 1) defective in representing irregular protein structures; 2) sensitive to rotations; 3) insufficient to characterize the protein surface; 4) unaware of protein size shift. To address the above issues, this work proposes EquiPocket, an E(3)-equivariant Graph Neural Network (GNN) for binding site prediction, which comprises three modules: the first one to extract local geometric information for each surface atom, the second one to model both the chemical and spatial structure of protein and the last one to capture the geometry of the surface via equivariant message passing over the surface atoms. We further propose a dense attention output layer to alleviate the effect incurred by variable protein size. Extensive experiments on several representative benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our framework to the state-of-the-art methods.

Experiments on several representative benchmarks report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the proposed geometric representation for this prediction task, with the reported evidence focused on identifying binding sites.
summary.tldr: EquiPocket improves protein binding-site prediction by combining surface geometry, chemical structure, and equivariant graph processing.

title: EquiPocket: an E(3)-Equivariant Geometric Graph Neural Network for Ligand Binding Site Prediction

abstract: Recent years have seen substantial advances in our understanding of high-dimensional ridge regression, but existing theories assume that training examples are independent. By leveraging techniques from random matrix theory and free probability, we provide sharp asymptotics for the in- and out-of-sample risks of ridge regression when the data points have arbitrary correlations. We demonstrate that in this setting, the generalized cross validation estimator (GCV) fails to correctly predict the out-of-sample risk. However, in the case where the noise residuals have the same correlations as the data points, one can modify the GCV to yield an efficiently-computable unbiased estimator that concentrates in the high-dimensional limit, which we dub CorrGCV. We further extend our asymptotic analysis to the case where the test point has nontrivial correlations with the training set, a setting often encountered in time series forecasting. Assuming knowledge of the correlation structure of the time series, this again yields an extension of the GCV estimator, and sharply characterizes the degree to which such test points yield an overly optimistic prediction of long-time risk. We validate the predictions of our theory across a variety of high dimensional data.
