paragraphs: Ridge regression theory often assumes independent training examples, even though observations in applications such as time series can be correlated. This paper develops sharp high-dimensional estimates of training and out-of-sample risk when data points have arbitrary correlations. The analysis uses random matrix theory and free probability to account for those dependencies.

The authors show that ordinary generalized cross-validation can fail to predict out-of-sample risk in this setting. When noise residuals share the same correlations as the data points, they construct CorrGCV, an efficiently computable modification. Under that condition, the estimator is unbiased and concentrates in the high-dimensional limit, providing a correction tailored to the correlation structure.

The analysis also covers test points correlated with the training set. Assuming the time series’ correlation structure is known, another extension of generalized cross-validation quantifies how such test points can make long-term risk look overly favorable. Experiments across high-dimensional datasets validate the theoretical predictions, connecting sample dependence to both risk estimation and its interpretation.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes ridge-regression risk under correlated samples and derives corrected cross-validation estimators under stated correlation assumptions.

title: Risk and cross validation in ridge regression with correlated samples

abstract: Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks (SE-GNNs) are popular explainable-by-design GNNs, but their explanations’ properties and limitations are not well understood. Our first contribution fills this gap by formalizing the explanations extracted by some popular SE-GNNs, referred to as Minimal Explanations (MEs), and comparing them to established notions of explanations, namely Prime Implicant (PI) and faithful explanations. Our analysis reveals that MEs match PI explanations for a restricted but significant family of tasks. In general, however, they can be less informative than PI explanations and are surprisingly misaligned with widely accepted notions of faithfulness. Although faithful and PI explanations are informative, they are intractable to find and we show that they can be prohibitively large. Given these observations, a natural choice is to augment SE-GNNs with alternative modalities of explanations taking care of SE-GNNs’ limitations. To this end, we propose Dual-Channel GNNs that integrate a white-box rule extractor and a standard SE-GNN, adaptively combining both channels. Our experiments show that even a simple instantiation of Dual-Channel GNNs can recover succinct rules and perform on par or better than widely used SE-GNNs.

paragraphs: Some graph neural networks produce explanations as part of their design, but the meaning and guarantees of those explanations need careful examination. This paper formalizes explanations produced by several popular models as Minimal Explanations and compares them with two established alternatives: Prime Implicant explanations and faithful explanations. The comparison asks what information each explanation actually provides.

Minimal Explanations coincide with Prime Implicant explanations for a restricted but significant family of tasks. Outside that family, they can convey less information and fail to align with accepted notions of faithfulness. The alternatives also present difficulties: the authors show that faithful and Prime Implicant explanations are intractable to find and can become prohibitively large.

These findings motivate Dual-Channel GNNs, which adaptively combine a standard self-explainable graph network with a white-box rule extractor. The additional channel supplies another form of explanation to address the identified limitations. Experiments show that even a simple version recovers concise rules while matching or improving on the predictive performance of widely used self-explainable GNNs.
summary.tldr: A formal analysis exposes limitations of graph explanations and motivates a dual-channel model that also extracts concise rules.

title: Beyond Topological Self-Explainable GNNs: A Formal Explainability Perspective

abstract: We theoretically characterize gradient descent dynamics in deep linear networks trained at large width from random initialization and on large quantities of random data. Our theory captures the “wider is better" effect of mean-field/maximum-update parameterized networks as well as hyperparameter transfer effects, which can be contrasted with the neural-tangent parameterization where optimal learning rates shift with model width. We provide asymptotic descriptions of both non-residual and residual neural networks, the latter of which enables an infinite depth limit when branches are scaled as $1/\sqrt{\text{depth}}$. We also compare training with one-pass stochastic gradient descent to the dynamics when training data are repeated at each iteration. Lastly, we show that this model recovers the accelerated power law training dynamics for power law structured data in the rich regime observed in recent works.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of how deep linear networks learn from random initialization. The analysis concerns large network widths and large quantities of random data. Although each layer is linear, the layered training problem provides a setting for examining how width, depth, data, and parameter scaling jointly influence gradient descent.

The theory captures the benefit of increasing width under mean-field or maximum-update parameterizations, along with effects that support transferring hyperparameters across widths. It contrasts these behaviors with neural-tangent parameterization, where optimal learning rates change with width. The authors analyze both residual and non-residual networks. For residual networks, scaling branches by the inverse square root of depth enables an infinite-depth limit.

The work also compares one-pass stochastic gradient descent with training that repeatedly uses the same data. Finally, the model reproduces accelerated power-law learning dynamics for data with power-law structure in the rich regime. Together, these results organize several scaling phenomena within one analytical framework, with the conclusions grounded in the stated deep-linear, large-width, random-data setting.
summary.tldr: A theory of deep linear networks connects training dynamics to width, depth, data reuse, and hyperparameter transfer.

title: Deep Linear Network Training Dynamics from Random Initialization: Data, Width, Depth, and Hyperparameter Transfer

abstract: Recent advances in latent diffusion models have demonstrated their effectiveness for high-resolution image synthesis. However, the properties of the latent space from tokenizer for better learning and generation of diffusion models remain under-explored. Theoretically and empirically, we find that improved generation quality is closely tied to the latent distributions with better structure, such as the ones with fewer Gaussian Mixture modes and more discriminative features. Motivated by these insights, we propose MAETok, an autoencoder (AE) leveraging mask modeling to learn semantically rich latent space while maintaining reconstruction fidelity. Extensive experiments validate our analysis, demonstrating that the variational form of autoencoders is not necessary, and a discriminative latent space from AE alone enables state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet generation using only 128 tokens. MAETok achieves significant practical improvements, enabling a gFID of 1.69 with 76$\times$ faster training and 31$\times$ higher inference throughput for 512$\times$512 generation. Our findings show that the structure of the latent space, rather than variational constraints, is crucial for effective diffusion models. Code and trained models will be released.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion models generate images through compressed representations produced by a tokenizer. This paper investigates which properties of those representations help diffusion learning and generation. Its theoretical and empirical analysis links better generation quality to more structured latent distributions, including fewer Gaussian mixture modes and features that distinguish semantic content more effectively.

Motivated by those findings, the authors introduce MAETok, an autoencoder trained with mask modeling. It aims to preserve reconstruction fidelity while creating a semantically rich latent space. The approach shows that an autoencoder can supply useful diffusion representations without requiring a variational formulation, focusing attention on the organization of the learned space.

Experiments report state-of-the-art ImageNet generation using 128 tokens. For images at 512 by 512 resolution, the paper reports a gFID of 1.69, training 76 times faster, and inference throughput 31 times higher in its comparisons. Together, these findings support latent-space structure as a crucial design consideration. They demonstrate that variational constraints are unnecessary for the reported success, rather than establishing that every ordinary autoencoder will produce equally effective diffusion representations.
summary.tldr: MAETok uses masked autoencoding to create structured image latents that enable strong diffusion generation with only 128 tokens.

title: Masked Autoencoders Are Effective Tokenizers for Diffusion Models

abstract: Developing algorithms to differentiate between machine-generated texts and human-written texts has garnered substantial attention in recent years. Existing methods in this direction typically concern an offline setting where a dataset containing a mix of real and machine-generated texts is given upfront, and the task is to determine whether each sample in the dataset is from a large language model (LLM) or a human. However, in many practical scenarios, sources such as news websites, social media accounts, and online forums publish content in a streaming fashion. Therefore, in this online scenario, how to quickly and accurately determine whether the source is an LLM with strong statistical guarantees is crucial for these media or platforms to function effectively and prevent the spread of misinformation and other potential misuse of LLMs. To tackle the problem of online detection, we develop an algorithm based on the techniques of sequential hypothesis testing by betting that not only builds upon and complements existing offline detection techniques but also enjoys statistical guarantees, which include a controlled false positive rate and the expected time to correctly identify a source as an LLM. Experiments were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Most text detection methods consider a fixed collection of samples and decide whether each was written by a person or generated by a language model. This paper studies a different setting: a source publishes text over time, and the detector must decide whether that source is an LLM as new evidence arrives.

The proposed algorithm uses sequential hypothesis testing by betting. It builds on existing offline detection techniques while organizing evidence into an ongoing statistical decision process. This makes it possible to study both how reliably the method identifies a machine source and how long identification takes in a stream.

The authors provide statistical guarantees covering the false positive rate and the expected time to correctly identify an LLM source. Experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to bring formal error and detection-time guarantees to an online setting, complementing tools designed for individual texts or fixed datasets. Its focus on a publishing source matches situations where evidence accumulates across successive pieces of content.
summary.tldr: A sequential betting-based detector identifies LLM text sources over time with guarantees on false positives and expected detection time.

title: Online Detection of LLM-Generated Texts via Sequential Hypothesis Testing by Betting

abstract: In sparse optimization, enforcing hard constraints using the $\ell_0$ pseudo-norm offers advantages like controlled sparsity compared to convex relaxations. However, many real-world applications demand not only sparsity constraints but also some extra constraints. While prior algorithms have been developed to address this complex scenario with mixed combinatorial and convex constraints, they typically require the closed form projection onto the mixed constraints which might not exist, and/or only provide local guarantees of convergence which is different from the global guarantees commonly sought in sparse optimization. To fill this gap, in this paper, we study the problem of sparse optimization with extra support-preserving constraints commonly encountered in the literature. We present a new variant of iterative hard-thresholding algorithm equipped with a two-step consecutive projection operator customized for these mixed constraints, serving as a simple alternative to the Euclidean projection onto the mixed constraint. By introducing a novel trade-off between sparsity relaxation and sub-optimality, we provide global guarantees in objective value for the output of our algorithm, in the deterministic, stochastic, and zeroth-order settings, under the conventional restricted strong-convexity/smoothness assumptions. As a fundamental contribution in proof techniques, we develop a novel extension of the classic three-point lemma to the considered two-step non-convex projection operator, which allows us to analyze the convergence in objective value in an elegant way that has not been possible with existing techniques. In the zeroth-order case, such technique also improves upon the state-of-the-art result from de Vazelhes et. al. (2022), even in the case without additional constraints, by allowing us to remove a non-vanishing system error present in their work.

Enforcing both kinds together can require a difficult projection onto their intersection. This paper studies additional constraints that preserve support and replaces that joint projection with a customized sequence of two projections.

title: Optimization over Sparse Support-Preserving Sets: Two-Step Projection with Global Optimality Guarantees

abstract: Reliable planning is crucial for achieving autonomous driving. Rule-based planners are efficient but lack generalization, while learning-based planners excel in generalization yet have limitations in real-time performance and interpretability. In long-tail scenarios, these challenges make planning particularly difficult. To leverage the strengths of both rule-based and learning-based planners, we proposed the Scenario-Aware Hybrid Planner (SAH-Drive) for closed-loop vehicle trajectory planning. Inspired by human driving behavior, SAH-Drive combines a lightweight rule-based planner and a comprehensive learning-based planner, utilizing a dual-timescale decision neuron to determine the final trajectory. To enhance the computational efficiency and robustness of the hybrid planner, we also employed a diffusion proposal number regulator and a trajectory fusion module. The experimental results show that the proposed method significantly improves the generalization capability of the planning system, achieving state-of-the-art performance in interPlan, while maintaining computational efficiency without incurring substantial additional runtime.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving planners must generate suitable trajectories while responding quickly to changing situations. Rule-based methods offer efficiency, while learned methods can generalize more broadly but face challenges in runtime and interpretability. The paper focuses on combining their strengths, particularly for uncommon scenarios that are difficult for either approach to handle alone.

SAH-Drive integrates a lightweight rule-based planner with a more comprehensive learning-based planner. A dual-timescale decision neuron determines the final trajectory, drawing inspiration from human driving behavior. The system also includes a regulator for the number of diffusion proposals and a trajectory fusion module, which are introduced to improve computational efficiency and robustness.

Experiments report improved generalization and state-of-the-art performance on interPlan, while maintaining computational efficiency without substantial additional runtime. These findings support the proposed hybrid design for the evaluated closed-loop planning setting. The contribution lies in coordinating the two planning approaches and managing their computational demands, so that greater planning capability can be obtained without a large increase in execution time.
summary.tldr: SAH-Drive coordinates rule-based and learned planners to improve driving generalization without substantial additional runtime in the reported evaluation.

title: SAH-Drive: A Scenario-Aware Hybrid Planner for Closed-Loop Vehicle Trajectory Generation

abstract: We introduce PokéChamp, a minimax agent powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) for Pokémon battles. Built on a general framework for two-player competitive games, PokéChamp leverages the generalist capabilities of LLMs to enhance minimax tree search. Specifically, LLMs replace three key modules: (1) player action sampling, (2) opponent modeling, and (3) value function estimation, enabling the agent to effectively utilize gameplay history and human knowledge to reduce the search space and address partial observability. Notably, our framework requires no additional LLM training. We evaluate PokéChamp in the popular Gen 9 OU format. When powered by GPT-4o, it achieves a win rate of 76% against the best existing LLM-based bot and 84% against the strongest rule-based bot, demonstrating its superior performance. Even with an open-source 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model, PokéChamp consistently outperforms the previous best LLM-based bot, Pokéllmon powered by GPT-4o, with a 64% win rate. PokéChamp attains a projected Elo of 1300-1500 on the Pokémon Showdown online ladder, placing it among the top 30%-10% of human players. In addition, this work compiles the largest real-player Pokémon battle dataset, featuring over 3 million games, including more than 500k high-Elo matches. Based on this dataset, we establish a series of battle benchmarks and puzzles to evaluate specific battling skills. We further provide key updates to the local game engine. This work establishes Pokémon as a benchmark to integrate LLM technologies with game-theoretic algorithms addressing general multi-agent problems. Videos, code, and dataset are available online.

title: PokéChamp: an Expert-level Minimax Language Agent

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful framework for generative modeling, with guidance techniques playing a crucial role in enhancing sample quality. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of the guidance effect remains limited. Existing studies only focus on case studies, where the distribution conditioned on each class is either isotropic Gaussian or supported on a one-dimensional interval with some extra conditions. How to analyze the guidance effect beyond these case studies remains an open question. Towards closing this gap, we make an attempt to analyze diffusion guidance under general data distributions. Rather than demonstrating uniform sample quality improvement, which does not hold in some distributions, we prove that guidance can improve the whole sample quality, in the sense that the ratio of bad samples (measured by the classifier probability) decreases in the presence of guidance. This aligns with the motivation of introducing guidance.

paragraphs: Guidance is widely used to improve samples from diffusion models, yet theoretical explanations have often covered only narrowly specified data distributions. This paper moves beyond analyses restricted to isotropic Gaussian classes or one-dimensional supports with extra conditions. It studies how guidance affects sample quality under more general data distributions.

A central distinction is between improving every sample and improving the population of generated samples. The authors explicitly observe that uniform quality improvement does not hold for some distributions. They therefore analyze the fraction of bad samples, with badness measured through classifier probability, instead of requiring each individual generated result to become better.

The paper proves that guidance can reduce this bad-sample ratio. This gives a theoretical meaning to overall quality improvement that is compatible with individual exceptions. The result matters because it supports the motivation for guidance beyond earlier special cases while keeping the guarantee tied to a specific aggregate measure of quality: the proportion of samples judged bad by classifier probability.
summary.tldr: For general data distributions, diffusion guidance can reduce the proportion of bad samples without improving every sample individually.

title: Provable Efficiency of Guidance in Diffusion Models for General Data Distribution

abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) is a principled framework for quantifying uncertainty in black-box learning models, by constructing prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Traditional approaches rely on scalar nonconformity scores, which fail to fully exploit the geometric structure of multivariate outputs, such as in multi-output regression or multiclass classification. Recent methods addressing this limitation impose predefined convex shapes for the prediction sets, potentially misaligning with the intrinsic data geometry. We introduce a novel CP procedure handling multivariate score functions through the lens of optimal transport. Specifically, we leverage Monge-Kantorovich vector ranks and quantiles to construct prediction region with flexible, potentially non-convex shapes, better suited to the complex uncertainty patterns encountered in multivariate learning tasks. We prove that our approach ensures finite-sample, distribution-free coverage properties, similar to typical CP methods. We then adapt our method for multi-output regression and multiclass classification, and also propose simple adjustments to generate adaptive prediction regions with asymptotic conditional coverage guarantees. Finally, we evaluate our method on practical regression and classification problems, illustrating its advantages in terms of (conditional) coverage and efficiency.

title: Optimal transport-based conformal prediction

abstract: Feature importance metrics are critical for interpreting machine learning models and understanding the relevance of individual features. However, real-world data often exhibit missingness, thereby complicating how feature importance should be evaluated. We introduce the distinction between two evaluation frameworks under missing data: (1) feature importance under the full data, as if every feature had been fully measured, and (2) feature importance under the observed data, where missingness is governed by the current measurement policy. While the full data perspective offers insights into the data generating process, it often relies on unrealistic assumptions and cannot guide decisions when missingness persists at model deployment. Since neither framework directly informs improvements in data collection, we additionally introduce the feature measurement importance gradient (FMIG), a novel, model-agnostic metric that identifies features that should be measured more frequently to enhance predictive performance. Using synthetic data, we illustrate key differences between these metrics and the risks of conflating them.

paragraphs: When some inputs are missing, asking which features matter can refer to different questions. It also cannot guide decisions when missingness continues during deployment. Observed-data importance addresses the actual measurement setting, yet neither perspective directly answers which features should be collected more often to improve predictions. That distinction separates interpretation from decisions about data collection.

To address the collection question, the authors introduce the feature measurement importance gradient, or FMIG. This model-agnostic metric identifies features whose more frequent measurement would enhance predictive performance. Synthetic-data examples illustrate how the metrics differ and why treating them as interchangeable can be misleading. The contribution is a clearer match between the question being asked and the feature-importance quantity used to answer it.
summary.tldr: The paper distinguishes feature importance under missing data from the value of measuring a feature more often, introducing FMIG for the latter.

title: Feature Importance Metrics in the Presence of Missing Data

abstract: Dynamic graph representation learning using Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) exploits the temporal spiking behavior of neurons, offering advantages in capturing the temporal evolution and sparsity of dynamic graphs. However, existing SNN-based methods often fail to effectively capture the impact of latency in information propagation on node representations. To address this, we propose Delay-DSGN, a dynamic spiking graph neural network incorporating a learnable delay mechanism. By leveraging synaptic plasticity, the model dynamically adjusts connection weights and propagation speeds, enhancing temporal correlations and enabling historical data to influence future representations. Specifically, we introduce a Gaussian delay kernel into the neighborhood aggregation process at each time step, adaptively delaying historical information to future time steps and mitigating information forgetting. Experiments on three large-scale dynamic graph datasets demonstrate that Delay-DSGN outperforms eight state-of-the-art methods, achieving the best results in node classification tasks. We also theoretically derive the constraint conditions between the Gaussian kernel’s standard deviation and size, ensuring stable training and preventing gradient explosion and vanishing issues.

paragraphs: Dynamic graphs change over time, so useful node representations must account for how information evolves and propagates. The method adjusts connection weights and propagation speeds through a mechanism based on synaptic plasticity. This allows past graph information to influence later node representations and is intended to reduce forgetting while strengthening temporal correlations.

The authors also derive constraints connecting the Gaussian kernel's standard deviation and size to stable training and the prevention of exploding or vanishing gradients. The contribution combines a mechanism for representing delayed information with theoretical guidance for training that mechanism, rather than treating propagation timing as incidental to the graph's evolution.
summary.tldr: Delay-DSGN learns how graph information arrives over time, improving node classification while deriving conditions for stable training.

title: Delay-DSGN: A Dynamic Spiking Graph Neural Network with Delay Mechanisms for Evolving Graph

abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) seeks to enable a model to sequentially learn new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. Balancing flexibility and stability remains a significant challenge, particularly when the task ID is unknown. To address this, our study reveals that the gap in feature distribution between novel and existing tasks is primarily driven by differences in mean and covariance moments. Building on this insight, we propose a novel semantic drift calibration method that incorporates mean shift compensation and covariance calibration. Specifically, we calculate each class’s mean by averaging its sample embeddings and estimate task shifts using weighted embedding changes based on their proximity to the previous mean, effectively capturing mean shifts for all learned classes with each new task. We also apply Mahalanobis distance constraint for covariance calibration, aligning class-specific embedding covariances between old and current networks to mitigate the covariance shift. Additionally, we integrate a feature-level self-distillation approach to enhance generalization. Comprehensive experiments on commonly used datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The source code is available at https://github.com/fwu11/MACIL.git.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning asks a model to learn new classes while retaining earlier ones, including when the task identity is unknown. Updating the model can move its feature representations, making old class knowledge harder to use. This study finds that differences in feature means and covariances primarily drive the distribution gap between new and existing tasks.

The proposed calibration method addresses both forms of movement. It represents each class mean by averaging sample embeddings, then estimates shifts using embedding changes weighted by proximity to the previous mean. For covariance, it applies a Mahalanobis distance constraint to align class-specific embedding covariances between the previous and current networks. These operations target changes in both where representations sit and how they are distributed.

The contribution is a concrete treatment of semantic drift through two statistical properties, connecting an observed source of representation mismatch to mechanisms designed to compensate for it as additional classes are learned.
summary.tldr: Mean-shift compensation and covariance calibration help preserve class representations as a model learns new classes without task identities.

title: Navigating Semantic Drift in Task-Agnostic Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: Pre-trained models have become the preferred backbone due to the increasing complexity of model parameters. However, traditional pre-trained models often face deployment challenges due to their fixed sizes, and are prone to negative transfer when discrepancies arise between training tasks and target tasks. To address this, we propose KIND, a novel pre-training method designed to construct decomposable models. KIND integrates knowledge by incorporating Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) as a structural constraint, with each basic component represented as a combination of a column vector, singular value, and row vector from $U$, $\Sigma$, and $V^\top$ matrices. These components are categorized into learngenes for encapsulating class-agnostic knowledge and tailors for capturing class-specific knowledge, with knowledge diversion facilitated by a class gate mechanism during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that models pre-trained with KIND can be decomposed into learngenes and tailors, which can be adaptively recombined for diverse resource-constrained deployments. Moreover, for tasks with large domain shifts, transferring only learngenes with task-agnostic knowledge, when combined with randomly initialized tailors, effectively mitigates domain shifts. Code will be made available at https://github.com/Te4P0t/KIND.

paragraphs: KIND changes pretraining so that a model can later be separated into useful components. The motivation is twofold: fixed model sizes complicate deployment under different resource budgets, and transferring a pretrained model can hurt performance when its original tasks differ substantially from the target task. Decomposable knowledge offers a way to address both issues.

The method uses singular value decomposition as a structural constraint. Each basic component combines a column vector, a singular value, and a row vector. During training, a class gate directs knowledge into two component types: learngenes capture knowledge shared across classes, while tailors capture knowledge specific to particular classes.

Experiments show that these components can be separated and recombined for deployments with different resource constraints. For tasks involving large domain shifts, transferring only learngenes and pairing them with randomly initialized tailors mitigates the shift. The findings connect model structure to transfer decisions: deployment can select reusable knowledge and avoid carrying over class-specific components that are less suitable for a new task.
summary.tldr: KIND pretrains decomposable models whose shared and class-specific components can be recombined for deployment and more selective transfer.

title: KIND: Knowledge Integration and Diversion for Training Decomposable Models

abstract: Generating samples from a high dimensional probability distribution is a fundamental task with wide-ranging applications in the area of scientific computing, statistics and machine learning. This article revisits the popular Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) sampling algorithms and provides a non-asymptotic error analysis in $\mathcal{W}_2$-distance in a non-convex setting. In particular, we prove an error bound $O(\sqrt{d} h)$, which guarantees a mixing time $ \tilde{O} (\sqrt{d} \epsilon^{-1})$ to achieve the accuracy tolerance $\epsilon$, under certain log-smooth conditions and the assumption that the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality, as opposed to the strongly log-concave condition used in (Li et al., 2019; 2022). This bound matches the best one in the strongly log-concave case and improves upon the best-known convergence rates in non-convex settings. To prove it, we establish a new framework of uniform-in-time convergence for discretizations of SDEs. Distinct from (Li et al., 2019; 2022), we start from the finite-time mean-square fundamental convergence theorem, which combined with uniform-in-time moment bounds of LMC and the exponential ergodicity of SDEs in the non-convex setting gives the desired uniform-in-time convergence. Our framework also applies to the case when the gradient of the potential $U$ is non-globally Lipschitz with superlinear growth, for which modified LMC samplers are proposed and analyzed, with a non-asymptotic error bound in $\mathcal{W}_2$-distance obtained. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Langevin Monte Carlo generates samples by discretizing a stochastic process. This paper analyzes its finite-computation error for non-convex targets using the Wasserstein-2 distance between distributions. Under certain log-smooth conditions and a log-Sobolev inequality, it proves an O(√d h) error bound, where d is dimension and h is the step size.

The framework also handles potentials whose gradients grow superlinearly and are not globally Lipschitz, with modified samplers and associated error bounds. Numerical experiments corroborate the analysis. Together, these results extend rigorous sampling guarantees to a broader set of non-convex problems.
summary.tldr: Under stated regularity and log-Sobolev assumptions, Langevin Monte Carlo achieves O(√d h) Wasserstein-2 error beyond strongly log-concave targets.

title: Non-asymptotic Error Bounds in $\mathcalW_2$-Distance with Sqrt(d) Dimension Dependence and First Order Convergence for Langevin Monte Carlo beyond Log-Concavity

abstract: Batch inference for agentic workloads stresses the GPU key–value (KV) cache in a sustained and cumulative manner, often causing severe throughput degradation well before memory capacity is exhausted. We identify this phenomenon as middle-phase thrashing, a previously under-characterized pathology in which cache efficiency collapses as long-lived agents accumulate state over time. We argue that mitigating this pathology requires moving beyond reactive, request-level cache management to proactive, agent-level admission control. Drawing inspiration from congestion control in distributed systems, we view the KV cache as a shared resource whose efficient utilization depends on feedback-driven regulation. Based on this insight, we present CONCUR, a lightweight control layer that regulates agent admission to bound aggregate cache pressure while preserving execution continuity. CONCUR adapts a cache-aware control algorithm to dynamically adjust the number of active agents using runtime cache signals. Across large models and real-world agent workloads, CONCUR prevents middle-phase thrashing and improves batch inference throughput by up to 4.09$\times$ on Qwen3-32B and 1.90$\times$ on DeepSeek-V3, while remaining compatible with existing LLM serving systems.

title: CONCUR: High-Throughput Agentic Batch Inference of LLM via Congestion-Based Concurrency Control

abstract: Consistency is an important property in dynamic submodular maximization and entails maintaining a near-optimal solution at all times, making only a small number of adjustments to the solution in each step. Prior work has explored this question for the insertion-only case, where the algorithm faces a stream of $n$ insertions, and has established lower and upper bounds for the cardinality-constrained version of the problem. We consider this question in the fully dynamic setting, where the stream of operations may contain both insertions and deletions. We develop a general framework for designing algorithms for this setting, and instantiate it to obtain the first constant-factor approximations with sublinear consistency. For cardinality constraints, we propose a $\tfrac 12 - O(\varepsilon)$ approximation that is $O\left(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ consistent. For rank-$k$ matroid constraints, we construct a $\tfrac 14 - O(\varepsilon)$ approximation to the dynamic optimum that is $O\left(\tfrac{\log k}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ consistent.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to keep a good selected set when available items continually arrive and disappear. The objective is submodular, meaning that adding an item offers diminishing returns as the selected set grows. Besides maintaining solution quality, the algorithm must preserve consistency: each update should require only a small number of changes to the selected set.

Earlier work considered streams containing only insertions. The authors develop a general framework that also handles deletions, and use it to obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees with sublinear consistency. This addresses two demands together: remaining competitive with the current best solution and limiting how much an existing selection must change.

For a cardinality constraint, the approximation is 1/2 minus O(ε), with O(1/ε²) consistency. For a rank-k matroid constraint, it is 1/4 minus O(ε), with O(log k/ε²) consistency. These bounds expose a trade-off: reducing ε improves the stated approximation factor while increasing the allowed number of adjustments. The contribution is a theoretical framework and guarantees for fully dynamic selection.
summary.tldr: A general framework maintains provably good submodular selections under insertions and deletions while limiting changes to the selected set.

title: A General Framework for Dynamic Consistent Submodular Maximization

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are pushing recommender systems (RecSys) toward content-grounded retrieval and ranking via cross-modal fusion. We find that while cross-modal consensus often mitigates conventional poisoning that manipulates interaction logs or perturbs a single modality, it also introduces a new attack surface where synchronised multimodal poisoning can reliably steer fused representations along stable semantic directions during fine-tuning. To characterise this threat, we formalise cross-modal interactive poisoning and propose VENOMREC, which performs Exposure Alignment to identify high-exposure regions in the joint embedding space and Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation to craft attention-guided coupled token–patch edits. Experiments on four real-world multimodal datasets demonstrate that VENOMREC consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving 0.73 mean ER@20 and improving over the strongest baseline by +0.52 absolute ER points on average, while maintaining comparable recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/VenomRec.

paragraphs: VENOMREC studies a poisoning threat to recommendation systems built on multimodal language models. Agreement between modalities can often reduce the effect of conventional attacks that alter interaction logs or only one modality. The authors find that coordinated manipulation across modalities creates a different vulnerability: poisoned inputs can steer fused representations in stable semantic directions during fine-tuning.

The paper formalizes this cross-modal interactive poisoning setting and introduces an attack with two components. Exposure Alignment identifies high-exposure regions in the shared embedding space. Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation then creates coupled text-token and image-patch edits guided by attention. The mechanism exploits the interaction between modalities within the learned recommendation representation.

Experiments on four real-world multimodal datasets report a mean ER@20 of 0.73, averaging 0.52 absolute ER points above the strongest baseline while retaining comparable recommendation utility. The findings show that ordinary recommendation quality can remain similar while targeted promotion becomes more effective. They identify synchronized multimodal poisoning as a distinct threat to systems that rely on cross-modal agreement.
summary.tldr: VENOMREC shows that coordinated text-and-image poisoning can promote targeted items in multimodal recommenders while maintaining comparable recommendation utility.

title: VENOMREC: Cross-Modal Interactive Poisoning for Targeted Promotion in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems

abstract: Modern computer-use agents (CUA) must perceive a screen as a structured state, what elements are visible, where they are, and what text they contain, before they can reliably ground instructions and act. Yet, most available grounding datasets provide sparse supervision, with insufficient and low-diversity labels that annotate only a small subset of task-relevant elements per screen, which limits both coverage and generalization; moreover, practical deployment requires efficiency to enable low-latency, on-device use. We introduce ScreenParse, a large-scale dataset for complete screen parsing, with dense annotations of all visible UI elements (boxes, 55-class types, and text) across 771K web screenshots (21M elements). ScreenParse is generated by Webshot, an automated, scalable pipeline that renders diverse urls, extracts annotations and applies VLM-based relabeling and quality filtering. Using ScreenParse, we train ScreenVLM, a compact, 316M-parameter vision language model (VLM) that decodes a compact ScreenTag markup representation with a structure-aware loss that upweights structure-critical tokens. ScreenVLM substantially outperforms much larger foundation VLMs on dense parsing (e.g., 0.592 vs. 0.294 PageIoU on ScreenParse) and shows strong transfer to public benchmarks. Moreover, finetuning foundation VLMs on ScreenParse consistently improves their grounding performance, suggesting that dense screen supervision provides transferable structural priors for UI understanding. The dataset, model and code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Computer-use agents need a structured view of the screen: visible elements, their locations, and their text. Sparse annotations cover only a small subset of those elements, limiting the supervision available for learning broader interface understanding. ScreenParse addresses this with dense annotations across 771,000 web screenshots containing 21 million elements.

The dataset includes element boxes, text, and types from 55 classes. An automated pipeline called Webshot renders varied URLs, extracts annotations, and uses a vision-language model for relabeling and quality filtering. The authors train ScreenVLM, a 316-million-parameter model that outputs compact ScreenTag markup, with extra training emphasis on tokens essential to the output structure.

ScreenVLM substantially outperforms much larger foundation models on dense parsing, including PageIoU of 0.592 versus 0.294 on ScreenParse, and transfers strongly to public benchmarks. Fine-tuning foundation models on the dataset also consistently improves grounding. These findings suggest that comprehensive screen supervision teaches reusable structural knowledge and can support strong parsing with a compact model.
summary.tldr: ScreenParse supplies dense screen annotations that enable a compact parsing model and improve foundation-model grounding through fine-tuning.

title: ScreenParse: Moving Beyond Sparse Grounding with Complete Screen Parsing Supervision

abstract: A common assumption in strategic classification is that the classifier is public knowledge. However, it remains unclear whether, and why, a system would choose to commit to full disclosure. We study a setting in which regulation requires the system to disclose some, but not all, of the information. This induces a learning task in which the learner must jointly optimize the classifier and the uncertainty surrounding it. To this end, we adopt from robust mechanism design the notion of ambiguity, which in our setting allows the learner to reveal a set or range of possible classifiers, while privately choosing which of them to ultimately realize. We investigate how ambiguity affects the learning task, develop efficient algorithms for computing best-responses and training, and empirically explore strategic learning and its outcomes in this novel setting and using our approach.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies prediction when the people being evaluated can respond to the decision rule. A common starting assumption is that everyone knows the classifier. This paper instead considers a regulatory setting that requires some disclosure while allowing the system to keep part of its decision process private.

The authors formalize partial disclosure through ambiguity, a concept drawn from robust mechanism design. The system announces a set or range of possible classifiers but privately chooses which one to use. Learning therefore involves two connected decisions: choosing the classifier and choosing the uncertainty that surrounds it. That uncertainty becomes part of the strategic environment to which evaluated individuals respond.

The paper examines how this additional choice changes learning and develops efficient algorithms for computing best responses and training classifiers. It also empirically explores strategic behavior and resulting outcomes in this setting. Its contribution is a framework for analyzing partial disclosure as an explicit design decision, rather than assuming that full disclosure is already settled. The abstract does not claim that ambiguity always improves outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper models partial classifier disclosure as a learnable choice and develops algorithms for strategic classification under that ambiguity.

title: Ambiguous Strategic Classification

abstract: Predicting molecular properties from three-dimensional structures is fundamentally hindered by limited labeled data. While researchers have adapted self-supervised pre-training techniques from computer vision and natural language processing to address this scarcity, these approaches frequently neglect the intrinsic physical principles unique to molecular systems. From a physical perspective, denoising pre-training can be formally proven equivalent to learning molecular force fields. However, existing methods indiscriminately apply uniform noise across all molecules, thereby introducing systematic bias into the modeling of molecular distributions. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MOES-Pred, a denoising pre-training framework featuring an energy sentinel mechanism that dynamically tailors noise perturbations to individual molecules. Leveraging chemical prior knowledge, our molecule-specific noising strategies enhance conformational sampling coverage and improve distribution modeling fidelity. Extensive experiments show that MOES-Pred surpasses mainstream approaches in both force prediction and downstream quantum chemical property prediction, demonstrating substantial improvements.

Self-supervised pretraining can help, but the paper argues that methods adapted from vision and language often neglect molecular physics. It highlights a physical connection: denoising pretraining can be formally related to learning molecular force fields.

The molecule-specific strategies improve coverage of sampled conformations and the fidelity of distribution modeling. The findings support treating noise design as part of the physical modeling problem: perturbations that account for molecular differences can produce representations useful for multiple prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: MOES-Pred adapts denoising perturbations to individual molecules, improving force and quantum chemical property prediction.

title: MOES-Pred: Molecular Structural Representation Learning by Adaptive Energy-Sentinel Vibration for Generalized Property Prediction

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to purely autoregressive language models because they can decode multiple tokens in parallel. However, state-of-the-art block-wise dLLMs rely on a “remasking" mechanism that decodes only the most confident tokens and discards the rest, effectively wasting computation. We demonstrate that recycling computation from the discarded tokens is beneficial, as these tokens retain contextual information useful for subsequent decoding iterations. In light of this, we propose Residual Context Diffusion (RCD), a module that converts these discarded token representations into contextual residuals and injects them back for the next denoising step. RCD uses a decoupled two-stage training pipeline to bypass the memory bottlenecks associated with backpropagation. We validate our method on both long CoT reasoning (SDAR) and short CoT instruction following (LLaDA) models. We demonstrate that a standard dLLM can be efficiently converted to the RCD paradigm with merely $\sim$300 million tokens. RCD consistently improves frontier dLLMs by 4–11 percentage points in accuracy with minimal extra computation overhead across a wide range of benchmarks. Notably, on the most challenging AIME tasks, RCD nearly doubles baseline accuracy and attains up to 4–5x fewer denoising steps at baseline’s peak accuracy.

This paper shows that discarded representations still contain useful context. Residual Context Diffusion, or RCD, aims to preserve that information for later decoding iterations.

RCD converts discarded token representations into contextual residuals and injects them into the next denoising step. On the most challenging AIME tasks, it nearly doubles baseline accuracy and requires up to four to five times fewer denoising steps at the baseline’s peak accuracy. The results show that information from discarded predictions can improve both answer quality and decoding efficiency.
summary.tldr: RCD recycles discarded diffusion-token representations as context, improving reported accuracy and reducing denoising steps needed to match baseline performance.

title: Residual Context Diffusion Language Models

abstract: This paper studies the critical problem of targeted adversarial attacks against closed-source MLLMs, which aim to generate highly transferable adversarial samples with open-source MLLMs. Previous approaches typically focus on maximizing the similarity of latent representations between adversarial samples and target samples. However, these approaches could overfit specific target samples with severely limited generalization ability to closed-source MLLMs. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Distribution-aware Adaptive Relational Transfer (DART) for adversarial attacks against closed-source MLLMs. The core of our DART is to adopt a statistical lens to characterize the intrinsic semantics of images for more generalized and robust alignment. In particular, each augmented image is considered an example from the intrinsic distribution of the original image. Then, we utilize non-parametric Energy Distance to measure the distribution divergence, which is naturally adopted for the semantic alignment in the hidden space. To further enhance transferability to specific target models, we learn a graph neural network (GNN) to explore the complex relations between source and target MLLMs on transferability and adaptively select surrogate models to maximize transferability across diverse targets. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the superior robustness and effectiveness of the proposed DART in comparison to various competing baselines.

paragraphs: DART studies targeted adversarial examples created using open-source multimodal language models and transferred to closed-source models. A central problem is overfitting: making an adversarial example closely resemble one target example in a source model’s hidden representation may not produce an attack that transfers well. The paper replaces this single-example alignment with a distributional view.

DART treats augmented versions of an image as samples from an underlying distribution associated with that image. It then uses Energy Distance, a non-parametric measure of distribution difference, to align these distributions in hidden representation space. This aims to capture image semantics more generally than matching particular representations alone.

A second component learns relationships between source and target models using a graph neural network. Those relationships guide adaptive selection of surrogate models for different targets. Benchmark experiments report better robustness and effectiveness than competing approaches. The results support combining broader semantic alignment with target-sensitive surrogate selection when studying how adversarial examples transfer between multimodal models.
summary.tldr: DART improves adversarial transfer through distribution-level image alignment and learned selection of surrogate multimodal models.

title: DART: Distribution-Aware Adaptive Relational Transfer for Adversarial Attacks against Closed-Source MLLMs

abstract: Multivariate time series anomaly detection remains challenging as it requires the joint modeling of variable relationships and temporal dependencies. Existing methods often struggle to balance channel relationship modeling and overlook the relative importance of different variables within multivariate time series. To address this, we propose TeamWork, an asymmetric role-aware channel modeling framework that decouples variables into dominant and auxiliary roles according to their contributions to uncertainty reduction. Dominant variables drive system evolution and their deviations more strongly disrupt normal patterns, while auxiliary variables provide complementary cues. These variables with different roles are integrated through a role-aware gated interaction module. Moreover, point and subsequence anomalies can exist in multiple periodic systems, and the same anomaly type may behave differently across short- and long-period series. To capture such variations, we introduce a period-aware masked modeling mechanism. It employs multiple specialized masking mechanisms spanning short to long periods to facilitate comprehensive temporal dependency learning. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that TeamWork achieves superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: TeamWork detects anomalies in time series containing multiple interacting variables. Such detection requires understanding both relationships between variables and patterns over time. The paper argues that existing methods often overlook differences in variables’ relative importance, making it difficult to model their contributions to normal system behavior effectively.

The framework assigns variables dominant or auxiliary roles according to how much they reduce uncertainty. Dominant variables drive system evolution, while auxiliary variables provide complementary information. A role-aware gated interaction module combines them while preserving this asymmetry. This gives the model a way to represent different contributions instead of treating all channels as equally influential.

TeamWork also uses period-aware masked modeling to learn temporal dependencies across short and long periods. Multiple specialized masking mechanisms address the fact that isolated-point and subsequence anomalies can appear differently across periodic systems. Experiments on several real-world datasets report stronger performance than state-of-the-art methods. The results support combining asymmetric channel relationships with temporal learning that explicitly spans different periods.
summary.tldr: TeamWork combines variable-specific roles with period-aware temporal modeling to improve multivariate time-series anomaly detection.

title: TeamWork: Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Asymmetric Role-aware Channel Modeling

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support human decision-making, rendering human-interpretable confidence essential. However, it remains unclear whether verbalized confidence calibration generalizes across heterogeneous tasks without degrading accuracy. We show that universal confidence calibration fails. Across diverse benchmarks, we identify two incompatible task families with distinct confidence semantics. In reasoning-centric tasks, confidence supervision transfers within the family, often improving calibration while preserving or even improving accuracy, and induces emergent behaviors such as confidence-dependent reasoning length and self-verification. Retrieval- and copy-oriented tasks also exhibit within-family transfer, but fail to generalize to reasoning tasks, with cross-family supervision degrading both calibration and accuracy. Motivated by this finding, we disentangle confidence into reasoning uncertainty and evidence localization uncertainty. This simple decomposition restores cross-family generalization using supervised fine-tuning alone, suggesting that effective confidence alignment requires task-aware semantics rather than a universal scalar notion.

paragraphs: When a language model states its confidence, that statement should help users judge whether its answer is reliable. This paper examines whether training models to express calibrated confidence transfers across different kinds of tasks. Across the studied benchmarks, the authors find that a single shared treatment of confidence fails because tasks attach different meanings to uncertainty.

Reasoning tasks form one family: confidence supervision transfers within that family and often improves calibration while preserving or improving accuracy. It also produces behaviors such as adjusting reasoning length with confidence and checking answers. Retrieval and copying tasks show their own within-family transfer, but supervision across the two families can worsen both calibration and accuracy.

The proposed remedy separates confidence into uncertainty about reasoning and uncertainty about locating the relevant evidence. Using this decomposition, supervised fine-tuning alone restores cross-family generalization in the reported study. The result suggests that useful confidence training should distinguish the source of uncertainty, rather than expecting one undifferentiated confidence value to retain the same meaning across heterogeneous tasks.
summary.tldr: Separating reasoning uncertainty from evidence-location uncertainty improves confidence transfer between task families that otherwise interfere.

title: Confidence is Not Universal: Task-Dependent Calibration and Emergent Behavior in LLMs

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often hypothesized to perform implicit Bayesian inference, yet a key coherence condition—the martingale property of predictive beliefs—has been shown to fail in controlled synthetic in-context learning settings. We revisit this question in a more typical usage regime: generic multiple-choice question answering. Exploiting the discrete answer space, we compute exact predictive distributions and study belief dynamics induced by autoregressive answer resampling. We introduce prompted predictive resampling (PPR), where an LLM generates a sequence of answers to the same question. Empirically, PPR reveals early-stage belief drift, indicating martingale violations. However, after sufficient resampling steps, the belief process self-stabilizes and converges to a coherent predictive distribution. Based on this observation, we further propose (i) a seed-answer prompting strategy to accelerate stabilization, and (ii) a self-consistency loss that amortizes early-stage drift into the model via fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple-choice QA benchmarks show that our methods substantially reduce belief drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: If a language model behaves like a coherent Bayesian predictor, its changing predictive beliefs should satisfy a condition called the martingale property. Roughly, its expected future belief should agree with its current belief. This paper examines that condition in ordinary multiple-choice question answering, where the discrete answer space allows exact predictive distributions to be computed.

The authors introduce prompted predictive resampling, which has the model generate a sequence of answers to the same question. They observe systematic belief drift early in this process, indicating violations of the coherence condition. Empirically, sufficient additional resampling leads the process to stabilize and converge to a coherent predictive distribution.

Building on this observation, the paper proposes seed-answer prompting to accelerate stabilization and a fine-tuning loss that incorporates self-consistency into the model. Across multiple-choice benchmarks, these methods substantially reduce drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy. The findings concern the consistency of the model’s evolving answer probabilities, providing a way to study and improve behavior beyond whether a final answer is correct.
summary.tldr: Repeated answer resampling reveals early belief drift, motivating prompting and fine-tuning methods that improve predictive coherence without reducing accuracy.

title: From Drift to Coherence: Stabilizing Beliefs in LLMs

abstract: Visual agents employ external visual tools within visual chains of thought to incorporate fine-grained evidence. While prior work has mainly studied these tools in visual search tasks, their role in more complex visual reasoning remains underexplored. In this paper, we move beyond simple visual search tasks to investigate more challenging tasks, including 3D spatial reasoning and medical visual question answering, where agents must integrate tool-acquired local evidence with the global context. We identify a tool-use collapse phenomenon: models progressively stop using tools while still achieving higher task accuracy. Moreover, we observe a clear asymmetry: (i) completely eliminating tool use degrades performance, whereas (ii) incentivizing tool use yields only marginal gains despite substantially increasing usage. We find that vanilla training and tool-use encouragement both reduce rollout diversity, explaining why higher tool use does not yield stronger reasoning performance. Motivated by these findings, we add an entropy regularization term to encourage diverse rollout exploration, achieving the best performance despite gradually declining tool usage. Overall, our findings suggest a training-time view of tools as scaffolding, where broader exploration over language generation and visual tool invocation improves reasoning despite tool-use collapse. Project page: https://scaffolded-exploration.github.io

paragraphs: Visual reasoning agents can call tools to inspect fine details, but complex tasks also require relating those details to a larger scene. This paper studies that interaction in settings including 3D spatial reasoning and medical visual question answering. It asks how tool use during training relates to the reasoning abilities agents develop.

The authors observe that models can become more accurate while progressively using tools less often. Removing tools entirely hurts performance, yet encouraging more calls produces only small gains despite substantially greater usage. Their analysis links this asymmetry to reduced diversity in generated reasoning trajectories: both ordinary training and explicit tool-use encouragement narrow the range of explored approaches.

The proposed change adds entropy regularization to encourage more varied exploration across language generation and tool invocation. This produces the best reported performance even as tool usage gradually declines. The findings support viewing tools as training scaffolding: they help agents explore useful evidence and reasoning strategies, while their eventual call frequency is an incomplete indicator of the reasoning benefit gained.
summary.tldr: The study finds that encouraging diverse reasoning trajectories improves visual agents more effectively than simply encouraging more tool calls.

title: Diversity Over Frequency: Rethinking Tool Use in Visual Chain-of-Thought Agents

abstract: Recent advances in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) have empowered large language models (LLMs) to tackle challenging reasoning tasks such as mathematics and programming, however existing RLVR methods often suffer from sparse reward signals and unstable policy gradient updates inherent to RL-based approaches. To address the challenges, we propose $\textbf{PACS}$, a novel RLVR framework that achieves im$\textbf{P}$licit $\textbf{A}$ctor $\textbf{C}$ritic coupling via a $\textbf{S}$upervised learning framework. By treating the outcome reward as a predictable label, we reformulate the RLVR problem into a supervised learning task over a score function parameterized by the policy model and optimized using cross-entropy loss. A detailed gradient analysis shows that this supervised formulation inherently recovers the classical policy gradient update while providing more stable and efficient training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACS significantly outperforms strong open-source models and RLVR baselines, yielding substantial average gains of $\textbf{+8.26%}$ (4B) and $\textbf{+9.57%}$ (8B) over base models offering a promising avenue for LLMs post-training with verifiable rewards. Our code and data are available as open source at https://github.com/ritzz-ai/PACS.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains models using outcomes that can be checked, including answers to mathematics or programming problems. However, sparse feedback and unstable policy-gradient updates can make training difficult. PACS approaches these difficulties by reformulating the reward-learning problem as supervised prediction.

The method treats the outcome reward as a label to predict. A score function parameterized by the policy model is trained with cross-entropy loss, creating an implicit coupling between acting and evaluating outcomes. The authors analyze the resulting gradients and show that this supervised objective recovers the classical policy-gradient update while supporting more stable and efficient training.

Experiments report significant improvements over strong open-source models and reinforcement-learning baselines. Relative to base models, the reported average gains are +8.26% for the 4B model and +9.57% for the 8B model. The contribution is a connection between supervised objectives and reward-driven policy improvement: changing the training formulation can preserve the relevant update structure while improving the reported learning behavior.
summary.tldr: PACS reformulates verifiable-reward training as supervised reward prediction while implicitly recovering policy-gradient updates.

title: Implicit Actor Critic Coupling via a Supervised Learning Framework for RLVR

abstract: The prevailing inference framework for diffusion models formulates generation fundamentally as a problem of numerical integration. This perspective casts the model as an accurate estimator, neglecting the inherent statistical uncertainty of the denoising process. In this work, we propose Forward-Process Aligned Diffusion prediction (DiFA), a training-free framework that reframes inference-time clean-signal prediction refinement within diffusion sampling as a sequential state estimation problem. Instead of discarding historical predictions, DiFA treats the inference trajectory as a sequence of correlated observations with varying uncertainties. Inspired by Kalman estimation, DiFA builds a logSNR-aware temporal consensus to align historical clean predictions. Crucially, to counteract the over-smoothing typically associated with temporal consensus, we introduce a deviation guidance mechanism that adaptively preserves residual details. Empirically, DiFA yields significant improvements on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across the evaluated metrics, including FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2, demonstrating that aligning inference with the forward statistical structure substantially improves generative fidelity.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation is commonly approached as numerical integration, with the model supplying estimates along a sampling trajectory. DiFA emphasizes that these estimates also contain statistical uncertainty. It treats successive predictions of the clean signal as correlated observations whose reliability changes during generation, making earlier predictions useful evidence for later ones.

The method refines predictions through sequential state estimation without additional training. Inspired by Kalman estimation, it builds agreement across historical clean-signal predictions while accounting for the logarithmic signal-to-noise ratio. This connects the refinement process to the statistical structure of forward diffusion rather than treating every prediction as an independent, equally reliable estimate.

Combining predictions can wash out detail, so DiFA adds adaptive deviation guidance to preserve residual information. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the authors report significant improvements across the evaluated FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2 metrics. The results support using uncertainty-aware prediction history to improve generative fidelity, with detail preservation playing an explicit role in the design.
summary.tldr: DiFA improves diffusion sampling without retraining by combining uncertain historical predictions while adaptively preserving detail.

title: DiFA: Inference-Time Forward-Process Alignment for Diffusion Models

abstract: We present AAD-1, an Asymmetric Adversarial Distillation framework for One-step autoregressive image-to-video generation. State-of-the-art methods adopt adversarial distillation but suffer from motion collapse and training instability, resulting in static videos. AAD-1 addresses these challenges through two key designs in architecture and training strategy. Our key architectural insight is to break the symmetry between generator and discriminator. While the generator remains causal to preserve autoregressive sampling capability, the discriminator attends bidirectionally over the full spatiotemporal context and produces a single holistic realism score for the entire video sequence. This asymmetric design enables the discriminator to effectively detect global temporal failures and long-range drift that cause motion collapse in autoregressive generation. To stabilize training, we introduce a phased strategy that first uses distribution matching to bootstrap a stable one-step generator, providing a warm-up phase that brings the student distribution closer to the teacher before adversarial distillation begins. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that AAD-1 achieves state-of-the-art performance in one-step autoregressive video generation.
originalAbstract: We present AAD-1, an Asymmetric Adversarial Distillation framework for One-step autoregressive image-to-video generation. State-of-the-art methods adopt adversarial distillation but suffer from motion collapse and training instability, resulting in static videos. AAD-1 addresses these challenges through two key designs in architecture and training strategy. Our key architectural insight is to break the symmetry between generator and discriminator. While the generator remains causal to preserve autoregressive sampling capability, the discriminator attends bidirectionally over the full spatiotemporal context and produces a single holistic realism score for the entire video sequence. This asymmetric design enables the discriminator to effectively detect global temporal failures and long-range drift that cause motion collapse in autoregressive generation. To stabilize training, we introduce a phased strategy that first uses distribution matching to bootstrap a stable one-step generator, providing a warm-up phase that brings the student distribution closer to the teacher before adversarial distillation begins. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that AAD-1 achieves state-of-the-art performance in one-step autoregressive video generation.

paragraphs: AAD-1 tackles a failure in fast image-to-video generation: a model can produce videos that barely move. The paper connects this motion collapse to unstable adversarial distillation, where a generator learns with feedback from a discriminator. Its goal is to retain one-step autoregressive generation while improving the quality of motion across the resulting sequence.

The main architectural change gives the two networks different access to context. The generator remains causal, preserving its ability to generate sequentially. The discriminator can examine the entire video in both temporal directions and assign one overall realism score. This wider view helps it detect failures that unfold over time, including long-range drift and collapsed motion.

abstract: Multi-label recognition with frozen Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is brittle under distribution shift: standard zero-shot inference scores labels independently, ignoring co-occurrence structure and producing incoherent label sets where dominant concepts suppress weaker but compatible labels. We introduce Bayesian Conditional Priors (BCP) Estimation, a gradient-free test-time adaptation method that injects label dependency without tuning the backbone. BCP views zero-shot logits as a proxy for marginal posteriors under a fixed image-text likelihood and attributes shift-induced errors mainly to a mismatched label prior. For each test image, it selects a high-confidence anchor label and applies an anchor-conditioned Bayesian refinement. This update is closed-form in logit space and admits a pointwise mutual information (PMI) interpretation, explicitly promoting compatible labels and suppressing incompatible ones. BCP operates without target annotations by estimating anchor-conditioned priors online from the unlabeled test stream via lightweight second-order co-occurrence statistics, adding negligible overhead beyond a single forward pass. Across standard multi-label benchmarks and multiple CLIP backbones, BCP consistently outperforms strong TTA baselines, e.g., improving RN50 average mAP from 57.31 to 69.22 and ViT-B/16 from 62.61 to 71.79.

title: Multi-Label Test-Time Adaptation with Bayesian Conditional Priors

abstract: Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising solution for fine-tuning LLMs under strict memory constraints, as it avoids the prohibitive memory cost of storing activations for backpropagation. However, existing ZO methods typically employ isotropic perturbations, neglecting the rich structural information available during the forward pass. In this paper, we identify a crucial link between gradient formation and activation structure: the gradient of a linear layer is confined to the subspace spanned by its input activations. Leveraging this insight, we propose Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order optimization (AGZO). Unlike prior methods, AGZO extracts a compact, activation-informed subspace on the fly during the forward pass and restricts perturbations to this low-rank subspace. We provide a theoretical framework showing that AGZO optimizes a subspace-smoothed objective and provably yields update directions with higher cosine similarity to the true gradient than isotropic baselines. Empirically, we evaluate AGZO on Qwen3 and Pangu models across various benchmarks. AGZO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art ZO baselines and significantly narrows the performance gap with first-order fine-tuning, while maintaining almost the same peak memory footprint as other ZO methods.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model usually requires storing intermediate activations for backpropagation, which can consume substantial memory. Zeroth-order optimization avoids that storage by estimating useful updates through parameter perturbations. AGZO addresses a weakness of existing approaches: their perturbations typically explore directions uniformly, ignoring structure already available during the forward computation.

AGZO extracts a compact representation of this subspace during the forward pass and restricts perturbations to it. This concentrates the search on directions informed by the layer's actual inputs, without retaining the full activation storage needed for ordinary backpropagation.

Experiments on Qwen3 and Pangu report consistent improvements over leading zeroth-order baselines and a smaller gap to first-order fine-tuning. These gains come with almost the same peak memory footprint as other zeroth-order methods.
summary.tldr: AGZO uses activation-informed perturbations to improve memory-efficient language-model fine-tuning while retaining nearly the same peak memory use as other zeroth-order methods.

title: AGZO: Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Optimization for LLM Fine-Tuning

abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of deep neural networks remains a significant challenge, particularly in elucidating how generic visual concepts emerge within latent spaces. In this work, we propose SAEs-BrainMap, a novel framework that utilizes human brain activation patterns from the ventral visual pathway as objective probes to guide the identification of features decomposed by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our quantitative and qualitative empirical results demonstrate a robust representational alignment between sparse model features and biological Regions of Interests (ROIs), confirming the feasibility of utilizing brain signals to characterize model functionality. By leveraging this alignment, we trace the hierarchical trajectory of generic concepts cross layers and utilize the brain’s hierarchical structure to visualize the model’s global processing flow, providing novel insights into model interpretability. Our code is available at this repository.
