paragraphs: Understanding how visual concepts emerge inside a deep model requires ways to characterize its internal features. SAEs-BrainMap uses human brain activity as an external reference for this task. It focuses on activation patterns from the ventral visual pathway to guide the identification of features extracted by sparse autoencoders.

The framework aligns sparse model features with biological regions of interest. The authors report robust representational alignment through both quantitative and qualitative analyses. This supports the feasibility of using brain signals to characterize model functionality: the measured relationships provide evidence for interpreting what particular model features represent.

The authors then use this alignment to follow generic concepts across model layers and visualize the model’s overall processing flow using the brain’s hierarchical organization. The contribution therefore extends from interpreting individual features to tracing how representations develop through the network. Its stated findings concern representational correspondence and interpretability, providing an empirical basis for connecting sparse feature analysis with a biologically organized view of visual processing.
summary.tldr: SAEs-BrainMap aligns sparse model features with visual brain responses to interpret concepts and trace their progression across network layers.

title: SAEs-BrainMap: Unveiling the Emergence of Specialized Concepts in Deep Models via Brain Alignment

abstract: To maximize hardware utilization, modern machine learning systems typically employ large constant or manually tuned batch size schedules, relying on heuristics that are brittle and costly to tune. Existing adaptive strategies based on gradient noise scale (GNS) offer a principled alternative. However, their assumption of SGD’s Euclidean geometry creates a fundamental mismatch with popular optimizers based on generalized norms, such as signSGD / Signum ($\ell_\infty$) and stochastic spectral descent (specSGD) / Muon (Schatten-$\infty$). In this work, we derive gradient noise scales for signSGD and specSGD that naturally emerge from the geometry of their respective dual norms. To practically estimate these non-Euclidean metrics, we propose an efficient variance estimation procedure that leverages the local mini-batch gradients on different ranks in distributed data-parallel systems. Our experiments demonstrate that adaptive batch size strategies using non-Euclidean GNS enable us to match the validation loss of constant-batch baselines while reducing training steps by up to 66% for Signum and Muon on a 160 million parameter Llama model.

paragraphs: Training systems often use large fixed batches or manually tuned schedules to keep hardware busy. Gradient noise scales offer a more principled way to adapt batch size by measuring variability in gradient estimates. However, existing versions assume the Euclidean geometry associated with stochastic gradient descent, which does not match optimizers whose updates follow other norms.

The authors derive noise scales tailored to signSGD and stochastic spectral descent, using the geometry of their respective dual norms. This connects the measure of gradient noise to the optimizer's own mathematical structure. They also propose an efficient estimator that uses local mini-batch gradients already available across workers in distributed data-parallel training.

Experiments with Signum and Muon on a 160-million-parameter Llama model show that these noise scales can guide adaptive batch sizes while matching the validation loss of fixed-batch baselines. Training steps fall by as much as 66%. The result demonstrates fewer optimization steps at comparable validation loss in the tested setting; the reported reduction is specifically in steps rather than elapsed training time.
summary.tldr: Optimizer-specific gradient noise scales guide adaptive batches that match baseline validation loss with up to 66% fewer training steps.

title: Adaptive Batch Sizes Using Non-Euclidean Gradient Noise Scales for Stochastic Sign and Spectral Descent

abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) methods often ignore causal dependencies and treat anomalies as outliers, which is brittle when anomalies are primarily mechanism violations rather than extreme values. We propose CausalAno, a causal-aware detector that trains a causal GAN on normal data and leverages its discriminator to learn mechanism-consistent representations. We score test samples by fitting a Gaussian model in this feature space and computing the Mahalanobis distance, measuring deviation from the normal causal manifold. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CausalAno with extensive experiments on 28 tabular datasets (18 continuous-only and 10 mixed-type), comparing against 16 SOTA baselines. Our results show consistent improvements across both mixed-type and numerical-only settings. Our ablation studies further confirm that the gains come from the causal factorization in the causal GAN rather than a generic GAN backbone. Our CausalAno offers a practical and effective solution for real-world applications where anomalies often arise from mechanism-violating behaviors.

paragraphs: An unusual record need not contain extreme values: it can instead violate the mechanisms connecting otherwise ordinary values. CausalAno addresses this form of tabular anomaly detection by learning representations that reflect causal dependencies in normal data. The aim is to make mechanism violations visible in the representation used for detection.

The method trains a causal generative adversarial network on normal examples and uses its discriminator to produce features. It then fits a Gaussian model in that feature space. Test records receive anomaly scores through Mahalanobis distance, which measures their departure from the fitted normal distribution while accounting for relationships among feature dimensions.

Experiments compare CausalAno with 16 baselines on 28 tabular datasets, including continuous-only and mixed-type data. The authors report consistent improvements in both settings. Ablations attribute the gains to the causal factorization rather than merely using a GAN. This supports the paper’s central idea that representing normal mechanisms can improve detection when anomalies involve broken relationships.
summary.tldr: CausalAno detects tabular anomalies through representations of normal causal mechanisms, improving results across continuous and mixed-type datasets.

title: Causal-aware Anomaly Detection for Tabular Data

abstract: We propose a Likelihood Matching approach for training diffusion models by first establishing an equivalence between the likelihood of the target data distribution and a likelihood along the sample path of the reverse diffusion. To efficiently compute the reverse sample likelihood, the equivalence, a quasi-likelihood is considered to approximate each reverse transition density by a Gaussian distribution with matched conditional mean and covariance, respectively. The score and Hessian functions for the diffusion generation are estimated by maximizing the quasi-likelihood, ensuring a consistent matching of both the first two transition moments between every two time points. A stochastic sampler is introduced to facilitate the computation that leverages both the estimated score and Hessian information. We establish consistency of the quasi-maximum likelihood estimation, and provide non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for the proposed sampler, quantifying the rates of the approximation errors due to score and Hessian estimation, dimensionality, and the number of diffusion steps. Empirical and simulation evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed Likelihood Matching and validate the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation follows a sequence of reverse transitions toward a data sample. This paper develops a training approach by establishing an equivalence between the likelihood of the target data distribution and a likelihood evaluated along that reverse path. The connection provides a basis for learning the generation process through its successive transitions.

Maximizing this quasi-likelihood estimates both score and Hessian functions, capturing information used to match the first two transition moments. A stochastic sampler then uses both estimates during generation, connecting the training objective to the sampling procedure.

Their error analysis accounts for score and Hessian estimation, dimensionality, and the number of diffusion steps. Empirical and simulation results support the approach and its theory. The contribution is a unified likelihood-based treatment of training and sampling that explicitly tracks errors introduced by estimation and approximation.
summary.tldr: Likelihood Matching trains diffusion models through Gaussian approximations of reverse transitions and provides estimation and sampling guarantees.

title: Likelihood Matching for Diffusion Models

abstract: Diverse Vision-language-action (VLA) models have been proposed and demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robotic manipulation. However, how to effectively ensemble VLAs to further enhance performance remains largely unexplored, as conventional ensemble techniques designed for discriminative tasks cannot be directly applied to generative action policies with high-dimensional, multimodal distributions. To address this challenge, we propose EnsembleVLA, an energy-based framework that enables principled ensemble of diverse VLA models. We establish a unified theoretical framework showing that both diffusion-based and flow-based VLA models can be formulated as energy-based models, where additive energy combination naturally induces policy composition at the distribution level. This theoretical foundation enables multiple pre-trained policies to be seamlessly aggregated into a stronger ensemble policy. Building upon this compositional framework, EnsembleVLA further incorporates learnable composition weights for dynamic policy balancing, coupled with a confidence-aware gating mechanism that adaptively modulates bounded residual corrections, collectively ensuring stable and robust task execution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EnsembleVLA achieves competitive performance across various tasks in both simulated and real-world environments.

paragraphs: EnsembleVLA studies how to combine vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation. These models produce distributions over complex actions, potentially with several distinct plausible outcomes. Conventional ensemble methods for discriminative predictions cannot be applied directly to these high-dimensional generative policies, motivating a framework that combines whole action distributions.

The authors show that both diffusion-based and flow-based VLA policies can be expressed as energy-based models. In this representation, adding energy functions provides a principled way to compose policies at the distribution level. This shared mathematical form allows multiple pretrained policies to contribute to one ensemble policy despite differences in their generation mechanisms.

The system also learns composition weights to balance policies dynamically. A confidence-aware gate regulates bounded residual corrections, supporting stable and robust execution. Experiments across simulated and real-world tasks show competitive performance. The contribution is thus a theoretical foundation for policy composition together with mechanisms for controlling how constituent policies influence actions, supported by evaluations in both types of environment.
summary.tldr: EnsembleVLA combines diffusion and flow action policies through energy-based composition, with learned balancing and confidence-controlled corrections.

title: EnsembleVLA: Ensemble Learning for Vision-Language Action Models

abstract: Post-training via supervised fine-tuning improves instruction-following, but often induces semantic mode collapse by biasing models toward low-entropy fine-tuning data at the expense of the high-entropy pretraining distribution. Crucially, we find this trade-off worsens with scale. To close this semantic diversity gap, we propose annotation-anchored training, a principled method that enables models to adopt the preference-following behaviors of post-training without sacrificing the inherent diversity of pretraining. Our approach is simple: we pretrain on documents paired with semantic annotations, inducing a rich annotation distribution that reflects the full breadth of pretraining data, and we preserve this distribution during post-training. This lets us sample diverse annotations at inference time and use them as anchors to guide generation, effectively transferring pretraining’s semantic richness into post-trained models. We find that models trained with annotation-anchored training can attain 6x less diversity collapse than models trained with SFT, and improve with scale.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning can make a model better at following instructions while narrowing the range of meanings it generates. This paper attributes that semantic narrowing to the relatively low diversity of fine-tuning data compared with pretraining data. The researchers find that this trade-off becomes worse as models scale, making diversity preservation an increasingly relevant training concern.

Their method, annotation-anchored training, begins during pretraining. Documents are paired with semantic annotations, allowing the model to learn an annotation distribution that reflects the breadth of the original material. That distribution is then preserved during post-training. At generation time, sampled annotations provide semantic guidance, giving the model a route back to the diversity learned earlier.

The reported models can achieve six times less diversity collapse than models trained with standard supervised fine-tuning, and the approach improves with scale. The finding suggests that annotations can connect preference-following behavior with a broader range of generated content. The intervention spans pretraining, post-training, and inference, with the preserved annotation distribution serving as the link between them.
summary.tldr: Preserving and sampling semantic annotations across training stages can substantially reduce the diversity loss associated with supervised fine-tuning.

title: Annotations Mitigate Post-Training Mode Collapse

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely deployed in user-facing applications, reaching hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Despite their widespread adoption, growing reliance on their outputs raises significant concerns, particularly as users may be exposed to model-inherent biases that disadvantage or stereotype certain groups. However, existing bias benchmarks commonly rely on simple templated prompts or restrictive multiple-choice questions that fail to capture the complexity of real-world user interactions. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a counterfactual framework that automatically generates realistic, open-ended questions for LLM bias evaluation. Through iterative question mutation, our approach systematically explores areas where models are most likely to exhibit biased behavior. Beyond just detecting harmful biases, we also capture increasingly relevant response dimensions, such as asymmetric refusals and explicit bias acknowledgment. Building on this, we construct CAB, a diverse and human-verified benchmark for realistic and nuanced bias evaluations on current frontier LLMs. Our evaluation using CAB highlights the continued need for fairness research by showing that all examined models exhibit persistent biases across certain scenarios.

paragraphs: Bias evaluations often ask models to complete templates or choose among fixed answers. These formats make testing manageable, but they capture only a narrow slice of ordinary conversation. This paper develops a way to generate open-ended questions that better reflect realistic interactions while probing whether responses disadvantage or stereotype particular groups.

The method uses a counterfactual framework and repeatedly mutates questions to explore situations where biased behavior is more likely to appear. This makes question construction adaptive rather than fixed in advance. The evaluation also examines response patterns beyond harmful content, including unequal refusals across cases and whether a model explicitly acknowledges bias.

The researchers use this process to build CAB, a diverse benchmark checked by humans. Evaluations find persistent biases in certain scenarios for every model examined. That finding concerns the tested models and scenarios, rather than establishing that every response is biased. The contribution is a more nuanced way to expose differences in how models handle socially sensitive, open-ended interactions.
summary.tldr: An adaptive, human-verified benchmark uses realistic open-ended questions to reveal persistent biases in certain scenarios across all examined models.

title: Adaptive Generation of Bias-Eliciting Questions for LLMs

abstract: Recently, the prominent performance of large language models (LLMs) has been largely driven by multi-task instruct-tuning. Unfortunately, this training paradigm suffers from a key issue, named cross-task interference, due to conflicting gradients over shared parameters among different tasks. Some previous methods mitigate this issue by isolating task-specific parameters, e.g., task-specific neuron selection and mixture-of-experts. In this paper, we empirically reveal that the cross-task interference still exists for the existing solutions because of many parameters also shared by different tasks, and accordingly, we propose a novel solution, namely Basic Abilities Decomposition for multi-task Instruct-Tuning (BADIT). Specifically, we empirically find that certain parameters are consistently co-activated, and that co-activated parameters naturally organize into base groups. This motivates us to analogize that LLMs encode several orthogonal basic abilities, and that any task can be represented as a linear combination of these abilities. Accordingly, we propose BADIT that decomposes LLM parameters into orthogonal high-singular-value LoRA experts representing basic abilities, and dynamically enforces their orthogonality during training via spherical clustering of rank-1 components. We conduct extensive experiments on the SuperNI benchmark with 6 LLMs, and empirical results demonstrate that BADIT can outperform SOTA methods and mitigate the degree of cross-task interference.

paragraphs: Training a language model on many instruction-following tasks can produce conflicting updates to shared parameters. Methods that allocate some parameters to particular tasks can still leave enough sharing for this interference to persist. This paper empirically identifies that remaining interference and investigates whether the model can instead be organized around reusable basic abilities.

The authors observe groups of parameters that consistently activate together. They use this observation to motivate an analogy: tasks could be expressed as combinations of distinct underlying abilities. BADIT implements that idea with orthogonal LoRA experts built around high-singular-value components. During training, spherical clustering of rank-one components dynamically maintains the separation between these experts.

The proposed organization therefore shares ability components across tasks while trying to keep those components from interfering with one another. The ability decomposition is a modeling motivation drawn from co-activation, rather than a demonstrated universal description of all tasks. Experiments on SuperNI using six language models show that BADIT can outperform state-of-the-art methods and reduce cross-task interference, supporting the practical value of this parameter organization.
summary.tldr: BADIT organizes instruction-tuning updates into orthogonal LoRA experts motivated by reusable abilities, reducing cross-task interference in experiments with six language models.

title: Decomposing the Basic Abilities of Large Language Models: Mitigating Cross-Task Interference in Multi-Task Instruct-Tuning

abstract: Emotional support plays an important role in dialogue systems, and its success depends on adapting to a user’s evolving and implicit needs across multi-turn interactions while leveraging the strong reasoning capacity of large language models. However, since signals about user needs are often weak, indirect, and can only be disambiguated through multi-turn interaction, existing emotional support methods often struggle to acquire and generalize relevant conversational knowledge efficiently. To bridge this gap, we introduce User-Aware Active Knowledge Acquisition (UKA), a gradient-free active dialogue learning framework that explicitly represents uncertainty about user needs and incorporates active learning into both knowledge acquisition and response selection. We propose a Theory-of-Mind uncertainty estimation mechanism that allows the model to prioritize responses, thereby eliciting more informative user feedback. UKA is capable of efficiently exploring user-aligned conversational knowledge during training while maintaining robustness at test time. Experiments across multiple dialogue benchmarks and model architectures demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms strong baselines in dialogue quality and user alignment.

Experiments across multiple dialogue benchmarks and model architectures consistently outperform strong baselines on dialogue quality and user alignment. These findings support actively reducing uncertainty over multiple turns as a way to improve support dialogue, where an initial interpretation of the user’s needs may be incomplete.
summary.tldr: UKA improves emotional-support dialogue by choosing responses that help clarify uncertain user needs and acquire relevant conversational knowledge.

title: User-Aware Active Knowledge Acquisition for Emotional Support Dialogue

abstract: Automating end-to-end GPU kernel generation with Large Language Models (LLMs) faces a critical tension between global performance and exploration efficiency. We present LEGO, a hierarchical framework that resolves this trade-off via a parallel multi-agent search over a recursive AND-OR FusionTree. LEGO synergizes two complementary flows: Top-Down Construction decomposes complex graphs into valid, context-isolated sub-problems to guarantee correctness and enable parallel exploration, while Bottom-Up Mutation speculatively fuses verified sub-plans to recover global locality for peak performance. This bi-directional mechanism effectively prunes the search space to avoid repetitive unguided sampling, while naturally parallelizing exploration and enabling the discovery of sophisticated fusion strategies. Evaluations demonstrate that LEGO achieves 2.18$\times$–13.48$\times$ speedups over PyTorch Eager and, compared to monolithic baselines, reduces end-to-end exploration time by up to 2.47$\times$ and token consumption by up to 7$\times$, across diverse end-to-end models.

paragraphs: LEGO tackles the cost of using language models to generate efficient GPU kernels for complete tensor computation graphs. Searching over an entire graph can be expensive, while optimizing isolated pieces can miss performance gains from combining operations. The framework organizes this search hierarchically in a recursive AND-OR FusionTree and uses multiple agents to explore alternatives in parallel.

Top-down construction divides a complex graph into valid subproblems with isolated contexts, providing correctness guarantees for that decomposition and enabling independent exploration. Bottom-up mutation then attempts to fuse verified subplans, recovering global locality that separate optimization can miss. This structure prunes repetitive exploration while allowing more sophisticated combinations of operations.

Across the evaluated end-to-end models, LEGO produces speedups of 2.18 to 13.48 times over PyTorch Eager. Compared with monolithic search baselines, it reduces overall exploration time by up to a factor of 2.47 and token use by up to a factor of seven. The results combine faster generated execution with a more economical optimization process.
summary.tldr: LEGO combines hierarchical decomposition and verified-plan fusion to generate faster GPU kernels with less search time and token use.

title: LEGO: An LLM-Enabled Hierarchical Optimizer for Tensor Computation Graphs with Structure-Aware Search and Compositional Synthesis

abstract: Visual token compression is widely used to accelerate large vision-language models (LVLMs) by pruning or merging visual tokens, yet its adversarial robustness remains unexplored. We show that existing encoder-based attacks cannot fully disclose the robustness vulnerabilities of compressed LVLMs, due to an optimization-inference mismatch: perturbations are optimized on the full-token representation, while inference is performed through a token-compression bottleneck. To address this gap, we propose the Compression-AliGnEd attack (CAGE), which aligns perturbation optimization with compression inference without assuming access to the deployed compression mechanism or its token budget. CAGE combines (i) expected feature disruption, which concentrates distortion on tokens likely to survive across plausible budgets, and (ii) rank distortion alignment, which actively aligns token distortions with rank scores to promote the retention of highly distorted evidence. Across diverse representative plug-and-play compression mechanisms and datasets, our results show that CAGEconsistently achieves lower robust accuracy than the baseline. This work highlights that robustness assessments ignoring compression can be overly optimistic, calling for compression-aware security evaluation and defenses for efficient LVLMs.

paragraphs: Visual token compression speeds up vision-language models by removing or merging image tokens. This paper argues that attacks optimized against the full visual representation may underestimate vulnerabilities after compression. The attack’s optimization and the model’s deployed inference then operate on different representations, leaving a mismatch in the robustness assessment.

CAGE addresses that mismatch without assuming knowledge of the deployed compression mechanism or its token budget. Its expected feature disruption component concentrates distortion on tokens likely to remain across plausible budgets. Its rank distortion alignment component aligns distortion with token-ranking scores, encouraging heavily distorted evidence to survive compression and reach the model.

Across multiple representative plug-and-play compression mechanisms and datasets, CAGE consistently produces lower robust accuracy than the evaluated baseline. Here, lower robust accuracy means the attack exposes more failures under adversarial input. The results suggest that apparent robustness can depend on whether the evaluation accounts for the compression bottleneck. The paper consequently motivates compression-aware assessment and defenses for efficient vision-language models, rather than treating compression as irrelevant to security testing.
summary.tldr: CAGE exposes vulnerabilities in compressed vision-language models by directing adversarial distortion toward visual evidence likely to survive compression.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Large Vision-Language Models under Visual Token Compression

abstract: While neural PDE solvers have demonstrated significant potential for accelerating engineering simulations, existing architectures remain constrained by high memory consumption and the "single-node bottleneck," where the maximum processable mesh resolution is strictly limited by the VRAM of a single compute unit. To address these challenges, we propose PGD-NO, a neural operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition, that relocates the computational overhead of geometric encoding to a deterministic pre-computation phase. By utilizing an iterative geometry decomposition algorithm to extract "geometry tokens," our model decouples feature extraction from solution querying. This architecture enables linear memory scalability, allowing high-fidelity learning on meshes exceeding 10 million nodes—a scale where existing architectures typically encounter memory exhaustion. PGD-NO demonstrates competitive predictive accuracy across diverse industrial benchmarks and provides intrinsic interpretability through attention mechanisms. By effectively overcoming traditional mesh-size constraints, PGD-NO offers a robust and efficient solution for the next generation of large-scale, high-fidelity industrial design applications.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for physical equations can accelerate engineering simulations, but large meshes create demanding memory requirements. The paper highlights a single-node bottleneck: the largest mesh an existing architecture can process may be limited by the memory of one compute unit. PGD-NO changes how geometry enters the learned solver to address this constraint.

An iterative geometry decomposition algorithm extracts geometry tokens in a deterministic preprocessing phase. Moving geometric encoding into this phase separates feature extraction from querying the physical solution. The resulting architecture provides linear memory scaling and supports learning on meshes with more than ten million nodes, a scale where existing architectures typically exhaust memory.

Across industrial benchmarks, the authors report competitive predictive accuracy and interpretability through attention mechanisms. The significance is the combination of useful prediction quality with substantially larger supported meshes. The claimed improvement concerns the organization and memory scaling of the solver, allowing high-fidelity geometric inputs to be used without making all geometric encoding part of the main solution-querying computation.
summary.tldr: PGD-NO precomputes geometry tokens to separate encoding from solution queries, enabling reported learning on meshes exceeding ten million nodes with competitive accuracy.

title: PGD-NO: A Neural Operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition for 3D Million-Scale Physics Simulations

abstract: Online matching has been a mainstay in domains such as Internet advertising and organ allocation, but practical algorithms often lack strong theoretical guarantees. We take an important step toward addressing this by developing new online matching algorithms based on a coarsening approach. Although coarsening typically implies a loss of granularity, we show that, to the contrary, aggregating offline nodes into capacitated clusters can yield near-optimal theoretical guarantees. We apply our methodology to heart transplant allocation to develop theoretically grounded policies based on structural properties of historical data. Furthermore, in simulations based on real data, our policy closely matches the performance of the omniscient benchmark, achieving competitive ratio 0.91, drastically higher than the US status quo policy’s 0.51. Our work bridges the gap between data-driven heuristics and pessimistic theoretical lower bounds.

paragraphs: Online matching makes allocation decisions as opportunities arrive, rather than with complete knowledge of the future. Practical policies can work well without having strong theoretical guarantees. This paper develops matching algorithms based on coarsening: grouping offline nodes into clusters that have capacities, instead of treating every node separately throughout the decision process.

Although grouping discards some granularity, the authors show that this approach can yield near-optimal theoretical guarantees. They apply the methodology to heart transplant allocation, using structural properties of historical data to construct theoretically grounded policies. The key idea is that an appropriately structured aggregate representation can support strong allocation decisions despite using a coarser description.

In simulations based on real data, the proposed policy achieves a competitive ratio of 0.91 against an omniscient benchmark, compared with 0.51 for the US status quo policy. These are simulated allocation results, rather than reported clinical deployment outcomes. Together with the theory, they show how data-informed structure can help connect effective practical policies with stronger performance guarantees.
summary.tldr: Clustering matching candidates yields near-optimal theoretical guarantees and a 0.91 competitive ratio in heart-allocation simulations based on real data.

title: Near-Optimal Dynamic Matching via Coarsening with Application to Heart Transplantation

abstract: This position paper argues that the machine learning community should prioritize early-stage quality assurance in annotation pipelines over the prevailing practice of late-stage validation. Data quality bottlenecks increasingly limit foundation model improvement, yet quality assurance research focuses almost exclusively on validation methods rather than validation timing. When validation occurs—not merely what validation methods are employed—fundamentally determines both error rates and annotation costs. This temporal neglect is puzzling given the well-established "shift-left" principle from software engineering, where empirical studies demonstrate 4–100$\times$ cost multipliers for defects detected in later development stages (Boehm, 1981; Shull et al., 2002). Annotation pipelines, we argue, exhibit analogous dynamics: errors caught before annotation begins cost a fraction of those discovered after review cycles complete. We propose a taxonomy of three QA trigger points—pre-annotation (T$_0$), post-annotation (T$_1$), and post-review (T$_2$)—that decompose annotation workflows into discrete validation opportunities. A survey of 47 recent papers reveals that only 4% report when validation occurs, a striking gap given timing’s demonstrated impact in adjacent fields. Without explicit attention to QA timing, the community risks optimizing validation methods while ignoring the structural variable that may matter most. We call on researchers to report QA timing configurations, on platform developers to expose timing as a first-class parameter, and on the community to conduct controlled experiments testing whether the shift-left principle transfers to annotation contexts.

paragraphs: This paper argues that annotation quality depends on when checks happen as well as which checks are used. Research largely emphasizes validation methods, leaving timing underexamined. The authors propose that catching problems before annotation begins could avoid costs that accumulate when errors are discovered only after annotation and review.

They organize workflows around three validation opportunities: before annotation, after annotation, and after review. A survey of 47 recent papers finds that only 4% report validation timing. This makes it difficult to understand how the placement of checks contributes to the quality and cost of an annotation pipeline.

The argument draws on software engineering’s experience with earlier defect detection, where later discovery has documented cost penalties. The authors propose analogous dynamics for annotation, while explicitly calling for controlled experiments to test that transfer. They recommend reporting timing configurations and making timing configurable in annotation platforms. The contribution is a framework and research agenda for studying a potentially important cost variable, rather than a demonstrated annotation-specific cost multiplier.
summary.tldr: The paper argues for earlier annotation checks and explicit reporting of validation timing, while calling for experiments to test the cost benefits.

abstract: We consider the bias and variance of value function estimation that are caused by using an empirical model instead of the true model. We analyze these bias and variance for Markov processes from a classical (frequentist) statistical point of view, and in a Bayesiansetting. Using a second order approximation, we provide explicit expressionsfor the bias and variance in terms of the transition counts and the rewardstatistics. We present supporting experiments with artificial Markov chains and with a large transactional database provided by a mail-order catalog firm.
originalAbstract: We consider the bias and variance of value function estimation that are caused by using an empirical model instead of the true model. We analyze these bias and variance for Markov processes from a classical (frequentist) statistical point of view, and in a Bayesiansetting. Using a second order approximation, we provide explicit expressionsfor the bias and variance in terms of the transition counts and the rewardstatistics. We present supporting experiments with artificial Markov chains and with a large transactional database provided by a mail-order catalog firm.

paragraphs: The paper examines uncertainty in value estimates when the underlying process is represented by a model learned from data. Its focus is the error introduced by substituting this empirical model for the true model. It separates that error into bias, meaning systematic displacement of estimates, and variance, meaning their sensitivity to the sampled observations.

The analysis treats Markov processes from both frequentist and Bayesian perspectives. Using a second-order approximation, the authors derive explicit expressions for bias and variance in terms of observed transition counts and reward statistics. This connects uncertainty in the final value estimate to information available in the data used to construct the model.

The approximation is central to how the results should be understood: the expressions characterize estimation error through that analytical treatment. Supporting experiments use artificial Markov chains and a large transaction database from a mail-order catalog business. Together, the analysis and experiments address how model estimation affects value estimation, rather than treating the learned transition and reward model as if it were exact.
summary.tldr: Second-order analysis links bias and variance in estimated values to transition counts and reward statistics in a learned Markov model.

title: Bias and variance in value function estimation

abstract: Ranking a set of retrieved documents according to their relevance to a query is a popular problem in information retrieval. Methods that learn ranking functions are difficult to optimize, as ranking performance is typically judged by metrics that are not smooth. In this paper we propose a new listwise approach to learning to rank. Our method creates a conditional probability distribution over rankings assigned to documents for a given query, which allows for gradient ascent optimization of the expected value of some performance measure. The rank probabilities take the form of a Boltzmann distribution, based on an energy function that depends on a scoring function composed of individual and pairwise potentials. Including pairwise potentials is a novel contribution, allowing the model to encode regularities in the relative scores of documents; existing models assign scores at test time based only on individual documents, with no pairwise constraints between documents. Experimental results on the LETOR3.0 data sets show that our method out-performs existing learning approaches to ranking.

paragraphs: Learning to rank documents is difficult because the measures used to judge a ranked list are typically not smooth. Small changes to document scores can change their order, complicating direct optimization. BoltzRank addresses this by learning a conditional probability distribution over possible rankings for a query and optimizing the expected value of a performance measure with gradient ascent.

The distribution has a Boltzmann form, with ranking probabilities determined by an energy function. Its scoring function includes both individual document terms and pairwise terms. The pairwise component lets the model express regularities in documents' relative scores, extending the individual-document scoring used at prediction time by the existing methods discussed in the abstract.

Experiments on the LETOR3.0 datasets report better performance than existing learning approaches to ranking. The contribution combines a probabilistic route to optimizing ranking gain with a richer way to score documents together. The reported advantage is empirical, tied to those datasets, while the methodological idea is to learn from whole rankings and relationships within them.
summary.tldr: BoltzRank optimizes expected ranking gain through a probability distribution over rankings that includes relationships between document scores.

title: BoltzRank: learning to maximize expected ranking gain

abstract: Although operator-valued kernels have recently received increasing interest in various machine learning and functional data analysis problems such as multi-task learning or functional regression, little attention has been paid to the understanding of their associated feature spaces. In this paper, we explore the potential of adopting an operator-valued kernel feature space perspective for the analysis of functional data. We then extend the Regularized Least Squares Classification (RLSC) algorithm to cover situations where there are multiple functions per observation. Experiments on a sound recognition problem show that the proposed method outperforms the classical RLSC algorithm.

We then extend the Regularized Least Squares Classification (RLSC) algorithm to cover situations where there are multiple functions per observation. Experiments on a sound recognition problem show that the proposed method outperforms the classical RLSC algorithm.

paragraphs: Functional data can describe an observation through functions, and the paper considers classification when each observation contains several of them. Operator-valued kernels had attracted attention in areas including multi-task learning and functional regression, but their associated feature spaces were less well understood. The authors make that feature-space perspective central to their investigation.

They explore how the perspective can support the analysis of functional data, then extend Regularized Least Squares Classification to handle multiple functions per observation. The methodological contribution combines a way of understanding the kernel representation with an adaptation of an established classification algorithm to this richer observation format.

Experiments on a sound-recognition problem show the proposed method outperforming classical Regularized Least Squares Classification. This provides empirical support for the extension in the application studied. The broader significance is that the form of an observation can guide both the feature-space analysis and the classifier design, allowing the learning method to address several functions as components of one observation.
summary.tldr: An operator-valued kernel perspective extends regularized least-squares classification to observations containing multiple functions.

title: Functional Regularized Least Squares Classication with Operator-valued Kernels

abstract: We propose a comprehensive survey of tree kernels through the lens of the mapping kernels framework. We argue that most existing tree kernels, as well as many more that are presented for the first time in this paper, fall into a typology of kernels whose seemingly intricate computation can be efficiently factorized to yield polynomial time algorithms. Despite this fact, we argue that a naive implementation of such kernels remains prohibitively expensive to compute. We propose an approach whereby some computations for smaller trees are cached, which speeds up considerably the computation of all these tree kernels. We provide experimental evidence of this fact as well as preliminary results on the performance of these kernels.
originalAbstract: We propose a comprehensive survey of tree kernels through the lens of the mapping kernels framework. We argue that most existing tree kernels, as well as many more that are presented for the first time in this paper, fall into a typology of kernels whose seemingly intricate computation can be efficiently factorized to yield polynomial time algorithms. Despite this fact, we argue that a naive implementation of such kernels remains prohibitively expensive to compute. We propose an approach whereby some computations for smaller trees are cached, which speeds up considerably the computation of all these tree kernels. We provide experimental evidence of this fact as well as preliminary results on the performance of these kernels.

paragraphs: Tree kernels provide ways to compare data organized as trees. This paper surveys them through the mapping-kernels framework, giving a common perspective on methods that can otherwise appear computationally intricate. The authors argue that most existing tree kernels, together with many introduced in the paper, fit into a shared typology.

Within that typology, the computations can be factorized to obtain polynomial-time algorithms. However, the authors emphasize that this computational classification does not by itself make a straightforward implementation practical. Even a polynomial-time method can require prohibitive computation, so the paper addresses implementation efficiency alongside the unifying mathematical framework.

The proposed improvement caches some computations for smaller trees so that they can be reused. Experiments show substantial speedups across the tree kernels considered, and the paper also reports preliminary results on their performance. Its contribution combines organization of the kernel family, efficient factorization, and a reuse strategy that makes those computations more practical.
summary.tldr: A mapping-kernel framework unifies tree kernels, while caching smaller-tree computations substantially speeds their evaluation.

title: Mapping kernels for trees
